Action Sports.overview: Action Sports covers skateboarding and snowboarding safety, equipment maintenance, park/slope etiquette, fundamental and intermediate maneuvers, and outdoor stewardship.

requirements.topic_heading: Hazards, Safety Gear & First Aid in Action Sports
requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in action sports (skateboarding or snowboarding) and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for hypothermia, frostbite, dehydration, sunburn, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, blisters, sprains, strains, fractures, head/concussion injuries, and spinal injuries. (c) Show your helmet, wrist guards, knee/elbow pads, boots, and bindings, and explain how to inspect and fit them properly.

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Action Sports Sub-Req 5a: Demonstrate three intermediate maneuvers or tricks approved by your counselor in a supervised skatepark or snow terrain park (p. 12).

Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: Action Sports Sub-Req 5b: Explain Leave No Trace and outdoor stewardship principles at mountain resorts and community skateparks, and explore careers or volunteer roles (such as National Ski) (p. 12).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: (a) Demonstrate three intermediate maneuvers or tricks approved by your counselor in a supervised skatepark or snow terrain park (p. 12).

Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: (b) Explain Leave No Trace and outdoor stewardship principles at mountain resorts and community skateparks, and explore careers or volunteer roles (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Preparation): Inspect the workspace, reference materials, and safety controls required for Action Sports Requirement 5 (p. 26).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Execution): Apply the official Action Sports pamphlet method for Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics while recording observations in your Scout Workbook (p. 26).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Buddy Check): Cross-check your Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics technique, measurements, and results with a patrol buddy using the EDGE method (p. 26).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Verification): Review your completed Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics evidence and demonstrate proficiency during your counselor conference (p. 26).

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain four features of the free enterprise system in the United States. Describe the difference between freedom and license. Tell how the Scout Oath and Scout Law apply to business and free enterprise. (b) Describe the Industrial Revolution and tell about the major developments that marked the start of the modern industrial era in the United States. Discuss three people who had a great influence on business or industry in the United States and describe what each did. (c) Identify and describe to your counselor the five primary areas of business. (d) Explain the history of labor unions in the United States and the importance of labor unions and employers working together. Identify two major labor unions currently in existence. (e) Discuss with your counselor how business impacts the local, national, and global economy.

pamphlet_excerpts: Free Enterprise System Features: He and many others wanted the United States, which had won itsindependence from Great Britain just a few years earlier, tobecome economically strong (p. 19).
Free Enterprise System Features Principle 2: They organized associations that promoted industrialization (p. 19).

Free Enterprise System Features Principle 3: Although more than three-fourths of the workingpopulation in the United States was involved in agriculture at the time, the Industrial Revolution spread (p. 19).
Free Enterprise System Features Principle 4: By the end of the century, the United Statesbecame the world leader in manufacturing and spurred what isknown as the Second Industrial Revolution (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Free Enterprise System Features): The United Statescontinues to be one of the world's largest producers of goods (p. 19).
Step 2 (Free Enterprise System Features): The result of globalization is a worldeconomy in which the borders between countries have blurred (p. 19).
Step 3 (Free Enterprise System Features): Technology, such as the internet, has helped makeglobal corporations and m ­ arkets possible (p. 19).
Step 4 (Free Enterprise System Features): Globalization has grown rapidly since the 1970s, but it has been an economic trend since the end of World War II in 1945 (p. 19).

Step 3 (Business Financial Statements): The three main financialstatements are the balance sheet, income statement, and cashflow statement (p. 48).
Step 4 (Business Financial Statements): The balance sheet provides an overview of assets, liabilities, andshareholders' equity as a snapshot in time (p. 48).

pamphlet_excerpts: Federal Economic and Trade Agencies: Employers also have a general duty under the OSH Act to provide their employees with work and a workplacefree from recognized, serious hazards (p. 60).
Federal Economic and Trade Agencies Principle 2: OSHA enforces the actthrough workplace inspections and investigations (p. 60).
Federal Economic and Trade Agencies Principle 3: Complianceassistance and other cooperative programs are also available (p. 60).
Federal Economic and Trade Agencies Principle 4: These provisions preempt many similar state laws (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Federal Economic and Trade Agencies): The Department of Labor (DOL) was established by President William Taft on March 4, 1913 (p. 60).
Step 2 (Federal Economic and Trade Agencies): Although the agency has enforced thousands ofregulations, the following are among the most notable (p. 60).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following, choosing a different group for each:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following, choosing a different group for each: (a) Go to a festival, celebration, or other event identified with one of the groups. Report on what you see and learn. (b) Go to a place of worship, school, or other institution identified with one of the groups. Report on what you see and learn. (c) Talk with a person from one of the groups about the heritage and traditions of the group. Report on what you learn. (d) Learn a song, dance, poem, or story that is traditional to one group, and teach it to a group of your friends. (e) Go to a library or museum to see a program or exhibit featuring one group's traditions. Report on what you see and learn.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Select two individuals from American history, one a political leader (a president, senator, etc.) and the other a private citizen (a writer, religious leader, etc.). Find out about each person's accomplishments and compare the contributions each has made to America's heritage. (b) With your counselor's approval, choose an organization that has promoted some type of positive change in American society. Find out why the organization believed this change was necessary and how it helped to accomplish the change. Discuss how this organization is related to events or situations from America's past. (c) With your counselor's approval, interview two veterans of the U. S. military. Find out what their experiences were like. Ask the veterans what they believe they accomplished. (d) With your counselor's approval, interview three people in your community of different ages and occupations. Ask these people what America means to them, what they think is special about this country, and what American traditions they feel are important to preserve.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Explain the National Register of Historic Places and how a property becomes eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places. Make a map of your local area, marking the points of historical interest. Tell about any National Register properties in your area. Share the map with your counselor, and describe the historical points you have indicated. (b) Research an event of historical importance that took place in or near your area. If possible, visit the place. Tell your counselor about the event and how it affected local history. Describe how the area looked then and what it now looks like. (c) Find out when, why, and how your town or neighborhood started, and what ethnic, national, or racial groups played a part. Find out how the area has changed over the past 50 years and try to explain why. (d) Take an active part in a program about an event or person in American history. Report to your counselor about the program, the part you took, and the subject. (e) Visit a historic trail or walk in your area. After your visit, share with your counselor what you have learned. Discuss the importance of this location and explain why you think it might qualify for National Register listing.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Watch two motion pictures (with the approval and permission of your counselor and parent or guardian) that are set in some period of American history. Describe to your counselor how accurate each film is with regard to the historical events depicted and also with regard to the way the characters are portrayed. (b) Read a biography (with your counselor's approval) of someone who has made a contribution to America's heritage. Tell some things you admire about this individual and some things you do not admire. Explain why you think this person has made a positive or a negative contribution to America's heritage. (c) Listen to recordings of popular songs from various periods of American history. Share five of these songs with your counselor, and describe how each song reflects the way people felt about the period in which it was popular. If a recording is not available, have a copy of the lyrics available.

Watch two motion pictures Principle 2: They can show the best of America, and they can show the worst of America (p. 48).
Watch two motion pictures Principle 3: They can tell stories about real events, and they can show what life was like during acertain time period (p. 48).
Watch two motion pictures Principle 4: Movies that deal with history should bewatched carefully (p. 48).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Watch two motion pictures): Directors sometimes have a certain point of view they want to get across to their audience (p. 48).
Step 2 (Watch two motion pictures): They may portray characters and events Thomasnegatively or positively so that the audience feels a certain Edisonway about the subject (p. 48).
Step 3 (Watch two motion pictures): For instance, many American Indians were portrayed asvillains in "spaghetti" Westerns, popular, low-budget films (p. 48).
Step 4 (Watch two motion pictures): This mayhave been because of prejudice on the part of moviemakers, orsimply to show the white characters as more heroic (p. 48).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Studying American heritagegives you these skills and makes you a sought-after candidate (p. 33).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Most people who want to work in American heritagemajor in history in college (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Some positions require a master'sor doctorate degree, especially if you want to teach (p. 33).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You alsomight consider being a museum curator, national park ranger, historic preservation officer, or archivist (p. 33).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): These fields requireknowledge of a specific part of history (p. 33).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): They also need to be able to find information, which requires research skills (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Different American Indian cultural areas: Pueblos were made of different types of materials (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 2: The Hopi and the Zuñi used stones that were mortared together and surfaced with plaster (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 3: Rio Grande Indians constructed their homes from adobe bricks of sun-dried earth mixed with straw (p. 7).
Different American Indian cultural areas Principle 4: They stretched log beams across the roofs and covered them with poles, brush, and plaster (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Sometimes the beams projectedbeyond the walls and were used as pegs to hang food for drying (p. 7).
Step 2 (Different American Indian cultural areas): The women owned the apartments and all of the furnishings (p. 7).
Step 3 (Different American Indian cultural areas): In the centralplaza of the village, the people dug kivas, underground chamberswhere men conducted sacred rituals (p. 7).
Step 4 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Men also used the kivas asclubhouses, and women usually were not allowed to enter (p. 7).

pamphlet_excerpts: American Indian Tribe: An American Indian tribe, group: Using dugout canoes, Plateau tribes traveled and tradedwidely along the Columbia and Fraser river systems (p. 57).
American Indian Tribe Principle 2: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 2: From thewest came sea otter pelts and ornamental shells (p. 57).
American Indian Tribe Principle 3: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 3: Deerskins, hemp for basketmaking, and bitterroot were brought from theinterior (p. 57).

American Indian Tribe Principle 4: An American Indian tribe, group Principle 4: All sorts of goods changed hands: dried salmon, candlefish oil, baskets, carvings, even the canoes in which the traderscarried their wares (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (American Indian Tribe): Step 1 (An American Indian tribe, group): When horses came to the Plateau in theearly 18th c­ entury, tribes like the Yakima, Nez Perce, and Cayusebecame expert horse raisers and traders (p. 57).
Step 2 (American Indian Tribe): Step 2 (An American Indian tribe, group): The Plateau Indians had a complex system of beliefs andceremonies (p. 57).

Step 3 (American Indian Tribe): Step 3 (An American Indian tribe, group): Everyone sought visits from guardian spirits, andwhen someone felt they were about to be healed by their guardian spirit, there was a ceremony (p. 57).
Step 4 (American Indian Tribe): Step 4 (An American Indian tribe, group): Shamans had visions and appeared to the people in the guise of grizzly bears (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Learn Common Terms in An: Learn 10 Common Terms: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and revivingtheir arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 17).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 2: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 2: Many havechosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 17).
Learn Common Terms in An Principle 3: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 3: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in themodern world (p. 17).

Learn Common Terms in An Principle 4: Learn 10 Common Terms Principle 4: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part ofmodern society (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 1 (Learn 10 Common Terms): There is no easy answer, and no one knowswhat the future holds (p. 17).
Step 2 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 2 (Learn 10 Common Terms): They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 17).
Step 3 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 3 (Learn 10 Common Terms): Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as "Hiawatha"), and Tecumseh, livedcenturies ago (p. 17).

Step 4 (Learn Common Terms in An): Step 4 (Learn 10 Common Terms): Others, like Geronimo, Ira Hayes, Ben Nighthorse Campbell, Ada Deer, and Wilma Mankiller, are people of the 20th and 21st centuries (p. 17).

Life Might Have Been Principle 2: Describe How Life Principle 2: Usethe information here as a starting point to learn more about American Indians and Ameri­can heritage (p. 9).

Step 3 (Life Might Have Been): Step 3 (Describe How Life): If you have anatural history museum in your area, ask the curator or personin charge for information (p. 9).
Step 4 (Life Might Have Been): Step 4 (Describe How Life): See if your town or city has an American Indian center, oran Indian tribal council or similar governing group (p. 9).

Step 3 (Union and Employer Organization Visit): The Labor Movement in the 20th Century Labor leaders promoted the ideas of union solidarity (a spirit of unity based on common interests) (p. 16).
Step 4 (Union and Employer Organization Visit): However, deep-rooted prejudice and fear oftenexerted a stronger influence on union members than idealism (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Labor Union Structure and Federation: Craft unions provide training to their members basedon the model of medieval craft guilds (p. 19).
Labor Union Structure and Federation Principle 2: A traineebegins as an apprentice, learning a trade at a unionsponsored school and acting as an assistant on thejob (p. 19).

Labor Union Structure and Federation Principle 4: The labor force serves two distinct parts of the nation'seconomy: the private sector and the public sector (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): The privatesector refers to the aspects of the economy that are under thecontrol of individuals and privately owned businesses (p. 19).
Step 2 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): The public sector is under the control of the federal, state, orlocal governments (p. 19).
Step 3 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): Another way to analyze the workforce is in terms ofunorganized versus organized labor (p. 19).
Step 4 (Labor Union Structure and Federation): In unorganized laborsituations, the individual employee addresses problemsone-on-one with his or her supervisor and the managerial chain (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: Adversarial vs. Cooperative Labor Models: Suppose you and two friends started a lawn-care business (p. 49).

Adversarial vs. Cooperative Labor Models Principle 3: All you have todo is maintain it, fuel it, and return it at the end of the summer (p. 49).
Adversarial vs. Cooperative Labor Models Principle 4: You and your friends have agreed to split the profits after payingexpenses, and everyone has a plan to spend his or her share (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Adversarial vs. Cooperative Labor Models): Did you notice how fast a simple plan becomes complicated (p. 49).
Step 2 (Adversarial vs. Cooperative Labor Models): Situations like that happen every day in businesses (p. 49).
Step 3 (Adversarial vs. Cooperative Labor Models): Conflicts of interest, if not negotiated, can easily escalate toanger (p. 49).
Step 4 (Adversarial vs. Cooperative Labor Models): Labor and management always have had a polarized relationship (p. 49).

pamphlet_excerpts: American Labor History Timeline: Us and Them: The Struggles Between Labor and Management (p. 16).
American Labor History Timeline Principle 2: Big business fought union efforts to have any influencein the workplace (p. 16).
American Labor History Timeline Principle 3: Management used the courts, private armies, and federal troops to put down labor activity (p. 16).
American Labor History Timeline Principle 4: Employers contracted with prisons to hire convicts as strikebreakers (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (American Labor History Timeline): Additionally, employers hired new immigrants, African Americans, and Latinos to break strikes, often causing racial unrest (p. 16).
Step 2 (American Labor History Timeline): Trade unionism grewin fits and starts in response to the success or failure of strikes, boom-and-bust business cycles, and union militancy (p. 16).
Step 3 (American Labor History Timeline): The Labor Movement in the 20th Century Labor leaders promoted the ideas of union solidarity (a spirit of unity based on common interests) (p. 16).
Step 4 (American Labor History Timeline): However, deep-rooted prejudice and fear oftenexerted a stronger influence on union members than idealism (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Major Labor Issue Case Study: Many nonunion businesses have informal open-door policies to address labor complaints (p. 43).
Major Labor Issue Case Study Principle 2: Workers are encouraged to discusstheir concerns with management without fear of any retaliatoryactions (p. 43).
Major Labor Issue Case Study Principle 3: Formal internal grievance procedures establish specificsteps an employee must take to challenge certain aspects of employment (p. 43).
Major Labor Issue Case Study Principle 4: The rights and responsibilities for labor and management aredetermined by union contracts and labor legislation (p. 43).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Major Labor Issue Case Study): Hard Hats and Thinking Caps, Two Sides of a Labor Issue You know by now that the goals of labor and the goals ofmanagement often conflict (p. 43).
Step 2 (Major Labor Issue Case Study): As you prepare to argue the issue (in person or on paper) from different points of view, imagine yourself as the mediatorin the labor-management (p. 43).
Step 3 (Major Labor Issue Case Study): Be objective and impartial so you cansee the facts beneath the issues (p. 43).
Step 4 (Major Labor Issue Case Study): Your goal is to defend each party's position within the limits of rights and responsibilities (p. 43).

pamphlet_excerpts: Collective Bargaining Negotiations: The foremost concern of a company owner (an individual or a group of investors) is to make a profit (p. 46).
Collective Bargaining Negotiations Principle 2: They makedecisions about whether to continue to invest in the companies based on the profitability of those businesses (p. 46).

Collective Bargaining Negotiations Principle 3: Just asmanagement may shut down a division in a company to cutcosts and improve profitability, the owner may sell an unprofitable company to protect (p. 46).
Collective Bargaining Negotiations Principle 4: Financial institutions, investment groups, and individuals oftenbuy shares of stock in a company (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Collective Bargaining Negotiations): Each share represents a piece of the company, a percentage of ownership (p. 46).
Step 2 (Collective Bargaining Negotiations): Some companies offeran employee stock-option plan thatallows employees to acquire shares of company stock and receive stockdistributions (p. 46).
Step 3 (Collective Bargaining Negotiations): Shareholders want a returnon their investment in the company (p. 46).

requirements.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf. (b) Option B, Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings. (c) Option C, Horse. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a useful saddle horse barn and exercise yard. (2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. (4) Visit a horse farm. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. (5) Outline the proper feeding of a horse doing light work. Explain why the amount and kind of feed will change according to the kind of horse and the work it does. Describe what colic is, what can cause it, and its symptoms. (d) Option D, Sheep or Goat. Choose one and do ALL of the following based upon the choice: (1) Make a sketch of a live lamb or goat. Show the location of the various wholesale and retail cuts. (2) Discuss how wools are sorted and graded. (3) List products that can be made from the milk. (4) Based on your choice, do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a lamb or goat from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm or ranch where sheep or goats are raised. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a sheep or goat farm or ranch, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on sheep or goats. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms for a sheep (wether, ewe, ram, and lamb) OR a goat (doe, nanny, kid, buck, and billy). (e) Option E, Hog. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of pork. Tell about the recommended USDA grades of pork. Tell the basis for each grade. (2) Outline in writing the proper feeding programs used from the breeding of a gilt or sow through the weaning of the litter. Discuss the feeding programs for the growth and finishing periods. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm where hogs are produced, or visit a packing plant handling hogs. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a hog production unit or packing plant, view a video from a packer or processor, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on hogs. Tell about your findings. (4) Define the following terms: gilt, sow, barrow, and boar. (f) Option F, Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf.

sub_requirements.text: Option F, Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

pamphlet_excerpts: General Knowledge: The history of animation is as old as the history of storytelling (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 2: The word animate means "alive." When early humans firstpainted animals and hunting scenes on cave walls, they lit fires to show off their work (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 3: The dancing flames cast irregular light in the caves, making the images of prehistoric animals appear to be alive and moving (p. 21).
General Knowledge Principle 4: Also, from the earliest times, children worldwide have used a light source to project hand shadows onto a wall to create theshapes of animals (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (General Knowledge): This kind of entertainment can beenjoyed by a group of friends (p. 21).
Step 2 (General Knowledge): The shared experience of creatinglifelike imitation is a key part of the attraction of animation (p. 21).
Step 3 (General Knowledge): The idea of projecting shadows led to the first magiclantern shows, starting around the mid to late 1700s and lastinguntil the introduction (p. 21).
Step 4 (General Knowledge): A primitive projection devicelike a wooden box with a candle inside was fitted with a lens (p. 21).

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles of Animation: The principles of animation are a set of 12 basic ideas applied toanimation to create appealing, believable results (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 2: They wereintroduced by two of the original Disney animators, Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas, in their book, Disney Animation: The Illusion (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 3: Since that time, the principles havebecome standard in the animation industry (p. 35).
Principles of Animation Principle 4: Straight Ahead Action and Pose to Pose Straight-ahead action and pose to pose are the two mainmethods for animating (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Principles of Animation): Using straight-ahead action, theanimator draws or animates frame by frame, doing the drawingsin order: 1, 2, 3, 4 (p. 35).
Step 2 (Principles of Animation): With pose-to-pose animation, incontrast, the animator draws or poses the main (key) frames of the animation before filling in the in-between (p. 35).
Step 3 (Principles of Animation): Using thepose-to-pose method, the animator might do drawing 1, thendrawing 25, and then drawing 47, before going back to do thedrawings (p. 35).
Step 4 (Principles of Animation): Most animators use the pose-to-pose method becauseit offers benefits in timing and frame composition (p. 35).

pamphlet_excerpts: Animation in our World: Scenes are created first with a rough sketch, then a simplifiedmock-up called an "animatic," and then the final image (p. 66).
Animation in our World Principle 2: The next time you watch an animated movie, watch thecredits at the end (p. 66).
Animation in our World Principle 3: You might be amazed by how manyartists are required to generate a full-length feature film (p. 66).
Animation in our World Principle 4: The different disciplines include animators, modelers, lighters, riggers, texture painters, effects artists (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Animation in our World): It is important to appreciate that the work isn't alldone by just one person (p. 66).
Step 2 (Animation in our World): Your unique learning experience should match your passionsas an artist (p. 66).

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles of Archaeological Science: Students of archaeology study a variety of subjects, including many sciences (p. 16).

Principles of Archaeological Science Principle 2: The scientific analysis of sites and artifactsrequires a knowledge of geology, paleontology, physics, chemistry, botany, zoology, and statistics (p. 16).
Principles of Archaeological Science Principle 3: Interdisciplinary programs that combine archaeology withvarious other fields of study are common (p. 16).
Principles of Archaeological Science Principle 4: Historical archaeologists usually major in anthropologyor history (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Principles of Archaeological Science): To work as a field archaeologist, previous experience isoften required (usually obtained by spending a summer in anarchaeological field) (p. 16).
Step 2 (Principles of Archaeological Science): Archaeological field schools provide the best way to learn howto properly excavate and document archaeological sites, andalso to find (p. 16).
Step 3 (Principles of Archaeological Science): You can begin now to prepare for your college courseworkby taking all of the science, history, and language classes (p. 16).
Step 4 (Principles of Archaeological Science): Strong communication skills are vital to an archaeologist, so you'll need a good grounding in writing, speech, and foreignlanguages (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Of the archaeological process: Archaeologists follow a careful step-by-step process designed to protect resources and obtain the most information possible (p. 33).
Of the archaeological process Principle 2: They sometimes study old letters, maps, journals, and other documents for clues to the locations of historic settlements or American Indian camps (p. 33).
Of the archaeological process Principle 3: They may use aerial photographs andpictures taken from satellites to homein on the places they are trying to find (p. 33).
Of the archaeological process Principle 4: They talk to people living in the area, Measuring an obsidian artifact from thewho often have the deepest knowledge (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Of the archaeological process): Nightfire Island site in Oregon Sites are sometimes found during surveys that may berequired before new roads, dams, apartment houses (p. 33).
Step 2 (Of the archaeological process): Archaeologists walk the entirearea, looking for anything made by humans that is more than 50 years old (p. 33).
Step 3 (Of the archaeological process): They may dig test pits or trenches in the pathway of the proposed construction (p. 33).
Step 4 (Of the archaeological process): If artifacts appear, the site may be excavated before construction machinery disturbs the area (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Combined Total of Five Archaeological: Learn About A Combined Total: This idea of relationships between objects is important (p. 14).
Combined Total of Five Archaeological Principle 2: Learn About A Combined Total Principle 2: Think of all the little parts that go together to make asmartphone (p. 14).

Combined Total of Five Archaeological Principle 3: Learn About A Combined Total Principle 3: If you take the individual parts out of a smartphone and study each one separately, will that tell you how the phonefunctions (p. 14).
Combined Total of Five Archaeological Principle 4: Learn About A Combined Total Principle 4: You must look at all of the parts in place inside the phone to see how they work together (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 1 (Learn About A Combined Total): Like a smartphone, an archaeological site is a complicated package that must be opened carefully and studiedas a whole if we are to make sense (p. 14).

Step 2 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 2 (Learn About A Combined Total): A researcher who looks at only a few stone tools and afew kernels of corn might find that, by themselves, the artifactsreveal little (p. 14).

Step 3 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 3 (Learn About A Combined Total): A few kernels of corn found in a space that did not have a hearth or any other artifacts would suggest that the room was probably a storeroom (p. 14).

Step 4 (Combined Total of Five Archaeological): Step 4 (Learn About A Combined Total): Compared with anisolated find, artifacts foundtogether at a site can provide more information about the people wholived there andeveryday activities (p. 14).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission, assist a qualified archaeologist for at least eight hours with a project being worked on. Projects may include surveying, site monitoring, site stabilization, surface excavation, laboratory analysis, use of digital archaeological technology, or public outreach. Describe your involvement in the project, what you learned about archaeology, and the steps of archaeological inquiry. Note: Visiting an archaeological site will require advance planning. An archaeological site during study can be a dangerous place. While there, you will need to closely follow the archaeologist's directions and comply with all the safety procedures. Be aware of the changing conditions at the site. (b) With your counselor's approval, take part in a simulated archaeological project designed by a qualified archaeologist. The project must include the use of a simulated archaeological site including artifacts and features for the site. Using the steps of archaeological inquiry, analyze the artifacts and features and document the spatial relationships of the artifacts and features at the simulated site. Explain how the environment and time can affect the interpretation of an artifact and the overall archaeological site. Tell how you would share the results of your analysis with other researchers and the public. Note: To find out how to make a simulated archaeological site, talk with a professional archaeologist, trained avocational archaeologist, museum school instructor, science teacher, advisor from a local archaeology society, or other qualified instructor.

Step 3 (Under the supervision of a qualified): Librarians can help you findbooks about the science of archaeology and about the peoples and periods of the past that interest (p. 28).
Step 4 (Under the supervision of a qualified): The internet also offers many opportunities for exploring the world of archaeology via computer (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment: You also can tell arrows apart by their fletchings. • Target arrows use small fletchings (p. 18).
Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment Principle 2: These can be feathers from 2 to 3 inches long or plastic vanes about 11/2 to 2 inches long (p. 18).
Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment Principle 3: These fletchings are most often used on blunt-tipped arrows (p. 18).
Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment Principle 4: They slow the arrow's flight and make it drop quickly. • Hunting arrows use longer fletchings, usually 4 to 5 incheslong (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment): The fletchings usually have a strong spiral that causes the arrow to rotate, which improves its flight when the pointis a broadhead (p. 18).
Step 2 (Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment): Modern arrow shafts are made from four principal materials: wood, aluminum, fiberglass, or carbon fiber (p. 18).
Step 3 (Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment): Beginning archersusually use arrows with wood shafts (p. 18).
Step 4 (Arrow Anatomy, Bowstrings & Equipment): Wood is the least expensive shaft material and is popular with many archers (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Archery Core Field Standard: Field archery is set up on a course or roving range similar to the field archery plan shown later in this chapter (p. 52).
Archery Core Field Standard Principle 2: Differenttarget faces and shooting distances are used for 14 targets (p. 52).
Archery Core Field Standard Principle 3: Stakes driven into the ground mark the exact shooting spot for each target (p. 52).
Archery Core Field Standard Principle 4: Outdoor target archery is set up in an open field, using 122-centimeter (48-inch) target faces (p. 52).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Archery Core Field Standard): In most cases, the targetposition is set and the shooting line is moved when differentdistances are shot (p. 52).
Step 2 (Archery Core Field Standard): Indoor target archery is shot in a building, using 60- or 40-centimeter targets at a distance of 18 meters (20 yards) (p. 52).
Step 3 (Archery Core Field Standard): Target archers straddle the firing line, with one foot in front of and one foot behind the line (p. 52).
Step 4 (Archery Core Field Standard): These four organizations govern archery tournaments (p. 52).

requirements.homework_verification_note: Verify completed Archery Workbook organizer table and practical demonstration for Req 4.

requirements.lead_text: Working under the supervision of a certified USA Archery Level 1 Instructor or a certified long-term camp staff member (i. e., a National Camping School [NCS] Range Activities Director; or a Rangemaster over age 18 who is trained by an NCS Range Activities Director or by a USA Archery Level 1 Instructor), do ONE of the following options: Note: When using a Genesis bow, apply the requirements in Option A.
requirements.req_text: Working under the supervision of a certified USA Archery Level 1 Instructor or a certified long-term camp staff member (i. e., a National Camping School [NCS] Range Activities Director; or a Rangemaster over age 18 who is trained by an NCS Range Activities Director or by a USA Archery Level 1 Instructor), do ONE of the following options: Note: When using a Genesis bow, apply the requirements in Option A. (a) Option A, Recurve Bow or Longbow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the recurve or longbow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store recurve bows and longbows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Demonstrate the proper way to string a recurve bow or longbow. (5) Using a bow square, locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a recurve bow or longbow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 60 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 80 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 80 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 50 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting 30 arrows in five-arrow ends at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target at 10 yards and using the 10 scoring regions, make a score of 150 points. (b) Option B, Compound Bow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the compound bow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store compound bows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Explain why it is necessary to have the string or cable on a compound bow replaced at an archery shop. (5) Locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a compound bow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 70 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 90 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 90 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 60 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

(4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 50 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting 30 arrows in five-arrow ends at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target at 10 yards and using the 10 scoring regions, make a score of 150 points.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Recurve Bow or Longbow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the recurve or longbow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store recurve bows and longbows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Demonstrate the proper way to string a recurve bow or longbow. (5) Using a bow square, locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a recurve bow or longbow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 60 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 80 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 80 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 50 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting 30 arrows in five-arrow ends at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target at 10 yards and using the 10 scoring regions, make a score of 150 points.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Compound Bow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the compound bow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store compound bows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Explain why it is necessary to have the string or cable on a compound bow replaced at an archery shop. (5) Locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a compound bow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 70 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 90 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 90 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 60 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Compound Bow. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and point to the parts of the compound bow you are shooting. (2) Explain how to properly care for and store compound bows. (3) Demonstrate and explain USA Archery's 11 Steps of Shooting for the bow you are shooting. (4) Explain why it is necessary to have the string or cable on a compound bow replaced at an archery shop. (5) Locate and mark with dental floss, crimp-on, or other method, the nocking point on the bowstring of the bow you are using. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Using a compound bow and arrows with a finger release, shoot a single round of ONE of the following: (1) An NFAA field round of 14 targets and make a score of 70 points (2) A Scouting America field round of 14 targets and make a score of 90 points (3) A World Archery/USA Archery indoor round and make a score of 90 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (4) An NFAA indoor round and make a score of 60 points (Indoor rounds may be shot outdoors if this is more convenient.) (b) Shooting at an 80-centimeter (32-inch) five-color target using the 10 scoring regions, make a minimum score of 160 points. Accomplish this in the following manner: Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 10 yards AND Shoot 15 arrows in five-arrow ends, at a distance of 15 yards.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Tour your community and list the different types of buildings you see. Try to identify buildings that can be associated with a specific period of history or style of architecture. Make a sketch of the building you most admire. (b) Select a historical architectural achievement that has had a major impact on society. Using resources such as the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission), books, and magazines, find out how this achievement has influenced the world today. Tell your counselor what you learned.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and approval, arrange to meet with an architect. Ask to see the scale model of a building and the drawings that a builder would use to construct this building. Discuss why the different building materials were selected. Look at the details in the drawings and the model to see how the materials and components are attached to each other during construction. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and approval, arrange to meet with an architect at a construction site. Ask the architect to bring drawings that the builder uses to construct the building. While at the site, discuss why the different building materials being used were selected. Discuss how the different building materials and components are attached to each other during construction. Note: To visit a construction site will require advance planning. You will need permission from a parent or guardian, counselor, the architect, and the construction site manager. A construction site is a very dangerous place. While there, you will need to closely follow the site manager's directions and comply with all the safety procedures, including wearing a hard hat, protective eyewear, and proper footwear. Be aware of the changing conditions at the site, and stay with the architect or site manager. (c) Interview someone who might be your client (such as a prospective homeowner or business owner) if you were an architect. pamphlet_excerpts: Discuss Forms Humankind Means: Your counselor: The question of what "art" is has occupied the minds ofphilosophers and critics ever since humankind began to think and argue (p. 8).

Discuss Forms Humankind Means Principle 2: Your counselor Principle 2: The term has been applied to many forms of visualmedia, especially to the fine arts, drawing, painting, sculpture, and printmaking (p. 8).
Discuss Forms Humankind Means Principle 3: Your counselor Principle 3: But it also includes architecture, industrialdesign, fashion design, pottery, and weaving (p. 8).

Discuss Forms Humankind Means Principle 4: Your counselor Principle 4: The differenceis that fine arts are concerned only with beauty and expression and the others, though the art may be beautiful, focus firston function (p. 8).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 1 (Your counselor): This merit badge pamphlet concentrates on two-dimensional art, specifically drawing and painting in various media (p. 8).
Step 2 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 2 (Your counselor): One requirement introduces you to design applications in thefields of graphic arts and industrial design (p. 8).
Step 3 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 3 (Your counselor): After you learnabout art history and design principles, you will understandhow these fields relate to fine art (p. 8).
Step 4 (Discuss Forms Humankind Means): Step 4 (Your counselor): Since prehistoric people first madecave paintings, artists have tried to portrayreality (p. 8).

pamphlet_excerpts: Elements of Art and Design Balance Balance is the visual stability of the composition (p. 16).
Elements of Art and Design Principle 2: If a work of art has visual balance, then the viewer feels that the elements have been arranged just right (p. 16).
Elements of Art and Design Principle 3: If there is an imbalance, then the viewer feels something's wrong, that the elementsneed to be rearranged (p. 16).
Elements of Art and Design Principle 4: A formal balance occurs whensimilar elements are placed on eachside of the central axis (a drawn orimaginary line through the center of the work) (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Elements of Art and Design): The differentelements of art, line, value, shape, space, color, and texture, all influence the visual weight of a composition (p. 16).
Step 2 (Elements of Art and Design): Forexample, a small area of bright color can balance a larger area of dull color (p. 16).
Step 3 (Elements of Art and Design): Elements of Art and Design Elements of Artand Design When you create art, you are expressing your ideas, your feelings, or your beliefs (p. 16).
Step 4 (Elements of Art and Design): If you intend to share your art with otherpeople, you need to know how to organize your design so thatthey will understand what your art is telling (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Principles of Design: Six Principles of Design: These principles are guidelines, notrules, to help you express yourself artistically (p. 23).
Principles of Design Principle 2: Six Principles of Design Principle 2: Understandingthese principles also will help you to appreciate how other artists try to communicate through their work (p. 23).
Principles of Design Principle 3: Six Principles of Design Principle 3: The six principles of design are rhythm, balance, proportion, variety, emphasis, and unity (p. 23).
Principles of Design Principle 4: Six Principles of Design Principle 4: Rhythm indicates movement by the repetition of a certain artelement or combination of elements (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Principles of Design): Step 1 (Six Principles of Design): The repeated element, a shape or line, for example, is called a motif (p. 23).
Step 2 (Principles of Design): Step 2 (Six Principles of Design): The artistuses the repetition of a motif to lead the viewer's eye around the work of art (p. 23).
Step 3 (Principles of Design): Step 3 (Six Principles of Design): Random rhythm happenswhen a motif is repeated in noapparent order, with irregularspacing between one motif and the next (p. 23).
Step 4 (Principles of Design): Step 4 (Six Principles of Design): Regular rhythm occurs whenidentical motifs with identicalspacing between them arerepeated (p. 23).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: An artist who makes art for personal pleasure does not have toget training (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: But if you want a career in the visual arts, you willneed some formal lessons (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Colleges and universities offer four- or five-year programs that lead to the bachelor of fine arts and master of fine artsdegrees (p. 61).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: In addition to the core courses common to all majorareas of study, these programs include art history and studioart classes (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A portfolio is a collection of samples of the artist'sbest work (p. 61).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Many art and design schools expect to see a portfolio and evaluate the student's talent and quality of work before they decide whether to accept him (p. 61).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Every year, various schoolshost a "portfolio day" so young artists can review their portfolios with representatives from many differentart (p. 61).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Independent schools of art and design offer two-year programs that lead to an associate of art or bachelor of fine artsdegree (p. 61).

intro_notes: NOTE: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) merit badge has no merit badge pamphlet. Instead, it has been designed for you to interact with the Scoutly chatbot on your learning journey as you work through the requirements. Scoutly can be found on the bottom right of your browser at https://scouting.org. If you have a question about a requirement, ask Scoutly! Hint: try asking Scoutly to Explain the "xxx" activity for requirement "yy" of the AI merit badge. This does not replace the requirement to identify and work with a counselor to complete the badge. Additional educational resources are available on our Counselor Information Page.

requirements.lead_text: Practical Application. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Practical Application. Do ONE of the following: (a) With your counselor's approval, choose an artificial intelligence project based on your personal interest or a community need. Develop a plan outlining the project's objectives, data requirements, and potential ethical considerations. Implement the project utilizing appropriate artificial intelligence tools, languages, or platforms. Share your project with your counselor. Discuss the steps you followed to create the project and your experience during the process. (b) With your counselor's approval, design a short lesson plan on AI and teach it to your patrol or a group of Scouts. The lesson should include an AI-generated age-appropriate explanation of AI, examples of how AI is used in both everyday life as well as in the workplace, and an interactive demonstration of how Scouts could utilize AI to assist them with a school assignment, Scouting activity, or rank advancement. Share information on the development process and teaching experience with your counselor.

requirements.lead_text: Career Exploration. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Career Exploration. Do ONE of the following: (a) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in artificial intelligence or automation. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Interview an artificial intelligence or automation professional. Learn about their day-to-day work, the challenges they face, and their vision for the future of artificial intelligence or automation. Inquire about training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Share what you learned with your counselor.

Step 3 (Light Pollution and Sky Observation): If light pollution interferes with your stargazing, trythese tricks (p. 24).
Step 4 (Light Pollution and Sky Observation): This willhelp prevent light from streetlights, passing cars, and the glowing sky itself from ruining your night vision (p. 24).

pamphlet_excerpts: Visible Planets: List The Names: Venus also appears only in the early evening or earlymorning sky, but it is much easier to see than Mercury (p. 35).
Visible Planets Principle 2: List The Names Principle 2: Sometimes called the morning or the evening star, diamondwhite and brilliant Venus is the brightest planet as seen from the Earth (p. 35).
Visible Planets Principle 3: List The Names Principle 3: If Venus is in the evening sky, you can't miss (p. 35).

Visible Planets Principle 4: List The Names Principle 4: Because different parts of their sunlit areas are visible from Earth at different times, Mercury and Venus have phasessimilar to the Moon's (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Visible Planets): Step 1 (List The Names): At different times, they appear full, gibbous (three-quarters full), half-full (like a first-quarter or lastquarter moon), as a crescent (p. 35).
Step 2 (Visible Planets): Step 2 (List The Names): When Mercury or Venus is on the same side of the Sun as Earth, the planet's unlit side faces Earth (p. 35).
Step 3 (Visible Planets): Step 3 (List The Names): As the planet movesaround the Sun away from Earth, its sunlit side becomes visible as a thin crescent and grows gradually as the planet (p. 35).
Step 4 (Visible Planets): Step 4 (List The Names): When Mercury or Venus is near the other side of the Sun, we can see almost all of its sunlit face, the full phase (p. 35).

Step 4 (Composition of the Sun, its relationship): It wasn't until 2011 that NASA's Kepler spacecraft discovered two Earth-sizedplanets beyond the solar system (p. 9).

requirements.lead_text: With your counselor's approval and guidance, do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: With your counselor's approval and guidance, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a planetarium or astronomical observatory. Submit a written report, a scrapbook, OR a video presentation afterward to your counselor that includes the following information: activities occurring there, exhibits and displays you saw, telescopes and other instruments being used, and celestial objects you observed. (b) Plan and participate in an observation session that includes using binoculars or a telescope and includes at least 10 celestial objects beyond those observed in requirement 4. These might be lunar features, Messier objects, additional constellations or planets, or artificial satellites including the International Space Station. List the celestial objects you want to observe and find each in a star chart, guidebook or by using an app. Prepare a log or notebook. Discuss with your counselor what you hope to observe prior to your observation session. Review your log or notebook with your counselor afterward. (c) Plan and host a star party for your Scout troop or other group such as your class at school. Use binoculars or a telescope to show and explain celestial objects to the group. (d) Help an astronomy club in your community hold a star party that is open to the public. (e) Personally take a series of photographs or digital images of the movement of the Moon, a planet, an asteroid, meteor, or a comet. In your visual display, label each image and include the date and time it was taken. Show all positions on a star chart or map. Show your display at school or at a troop meeting. Explain the changes you observed. (f) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, use online observing opportunities such as SkyNet to observe planets, comets, galaxies, and/or the sun. Describe your experience to your counselor.

Step 3 (Guidance Do ONE): Step 3 (Your Counselor's Approval and Guidance): Modern digital cameras are very sensitive to light, and objects appear brighter and clearer in photographs than through a telescope or binoculars (p. 64).

Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in astronomy to pursue a personal hobby. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Like anyone else, athletes can get injured or sustain an illness (such as a heat-related sickness) (p. 57).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Proper training and conditioning will help keep you healthy (p. 57).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: However, you should knowwhat to do in the event of common injuries or illnesses (p. 57).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: As a young athlete, to help prevent or reduce the chance of injuries, you should try to match your physique with your desired activity (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Muscular athletes might consider basketball, football, or soccer (p. 57).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In weightlifting competitions, for example, athletes compete against others in their own weight class (p. 57).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Take responsibility and precautions for minimizingrisk and avoidinginjury by following the information in the "Ready, Set, Go" chapter (p. 57).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If you are injured, you should not try to play through the pain (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check: Calciumis found in dairy products such as milk, cheese, and yogurt, and foods such as nuts, beans, broccoli, and canned salmon (p. 7).
Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 2: Making sure you have at least four servings of calcium daily will help ensure that your bones stay strong throughout your life (p. 7).
Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 3: If you do not get enough calcium in your diet while you are young, you could be at risk for the bone-thinning diseasecalled osteoporosis (p. 7).
Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check Principle 4: Failing to fuel and refuel your body with good foods canlead to fatigue and injury; you will also be more likely to getsick (p. 7).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): Develop good eating habits now so that they will becomesecond nature to you throughout your lifetime (p. 7).
Step 2 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): For more information aboutnutrition andphysical fitness, read the Cooking and Personal Fitness meritbadge pamphlets (p. 7).
Step 3 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): To be a strong, healthy performer in athletics and in life, avoid tobacco, alcohol, and other harmful substances (p. 7).
Step 4 (Pre-Participation Physical & Health Check): Smoking makes you cough and wheeze, and it interferes withproper lung growth and lung function (p. 7).

Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): This includes treating opponents, teammates, coaches, officials, and spectators with respect (p. 21).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Athletes shouldshake hands and congratulate opponents after participating inan event, whether or not they have won (p. 21).

requirements.lead_text: Complete the activities in FOUR of the following options and show improvement over a three-month period:
requirements.req_text: Complete the activities in FOUR of the following options and show improvement over a three-month period: (a) Option A, Sprinting. Do ALL of the following: (1) 100-meter dash (2) 200-meter dash (b) Option B, Long-Distance Running. Do ALL of the following: (1) 3k run (2) 5k run (c) Option C, Long Jump OR High Jump. Do ALL of the following: (1) Running long jump OR running high jump (best of three tries) (2) Standing long jump OR standing high jump (best of three tries) (d) Option D, Swimming. Do ALL of the following: (1) 100-meter swim (2) 200-meter swim (e) Option E, Pull-Ups AND Push-Ups. Do ALL of the following: (1) Pull-ups in two minutes (2) Push-ups in two minutes (f) Option F, Baseball Throw. Do ALL of the following: (1) Baseball throw for accuracy, 10 throws at a target (distance to be determined by age): ages 11 to 12, 20 feet; ages 13 to 15, 30 feet; ages 16 to 17, 40 feet (2) Baseball throw for distance, five throws (total distance) (g) Option G, Basketball Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Basketball shot for accuracy, 10 free-throw shots (2) Basketball throw for skill and agility, the following shots: (a) Left-side layup (b) Right-side layup (c) Left side of hoop, along the key line (d) Right side of hoop, along the key line (e) Where key line and free-throw line meet, left side (f) Where key line and free-throw line meet, left side (g) Top of the key (h) Another spot along the three-point line (h) Option H, Football Kick OR Soccer Kick. Do ALL of the following: (1) Goals from the 10-yard line, eight kicks (2) Football kick or soccer kick for distance, five kicks (total distance) (i) Option I, Weight Training. Do ALL of the following: (1) Chest/bench press, two sets of 15 repetitions each (2) Leg curls, two sets of 15 repetitions each

Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You may want to practice and train throughout the week and then test yourself each Saturday (p. 21).

intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-12-31). The Auctioneering Badge is a dynamic blend of public speaking and salesmanship that offers Scouts the opportunity to develop essential communication and persuasion skills. Scouts will learn about the history of auctioneering, develop presentation techniques, and build rapport with an audience. They’ll engage in mock auctions to practice creating demand and closing deals while also learning how to handle challenges and uphold ethical standards. This badge fosters confidence and critical thinking skills that are powerful tools for personal growth, leadership roles, and future success.

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.

intro_notes: NOTE: You will need access to a car or truck and its owner's manual to meet some requirements for this merit badge. If you do not have your own vehicle, you should work with your counselor or other trusted adult to obtain access to a vehicle and the owner's manual for that vehicle.
NOTE: The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

requirements.lead_text: Safety and Registration. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Safety and Registration. Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the hazards you are most likely to encounter during automotive maintenance activities, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, or lessen these hazards. (b) Discuss with your counselor the safety equipment, tools, and clothing used while checking or repairing a motor vehicle. Use this equipment, tools, and/or clothing (when needed or called for) in meeting the requirements for this merit badge. (c) Explain the different ways motor vehicles are powered. (d) Explain the safety considerations when performing maintenance on a vehicle equipped with a high-voltage electrical system. (e) Review the maintenance chart in the vehicle owner's manual. Explain the requirements and time limits. (f) Explain the purpose, importance, and limitations of safety belts and passive restraints. (g) Find out the requirements for your state's emissions and safety inspections (as applicable), including how often a vehicle needs to be inspected. (h) Explain the importance of registering a vehicle and find out the annual registration fee for renewing your family car's registration.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Air bags are required on all new passenger vehicles sold in the United States (p. 20).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If a front-end crash occurs, sensors in the air bags notice that the car has suddenly sloweddown or even stopped (a process called deceleration) (p. 20).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): This triggers a chemical reaction that fills the air bags with gas (p. 20).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In lessthan 1/20 of a second, the air bags balloon out, cushioning thedriver and passenger (p. 20).

requirements.lead_text: General Maintenance. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: General Maintenance. Do the following: (a) Demonstrate how to check the following: (1) Brake fluid (2) Engine oil (3) Coolant (4) Power steering fluid (5) Windshield washer fluid (6) Transmission fluid (7) Battery fluid (if possible) and condition of the battery terminals (b) Locate the fuse boxes; determine the type and size of fuses. Demonstrate the proper replacement of burned-out fuses. (c) Demonstrate how to check the condition and tension of belts and hoses. (d) Check the vehicle for proper operation of its lights, including the interior overhead lights, instrument lights, warning lights, and exterior bulbs. (e) Locate and check the air filter(s).

pamphlet_excerpts: Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard: An electric vehicle (EV) works differently than a traditionalgasoline car (p. 30).

Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard Principle 2: Instead of using an internal combustion engine that runs on gasoline, an EV uses an electric motor powered byelectricity stored in a large battery (p. 30).
Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard Principle 3: EVs have a big battery pack, usually located under thefloor or in the back of the car (p. 30).
Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard Principle 4: This battery stores electricity, much like how your phone stores power (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): The battery is chargedby plugging it into a charging station or a wall outlet. 2 (p. 30).
Step 2 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): The electric motor in an EV is like the enginein a regular car, but it runs on electricity (p. 30).
Step 3 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): When you step on the accelerator pedal, the electric motor receives electricity from the battery and uses it to generate motion (p. 30).
Step 4 (Automotive Maintenance Core Field Standard): The controller manages the flow of electricity from the battery to the electric motor (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Cooling System: Manufacturers generally recommend an equal mixture of water and ethylene-glycol antifreeze (p. 60).
Cooling System Principle 2: This coolant mixture offers goodcooling during the summer and protects the engine down toabout 35 degrees below zero Fahrenheit in the winter (p. 60).
Cooling System Principle 3: When youuse this type of coolant, you should not add water (p. 60).
Cooling System Principle 4: Coolant should be checked regularly and replaced about every 30,000 miles or two years, or up to five years in some newervehicles (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Cooling System): The system also might need to be flushed if there is toomuch dirt and rust in the coolant (p. 60).
Step 2 (Cooling System): To check the car's coolant in most new cars, you needonly to check the coolant level on the plastic coolant reservoir and, if necessary, add coolant (p. 60).
Step 3 (Cooling System): If your car does not have one of these reservoirs, you willneed to remove the radiator cap to check the fluid, but only if the engine is cool (p. 60).
Step 4 (Cooling System): To remove the cap, wrap a cloth around thecap and slowly loosen it to the first stop (p. 60).
