pamphlet_excerpts: Ignition and Electrical Systems: A voltage regulator controls the amount of recharging (p. 69).
Ignition and Electrical Systems Principle 2: The lighting system includes the interior overhead lights, instrument lights, headlights, taillights, turn signals, warning lights, hazard lights (p. 69).
Ignition and Electrical Systems Principle 3: When you open a car door, plunger-type switches close a circuit to the interior lights and make them (p. 69).
Ignition and Electrical Systems Principle 4: When you apply the brakes, a switch under the pedal closes a circuit to the brake light bulbs so they light (p. 69).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): Wires connect the battery to many other accessories, including the sound system, heating and cooling systems, and (if the carhas them) power (p. 69).
Step 2 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): In some cases (such as the sound system and theheating and cooling systems), you must also turn the ignitionswitch on to close the circuit (p. 69).
Step 3 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): A solenoid is a coil of wire that wraps around a metalcore (p. 69).
Step 4 (Ignition and Electrical Systems): Electricity magnetizes the coil and makes the coremove, opening or closing an electrical circuit (p. 69).

pamphlet_excerpts: Drive Train: You may have seen this idea at work on a bicycle (p. 33).
Drive Train Principle 2: If your chain is on a small chain ring in the front and a large sprocketin the back, it will help you climb a very steep hill (p. 33).
Drive Train Principle 3: If it is on a large chain ring and a small sprocket, it will help you pedalalong a flat road at high speed (p. 33).
Drive Train Principle 4: A key difference between a car transmission and a bicyclegear set is that on a bicycle, you can use any chain ring withany sprocket (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Drive Train): On a car, however, the gears on the input shaft (coming from the engine) and the output shaft (going toward the wheels) are always connected in pairs (p. 33).
Step 2 (Drive Train): Each time you shiftgears, the transmission tells a different pair of gears to sendpower to the wheels (p. 33).
Step 3 (Drive Train): There are two basic types of transmissions: manual and automatic (p. 33).
Step 4 (Drive Train): With a manual transmission, just before shifting gears, thedriver must push a pedal down to release the clutch (p. 33).

Step 3 (Brake System): Have your friend start the engine, apply the brakes, and shift into reverse while youcheck the backup lights (p. 46).
Step 4 (Brake System): Return the carto park and turn off then engine, thenturn on the hazard light switch andturn indicator (p. 46).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Determine the value of three different vehicles you are interested in purchasing. One must be new and one must be used; the third vehicle can be new or used. For each vehicle, find out the requirements and cost of automobile insurance to include basic liability and options for collision, comprehensive, towing, and rental car. Using the three vehicles you chose and with your counselor's assistance, complete the operation/maintenance chart provided in the Automotive Maintenance merit badge pamphlet. Use this information to determine the operating cost per mile for each vehicle, and discuss what you learn with your counselor. (b) Choose a car cleaner and wax product for a vehicle you want to clean. Explain clear-coat paint and the precautions necessary for care. Clean the vehicle, both inside and out, and wax the exterior. Use a vinyl and rubber protectant (on vinyl tops, rubber door seals, sidewalls, etc.) and explain the importance of this protectant. (c) Locate the manufacturer's jack. Use the jack to demonstrate how to engage the jack correctly on the vehicle, then change a tire correctly. (d) Perform an oil filter and oil change on a vehicle. Explain how to properly dispose of the used oil and filter.

requirements.topic_heading: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight
requirements.lead_text: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Aviation Basics and Mechanics of Flight. Do the following: (a) Define "aircraft." Describe three kinds of aircraft today, and their typical uses. (b) Provide a brief overview of the evolution of flight, and discuss three notable times in history important to aviation. (c) Explain the difference between a fixed wing and a rotary wing aircraft, and the benefits of each. (d) Explain the operation of piston, turbine, and jet engines. (e) Using a model aircraft, describe the four forces that act on an aircraft in flight. (f) Explain how an airfoil generates lift, specifically noting Bernoulli's principle. (g) Identify and describe the aerodynamic control surfaces on the aircraft of your choice, and explain how they operate to control its attitude and direction of flight. (h) Explain the purposes and functions of the various instruments found in a typical single-engine aircraft: attitude indicator, heading indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator, turn and bank indicator, vertical speed indicator, compass, navigation, communication, and engine performance indicators.

requirements.req_text: Principles of Flight. Do ONE of the following: (a) Build a model FPG-9. Get others in your troop or patrol to make their own model, then organize a competition to test the precision of flight and landing of the models. (b) Build a rubber-band driven balsa wood airplane. Fly the plane for 25 feet in a straight line, with a smooth landing. (c) Build (or obtain) a fuel-driven or battery-powered electric model aircraft or drone. Obtain The Recreational UAS Safety Test (TRUST) certification, and fly the aircraft with a successful take-off and landing.

requirements.lead_text: Flight Operations. Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Flight Operations. Do TWO of the following: (a) Using a flight simulator software package, set a course and fly the headings you have established with a successful take-off and landing. (b) Under supervision, perform a preflight inspection of an aircraft. (c) Observe and/or participate in an aircraft maintenance activity. Describe the maintenance schedule and requirements for an aircraft of your choice. (d) Obtain and learn how to read an aeronautical chart. Measure a true course on the chart; correct it for magnetic variation, compass deviation, and wind drift to determine a navigational heading for an aircraft. (e) With your parent or guardian's permission, take a discovery flight in an aircraft. Record the date, place, type of aircraft, and duration of flight. Report on your impressions of the flight.

Flight Operations Principle 2: In every aircraft, you will find a deviation card mounted near the compass that tells us how to correct the magnetic course for deviation (p. 50).
Flight Operations Principle 3: Remember, the magnetic course from Indianapolis International (IND) to Crawfordsville Airport (CFJ) is 300 degrees (p. 50).
Flight Operations Principle 4: Our deviation card tells us that for a magnetic course of 300 degrees, we should steer a course of 301 degrees (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Flight Operations): In other words the compass deviation in our airplane at thiscourse is 1 degree higher than the magnetic course (p. 50).
Step 2 (Flight Operations): We can now proceed to steer at 301 degrees, confident that we will soon see the Crawfordsville Airport (p. 50).
Step 3 (Flight Operations): For requirement 2(e), you learned that your airspeed indicatorshows how fast you are passing through the air, not over the ground (p. 50).
Step 4 (Flight Operations): If you are flying into a 25-knot headwind, you areactually traveling over the ground at 25 knots less than your airspeed (p. 50).

pamphlet_excerpts: Airport Operations: Providing weather and information services for all pilots is the primary responsibility of the flight service station (p. 73).
Airport Operations Principle 2: As its name suggests, a control tower is an elevated structure from which airport controllers operate (p. 73).
Airport Operations Principle 3: The people in the control tower have four primary responsibilities (p. 73).
Airport Operations Principle 4: Theactual TRACON facility might not be located in the controltower or even on the airport site (p. 73).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Airport Operations): When you visit a terminal radar control facility, expect to enter a darkened room lit only by the glow of radarscreens (p. 73).
Step 2 (Airport Operations): Controllers skillfully observe and maneuver the "blips" that appear on their screens; each blip represents an aircraft (p. 73).
Step 3 (Airport Operations): If you have ever played a computer orvideo game, you have some idea of the intense nature of this responsibility (p. 73).
Step 4 (Airport Operations): Most of the facilities mentioned welcome visitors, and you can find their phone numbers in your phone book (p. 73).

requirements.req_text: Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities. Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities Principle 2: Mostimportantly, thepilot can fly onlyduring daylighthours and inairspace wherehe or she does notneed to communicate with airtraffic control (p. 57).
Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities Principle 3: Of all the certificates and ratings, the recreational pilot certificateis the easiest to obtain (p. 57).
Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities Principle 4: It requires 30 hours of flight instruction (three hours of which must be solo flight time) (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): The recreationalpilot may earn additional privileges (p. 57).

Step 2 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): The FAA created the sport pilot's license in 2004 to help lower the barriers of entry-level aviation by making flying moreaffordable and accessible (p. 57).
Step 3 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): If you are an enthusiast of light-sport aircraft (LSA), consider a sport pilot certificateif you want to fly one (p. 57).

Step 4 (Personal & Professional Aviation Opportunities): Like the recreational pilotcertificate, this certificate will allow the pilot to carry only onepassenger at up to 10,000 feet above sea (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards: There are two types of venomous snakes in the United States (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 2: Pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths) have triangular heads with pit marks on both sides of the head (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 3: Coral snakes have black snouts and bands of red andyellow separated by bands of black (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 4: Coral snakes injectpowerful venom that works on the victim's nervoussystem; pit-viper venom affects the circulatory system (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): A hiking stick does double duty when youwalk through places where snakes might lurk (p. 22).
Step 2 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): Walk slowly and use the stick to poke amongstones and brush ahead (p. 22).
Step 3 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): Watch whereyou put your hands as you collect firewoodor climb over rocks and logs (p. 22).
Step 4 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): The bite of a nonvenomous snake causes onlyminor puncture wounds (p. 22).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off andstow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, butrespect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: If you encounter horsebackriders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while theanimals pass (p. 61).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If you encounter other hikers or backpackersgoing uphill when you are going downhill, give them the right of-way (p. 61).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact (p. 61).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If possible, campaway from trails and other visitors (p. 61).

That you can read topographic maps Principle 2: One of the secrets of safebackcountry hiking is the use of thumbnail navigation (p. 74).
That you can read topographic maps Principle 3: This technique calls for your constant awareness of your position (p. 74).
That you can read topographic maps Principle 4: You must carry atopographic map where you can easily refer to it, that is, in your shirt or pants pocketrather than in your pack (p. 74).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (That you can read topographic maps): As you hike, you shouldcontinuously try to matchup features around you withpoints on your map (p. 74).
Step 2 (That you can read topographic maps): Not only will this prevent you from getting too far off your route if you take a wrong turn, it will keep your map-readingskills sharp (p. 74).
Step 3 (That you can read topographic maps): With a basic knowledge of route finding and theuse of thumbnail navigation, there is little chance of becomingtruly lost (p. 74).
Step 4 (That you can read topographic maps): If you find you can't determine your position, the bestthing to do is stop walking (p. 74).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off andstow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, butrespect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: If you encounter horsebackriders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while theanimals pass (p. 61).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If you encounter other hikers or backpackersgoing uphill when you are going downhill, give them the right of-way (p. 61).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact (p. 61).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If possible, campaway from trails and other visitors (p. 61).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Write a plan for a backpacking trek of at least five days using at least three different campsites and covering at least 30 miles. Your plan must include a description of and route to the trek area, a schedule (including a daily schedule), a list of food and equipment needs, a safety and emergency plan, and a budget. (b) Following the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code, take the trek as planned in requirement 11(a) that is at least five full days, covering at least 30 miles and utilizing at least three different campsites. While on trek, complete at least one service project approved by your counselor. (c) Keep a daily journal during the trek that includes a day-by-day description of your activities, including notes about what worked well and thoughts about improvements that could be made for the next trek.

pamphlet_excerpts: Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed: Your counselor that you are able: The following are common weaves used in this pamphlet (p. 11).

Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 2: Your counselor that you are able Principle 2: Sometimes called over-under weave, the plainweave is done with rigid stakes or spokes, and weavers thatwrap around the stakes in an over-one (p. 11).
Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 3: Your counselor that you are able Principle 3: Spokes and stakes usually are more rigid and thicker reedthan weavers (p. 11).
Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed Principle 4: Your counselor that you are able Principle 4: Continuous weave looks much the same as plainweave, but it is woven with a different technique (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 1 (Your counselor that you are able): This weave is created over an odd number of stakes (p. 11).

Step 2 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 2 (Your counselor that you are able): It is not done one row at a time, but continuously from beginning to end, with additional weavers added whenmore length is needed (p. 11).

Step 3 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 3 (Your counselor that you are able): This method of weaving involves the weaverpassing over two or more stakes and under two or more stakesat a time (p. 11).

Step 4 (Baskets Plaited Coiled Ribbed): Step 4 (Your counselor that you are able): This weave, sometimes called pairing, involvestwo weavers, each alternately twisting over and underconsecutive spokes (p. 11).

pamphlet_excerpts: Need for Bird Study: Birds lend life, color, and music to the outdoors, and they are an important part of the ecosystems that keep thisplanet healthy (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 2: Because they are sensitive to changes in theenvironment, birds are valuable indicators of trouble, includingpollution and habitat loss (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 3: It was the near-disappearance of baldeagles, peregrine falcons, and brown pelicans decades ago thatalerted people to the dangers of many (p. 10).
Need for Bird Study Principle 4: Major, rapiddeclines in the number of songbirds have shown that we mustpreserve large areas for wildlife habitat (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Need for Bird Study): Each species is lumped with its closest relatives to form a genus, usually on the basis of physical characteristicslike the shapes of certain bones (p. 10).
Step 2 (Need for Bird Study): Closely related genera (theplural of "genus") are grouped together to form a family (p. 10).
Step 3 (Need for Bird Study): Most field guides are arranged in this taxonomic order (p. 10).
Step 4 (Need for Bird Study): Because related birds often act and look somewhat the same, knowing these relationships can help you identify a new, puzzling species (p. 10).

pamphlet_excerpts: Certain Orders of Birds: Juncos have white flashmarks on the sides of their tails (p. 29).
Certain Orders of Birds Principle 2: A bird doesn't really have a mustache, that's just the nickname for dark markings that extend back from the base of the bill (p. 29).
Certain Orders of Birds Principle 3: Rump patches are white or colorful feathers just above the tail, found on species such as northern flickers and yellowrumped warblers (p. 29).
Certain Orders of Birds Principle 4: Common birds such as sparrows, robins, or crows can be used for size references, while shape candistinguish birds with similar markings (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Certain Orders of Birds): A wood thrush and abrown thrasher, for instance, are colored much the same, rustybrown on top, with a white breast spotted in black (p. 29).
Step 2 (Certain Orders of Birds): But the thrushis plump, with a fairly short tail and a short beak (p. 29).
Step 3 (Certain Orders of Birds): The thrasher isslender and slinky, with a long tail and a long, pointed beak (p. 29).
Step 4 (Certain Orders of Birds): Another important clue to a bird's identity is how itbehaves (p. 29).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Go on a field trip with a local club or with others who are knowledgeable about birds in your area. (1) Keep a list or fill out a checklist of all the birds your group observed during the field trip. (2) Tell your counselor which birds your group saw and why some species were common and some were present in small numbers. (3) Tell your counselor what makes the area you visited good for finding birds. (b) By using a public library, the internet, or contacting the National Audubon Society, find the name and location of the Christmas Bird Count nearest your home and obtain the results of a recent count. (1) Explain what kinds of information are collected during the annual event. (2) Tell your counselor which species are most common, and explain why these birds are abundant. (3) Tell your counselor which species are uncommon, and explain why these were present in small numbers. If the number of birds of these species is decreasing, explain why, and what, if anything, could be done to reverse their decline. (c) Participate in a bird banding program with an approved federal or state agency, university researcher, bird observatory, or certified private individual. (1) Explain who is able to band birds and why. (2) Explain why birds get banded. (3) Explain what kinds of birds get banded. (4) Tell how the birds were captured, the number of bird species recorded during your visit, and your role in the program.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Go on a field trip): The North American Migration Count is a warm-weather version of the Christmas Bird Count and is designed to provide a kind ofsnapshot of bird (p. 57).
Step 2 (Go on a field trip): Unlike the CBC, however, the NAMC covers entire counties, andparticipation is free (p. 57).
Step 3 (Go on a field trip): Participants are asked to watch their feeders for part or all of a two-day period every two weeks, from late autumn untilearly spring (p. 57).
Step 4 (Go on a field trip): The information from Project Feeder Watch helpsscientists track bird movements and see whether some species are increasing or decreasing (p. 57).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: But beyond the pleasure of bird watching, there are paid and unpaid careersin bird study (p. 52).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Veterinarians and veterinarytechnicians can serve in the specializedfield of avian medicine and surgery (p. 52).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Volunteer activities may include bird census counting, monitoring the nesting sites of endangered species, andreporting hatchling survival (p. 52).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Many of these activities aremanaged by governmental agencies such as state and federalwildlife departments (p. 52).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Use a field notebook small enough to fit easily in a shirtpocket or outside compartment of a pack (p. 52).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You mightdecide to devote an entire page to one species of bird, noting itscolor, pattern, song, or behavior (p. 52).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in camping activities and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Discuss with your counselor why it is important to be aware of weather conditions before and during your camping activities. Tell how you can prepare should the weather turn bad during your campouts. (c) Show that you know first aid for and how to prevent injuries or illnesses that could occur while camping, including hypothermia, frostbite, heat reactions, dehydration, altitude sickness, insect stings, tick bites, snakebite, blisters, and hyperventilation.

Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: You also will be in a stronger position to provide assistance if an emergency does arise (p. 13).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Lastly, let others know when you are having difficulties orare aware of a concern that might affect you or the group (p. 13).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Stopping for a few moments to deal with a hot spot on a heel canhelp avoid bringing the group to a long halt later in the day whenblisters break (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Speaking up about changes you notice in theweather or asking questions you have about whether a campsiteis appropriate can help everyone (p. 13).

pamphlet_excerpts: Features of four types of tents: All good things must come to an end, and that includes camping trips (p. 37).
Features of four types of tents Principle 2: As you break camp, keep in mind these suggestions: • Leave the dining fly in place until you are almost ready togo (p. 37).
Features of four types of tents Principle 3: Leave the campsite looking better than you found (p. 37).
Features of four types of tents Principle 4: Going to just leave that pack on the floor when you get home (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Features of four types of tents): Taking care of your gear lengthens the life of your gear, too. • Clean and air out all of your gear, including sleeping bags (p. 37).
Step 2 (Features of four types of tents): The next time you want to go camping, and it won't be long, you willalready be well on your way to thegreat out-of-doors (p. 37).
Step 3 (Features of four types of tents): Mix geometry, modern materials, and the imaginations of tent makers, and you get an astounding variety ofshapes (p. 37).
Step 4 (Features of four types of tents): Among the most interesting are hybrid tents thatcombine features of A-frames and domes (p. 37).

pamphlet_excerpts: Overnight Campout With Your Patrol: Prepare for an overnight campout: You have planned a campout and gathered your food and gear (p. 42).

Overnight Campout With Your Patrol Principle 2: Prepare for an overnight campout Principle 2: After loading everything intoyour pack, there should be little left to doexcept head out the door and let theadventure begin (p. 42).
Overnight Campout With Your Patrol Principle 3: Prepare for an overnight campout Principle 3: Besides your own gear, you probably will carry some group equipment (p. 42).
Overnight Campout With Your Patrol Principle 4: Prepare for an overnight campout Principle 4: Your share might include several pots, part of atent, a camp stove, and some food (p. 42).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Overnight Campout With Your Patrol): Step 1 (Prepare for an overnight campout): Arrangesoft items in your pack so they will cushionyour back (p. 42).

Step 2 (Overnight Campout With Your Patrol): Step 2 (Prepare for an overnight campout): Keep your rain gear, flashlight, first-aid kit, water bottle, and hike food near the top of your pack orin its outside pockets where you can reach (p. 42).
Step 3 (Overnight Campout With Your Patrol): Step 3 (Prepare for an overnight campout): If there is room, stow your sleeping bag inside your pack (p. 42).
Step 4 (Overnight Campout With Your Patrol): Step 4 (Prepare for an overnight campout): Otherwise, cover it with a ground cloth or a plastictrash-can liner to protect it from the elements (p. 42).

requirements.lead_text: Show experience in camping by doing the following:
requirements.req_text: Show experience in camping by doing the following: (a) Camp for at least 20 nights at designated Scouting activities or events. One long-term camping experience of up to six consecutive nights may be applied toward this requirement. Two nights may be counted toward the total for each additional long-term camping trip. Each night must be spent either under the sky, in a tent you have pitched yourself (if a tent is provided and already set up, you do not need to pitch your own), in a hammock that is safely strung outdoors, in a lean-to, or other three-sided shelter with an open front. Nights spent in indoor lock-in events, cabin camping, hotel stays, or other covered accommodations do not count toward the 20 nights. (b) On any of these camping experiences, you must do TWO of the following, only with proper preparation and under qualified supervision. (1) Hike up a mountain, gaining at least 1,000 vertical feet. (2) Backpack, snowshoe, or cross-country ski for at least 4 miles. (3) Take a bike trip of at least 15 miles or at least four hours. (4) Take a nonmotorized trip on the water of at least four hours or 5 miles. (5) Plan and carry out an overnight snow camping experience. (6) Rappel down a rappel route of 30 feet or more. (c) On any of these camping experiences, perform a conservation project approved by the landowner or land managing agency. This can be done alone or with others.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Experience in camping by doing): As you leave civilization behind, a great world of possibilities and responsibilities opensbefore (p. 21).

Step 3 (Experience in camping by doing): You can spend time near remote lakes, in deep forests, and in desert terrain (p. 21).
Step 4 (Experience in camping by doing): Best of all, you can relyon your own skill and determination to make the most ofliving for a while beyond the usual bounds of civilization (p. 21).

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Because canoeing is a physicalactivity that takesplace in the outdoors, participants are at risk for arange of injuries (p. 16).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Following the nine points of Safety Afloat reduces many of theserious risks in canoeing, but some major and minor injuriesstill might occur (p. 16).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: First aid for some of the temperature-relatedinjuries can be lifesaving while treatment for other conditions isless urgent (p. 16).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: There are two primary cold related dangers encountered incanoeing (p. 16).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): The first is cold-water shock which a paddler canexperience by falling into cold water (p. 16).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): The second danger is hypothermia, which is a gradual lowering of the body's core temperature caused by spending minutes to hours in water (p. 16).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Cold-water shock occurs when a paddler falls into verycold water, especially below 60 degrees (p. 16).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): The colder the water, the more severe the effects (p. 16).

pamphlet_excerpts: Out The Major: Name and point out the major: Gunwales (pronounced "gunnels") are rails that run along the top edge of both sides of the canoe (p. 27).
Out The Major Principle 2: Name and point out the major Principle 2: Gunwales add strength to the hull and help it keep its shape (p. 27).
Out The Major Principle 3: Name and point out the major Principle 3: Braces, called thwarts (pronounced "thorts"), span the width of the canoe and provide rigidity and support (p. 27).
Out The Major Principle 4: Name and point out the major Principle 4: Some canoes also have a small keel, a ridge that runs the length of the bottom of the canoe alongits center line (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Out The Major): Step 1 (Name and point out the major): A keel improves a canoe's ability to travel in astraight line but hinders its ability to turn (p. 27).

Step 2 (Out The Major): Step 2 (Name and point out the major): When you are facing forward in your canoe, ahead is the direction in front of thebow, and astern is the direction behind the boat (p. 27).
Step 3 (Out The Major): Step 3 (Name and point out the major): A canoe's dimensions affect how the canoe will perform on water (p. 27).
Step 4 (Out The Major): Step 4 (Name and point out the major): A keel further improves a canoe's tracking ability (p. 27).

pamphlet_excerpts: Size Paddler Sitting Position: Name and point out the parts: In the kneeling position, the paddler's center of gravity islower than in the seated position (p. 38).
Size Paddler Sitting Position Principle 2: Name and point out the parts Principle 2: This puts the paddler in amore stable position in the boat (p. 38).

Size Paddler Sitting Position Principle 3: Name and point out the parts Principle 3: When kneeling in the canoe, the paddler should sit up straight with their buttocks leaningagainst the seat or thwart behind them (p. 38).
Size Paddler Sitting Position Principle 4: Name and point out the parts Principle 4: Avoid kneeling with theback and upper legs in alignment (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Size Paddler Sitting Position): Step 1 (Name and point out the parts): The body should be slightlyshifted to the paddling side of the paddler so the knee is in thecurved part of the hull (p. 38).
Step 2 (Size Paddler Sitting Position): Step 2 (Name and point out the parts): A kneeling cushion or pad of closedcell foam is almost always needed for the kneels even for shorttrips (p. 38).

Step 3 (Size Paddler Sitting Position): Step 3 (Name and point out the parts): Some canoes are not designed for the kneeling position with little room under the seat for the feet and lower legs (p. 38).
Step 4 (Size Paddler Sitting Position): Step 4 (Name and point out the parts): In these canoes, avoid getting the legs entangled by using only thesitting position (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: General Care and Maintenance: Review with your counselor the general: Store canoes out of the water and upside down in acovered area away from direct sunlight and extremeheat or cold (p. 30).
General Care and Maintenance Principle 2: Review with your counselor the general Principle 2: Do not store canoes with wooden gunwales on the ground (p. 30).

General Care and Maintenance Principle 3: Review with your counselor the general Principle 3: To prevent damage, do not drag a canoe across the ground or run it up onto the shoreor into trees or rocks (p. 30).

General Care and Maintenance Principle 4: Review with your counselor the general Principle 4: Make sure to wipe sand, mud, and other debris out of the canoe after each trip, and make repairs as needed (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (General Care and Maintenance): Step 1 (Review with your counselor the general): Oil wooden gunwales, seats, and thwarts of a canoe at least twice a year (p. 30).

Step 2 (General Care and Maintenance): Step 2 (Review with your counselor the general): Paddling using a small blade, for example, 110 squareinches, takes less energy and can be less tiring than a largerpaddle blade with 140 square (p. 30).

Step 3 (General Care and Maintenance): Step 3 (Review with your counselor the general): However, the same results can be achieved by pulling less hard with a slightly larger blade, making paddling just as efficient on extended (p. 30).
Step 4 (General Care and Maintenance): Step 4 (Review with your counselor the general): Rectangular shaped blades with rounded or square cornersat the bottom are usually wider and shorter (p. 30).

Companion Use A Properly Equipped Principle 2: Most canoeing injuries on flatwatertake place while carrying, entering, or exiting the canoe (p. 37).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Companion Use A Properly Equipped): A bridged canoe is unstable and stepping into onecan result in injury to the paddler or damage to the boat (p. 37).
Step 2 (Companion Use A Properly Equipped): Enter, exit, ormove about thecanoe only whenboth hands arefree of equipmentor gear. • Never enter or exit a canoe with something in your hands (p. 37).
Step 3 (Companion Use A Properly Equipped): Place all equipment including paddles, pads, water containers, sunscreen, etc. in the boat before entering (p. 37).
Step 4 (Companion Use A Properly Equipped): Thecanoe must be floating when you enter it and remain floatingafter both paddlers are situated (p. 37).

requirements.lead_text: With a companion, use a properly equipped canoe to demonstrate the following:
requirements.req_text: With a companion, use a properly equipped canoe to demonstrate the following: (a) Safely exit the canoe in deep water without losing contact with the canoe. Reenter the canoe with the assistance of the other paddler without capsizing the boat. (b) Safely perform a controlled capsize of the canoe and demonstrate how staying with a capsized canoe will support both paddlers. (c) Swim, tow, or push a swamped canoe 50 feet to shallow water. In the shallow water, empty the swamped canoe and reenter it. (d) In deep water, rescue a swamped canoe and its paddlers. After checking that those in the water do not need immediate assistance, empty the swamped canoe and help the paddlers safely reenter their boat without capsizing. (e) Perform a canoe rescue of a conscious swimmer. (f) Using a rescue (throw) bag from shore, lay the line within 3 feet of a conscious swimmer 30 feet away. Show how to repack the bag when done.

requirements.lead_text: With a companion, using a properly equipped canoe to demonstrate the following tandem maneuvers while paddling in unison on opposite sides and without changing sides. Each paddler must demonstrate these maneuvers in both the bow and stern and on both sides of the canoe while maintaining trim and balance of the canoe:
requirements.req_text: With a companion, using a properly equipped canoe to demonstrate the following tandem maneuvers while paddling in unison on opposite sides and without changing sides. Each paddler must demonstrate these maneuvers in both the bow and stern and on both sides of the canoe while maintaining trim and balance of the canoe: (a) Pivot (spin) the canoe 180° (half circle) to the right from a stationary position, stop, and return to the starting position by pivoting to the left using draw and pushaway strokes or using forward and reverse sweeps staying within 2 boat lengths of the starting position. (b) Move a canoe sideways (abeam) in one direction for 10 feet and then return to the starting position using the draw and pushaway strokes. (c) While in forward motion, stop the canoe within two boat lengths using the backstroke. (d) While in the stern position and without assistance from the bow paddler, paddle in a straight line 15-20 boat lengths using an appropriate steering stroke, e. g., the J-stroke or thumb-down rudder stroke with or without a stern pry. (e) Move the canoe in a straight line 15-20 boat lengths with the bow paddler using as necessary the forward stroke, draw stroke or forward sweep and the stern paddler using an appropriate steering stroke, e. g., the J-stroke or thumb-down rudder stroke with or without a stern pry. (f) While maintaining forward motion, turn the canoe 90° in an arc to the right in 5-10 boat lengths with the bow paddler using as necessary either the draw stroke or forward sweep and the stern paddler using only the forward stroke. Repeat the maneuver turning the canoe 90° to the left. (g) Move the canoe backwards in a straight line 3-4 boat lengths using as necessary the back stroke, reverse sweep or draw stroke in the bow or the stern. (h) Complete a figure of 8 course around markers 3-4 boat lengths apart using appropriate strokes including the draw stroke, and the forward and reverse sweeps.

pamphlet_excerpts: Companion Using A Properly Equipped: Imagine a box about as wideas your shoulders, as high as the top of your head, andas low as the top of the gunwales (p. 51).
Companion Using A Properly Equipped Principle 2: It extends forward from your back to as far as your arms will reach while keeping good posture (p. 51).
Companion Using A Properly Equipped Principle 3: It is also the safest way to paddle becausestaying in the box protects your shoulder joints frombeing put in unstable positions (p. 51).
Companion Using A Properly Equipped Principle 4: If you rotate your upperbody to perform each stroke, the large, strong muscles of the torso will power the stroke and prevent fatigue (p. 51).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Companion Using A Properly Equipped): As you paddle, imagine your torso twisting around your backbone (p. 51).
Step 2 (Companion Using A Properly Equipped): Following the paddle blade with your eyes will help you learn to rotate your torso through eachstroke (p. 51).
Step 3 (Companion Using A Properly Equipped): Course Direction is a Team Effort The paddler in the stern position is better able to steer thecanoe since the stern paddler is further (p. 51).
Step 4 (Companion Using A Properly Equipped): That is why the J-stroke and Thumb-down rudderstroke are only performed in the stern (p. 51).

requirements.lead_text: Chemistry and Safety. Do the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Chemistry and Safety. Do the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Obtain safety data sheets (SDS) for sucrose (sugar), isopropyl alcohol (rubbing alcohol), and a waterproofing spray. Compare their properties and potential hazard(s), including handling and disposal guidelines and toxicity information. (b) What types of personal protective equipment (PPE) are recommended for each, and why? How does the recommended PPE change with toxicity and route of exposure? (c) Review the pictograms in Section 2 of each SDS. What do they mean, and how do you see them used in your community? (d) Discuss the safe storage of chemicals. How does the safe storage of chemicals apply to your home, school, community, and the environment?

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Chemistry and Cooking): Youeat complex molecules of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins (p. 15).
Step 2 (Chemistry and Cooking): Your body uses these molecules for energy and to make new biomolecules for tissues such as muscle, hair, and nails (p. 15).
Step 3 (Chemistry and Cooking): Combustion is one way to tell if achemical change has taken place (p. 15).
Step 4 (Chemistry and Cooking): Trythis experiment with a flame, one sign of chemical change (p. 15).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a research laboratory, and discuss the research performed there with a chemist or chemical technician. Learn what education and training they received. (b) Visit a company or plant that makes chemical products or uses chemical processes. Learn about their products or processes, and talk with someone who works there. Learn what they do, and what education and training they received. (c) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in chemistry. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career.

Step 3 (Chess Core Field Standard): You must analyze orcompare the risks and make the best decision (p. 13).
Step 4 (Chess Core Field Standard): You might have to use your creativity and try something that you think might work, perhaps a play you have never triedbefore (p. 13).

Step 4 (You Know): Step 4 (Your Counselor That You Know): The game is automatically a draw if the player whose turn it is to move is not incheck but has no legal move (p. 24).

Scorekeeping using the algebraic system Principle 3: The openings which begin 1. d4 d5 are called closed games and areknown for more subtle positional play and less aggressive maneuvering (p. 37).
Scorekeeping using the algebraic system Principle 4: Games in which White begins with 1. e4 and Black replies with a move other than 1. . e5 are called semi-open games (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Scorekeeping using the algebraic system): They are known for unbalanced and exciting play, often with the twoplayers attacking in different sectors of the board (p. 37).
Step 2 (Scorekeeping using the algebraic system): Experiment with many different openings and find ones which you are most comfortable playing (p. 37).
Step 3 (Scorekeeping using the algebraic system): It is possible to lose (or win) a game of chess in only two or fourmoves (p. 37).
Step 4 (Scorekeeping using the algebraic system): The most common types of quick checkmates (which often happen to beginners because they ignore the "openingprinciples") are the fool's mate (p. 37).

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain four of the following elements of chess strategy: exploiting weaknesses, force, king safety, pawn structure, space, tempo, and clock management. (b) Explain any five of these chess tactics: clearance sacrifice, decoy, discovered attack, double check, double attack, fork, interposing, overloading, overprotecting, pin, skewer, remove the defender, zwischenzug, and zugzwang. (c) Set up a chessboard as follows and with White to move first, demonstrate how to force checkmate on the Black king: (1) White king on e1, the White rooks on a1 and h1, and the Black king on e5 (2) White king on e1, White queen on d1, Black king on e5 (3) White king on e1, White rook on a1, Black king on e5 (d) With White king on d4, White pawn on e3, and Black king on e6: (1) With White to move, demonstrate how White can force Black to allow their pawn to reach the last rank and be promoted to a queen. (2) With Black to move, demonstrate how Black can force a draw. (e) Set up and solve five direct-mate problems provided by your counselor.

Share how your actions represent alignment with the Scout Oath and Scout Law. (c) Explain to your counselor how you plan to use what you have learned to assist you when that time comes, and what action(s) you can take to serve as an upstander and help other people at all times.

requirements.lead_text: Repeat the Scout Oath and Scout Law for your counselor. Choose TWO of the following scenarios and discuss what you could do as a Scout to demonstrate leadership and your understanding of what it means to help others who may seem different from you:
requirements.req_text: Repeat the Scout Oath and Scout Law for your counselor. Choose TWO of the following scenarios and discuss what you could do as a Scout to demonstrate leadership and your understanding of what it means to help others who may seem different from you: (a) Scenario 1: While at camp, a youth accidentally spills food on another camper. The camper who gets spilled on gets angry and says something that is offensive to people with disabilities; their friends laugh. What could/should you do? (b) Scenario 2: Your friend confides in you that some students in school are making insulting comments about one of their identities, and that those same students created a fake social media account to impersonate your friend online and post messages. What could/should you do? (c) Scenario 3: A new student in your class was born in another country (or has a parent who was born in another country). Your friends make rude comments to the student about their speech or clothes and tell the student to "go back home where you came from." What could/should you do?

requirements.lead_text: With your parent or guardian's approval, connect with another Scout or youth your own age who has an identity that's different from yours. (This means a trait, belief, or characteristic different from you.)
requirements.req_text: With your parent or guardian's approval, connect with another Scout or youth your own age who has an identity that's different from yours. (This means a trait, belief, or characteristic different from you.) (a) Share with each other what makes the different aspects of your identity meaningful/special to you (b) Share with each other ONE of the following options: (1) Option 1, A time you felt excluded from a group: What was the situation? How did it make you feel? What did you do? Did anyone stand up for you? What did you learn? Would you do anything differently today? (2) Option 2, This imaginary situation: You're attending a new school and don't know anyone there yet. You notice they dress very differently than you do. At lunchtime, you decide you'll try to sit with a group to get to know other students. People at two tables tell you there is someone sitting at the currently empty seat at their table, so you end up eating by yourself. Discuss: How would that make you feel? What could the students have done? If that happened at your school, what would you do? (c) Discuss with your counselor what you learned from the discussion with the other Scout or youth.

Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion Principle 2: Citizenship in Society Sub-Req 7b: Discuss with your counselor what you learned and how you can apply it in your life (p. 40).

Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion Principle 3: Identify and interview an individual in your community, school, and/or Scouting who has had a significant positive impact in promoting diversity, equity (p. 40).

Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion Principle 4: If you feel your community, school, or local Scouting group does not have such an individual, then research a historical figure who meets these criteria (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion Preparation): Inspect the workspace, reference materials, and safety controls required for Citizenship in Society Requirement 7 (p. 34).

Step 2 (Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion Execution): Apply the official Citizenship in Society pamphlet method for Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion while recording observations in your Scout Workbook (p. 34).

Step 3 (Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion Buddy Check): Cross-check your Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion technique, measurements, and results with a patrol buddy using the EDGE method (p. 34).

Step 4 (Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion Verification): Review your completed Community & Historical Leaders in Inclusion evidence and demonstrate proficiency during your counselor conference (p. 34).

requirements.req_text: Scouting strives to develop young people to be future leaders in their workplaces, schools, and community environments. As you look at your current involvement in school, your family, Scouting, your job, and/or community, think about how you can have a positive impact in diversity, equity, and inclusion. (a) Describe your ideas on how you can and will support others with different identities to feel included and heard at your school, workplace, and/or social settings in your community. (b) Explain how including diverse thoughts and opinions from others with different identities can: Make your interactions more positive. Help everyone benefit by considering different opinions. (c) Give three examples of how limiting diverse input can be harmful. (d) Give three examples of how considering diverse opinions can lead to innovation and success.

pamphlet_excerpts: Citizenship in The Community Means: Public policy includes the goals the government sets as well as theactions required to achieve those goals (p. 10).
Citizenship in The Community Means Principle 2: Some citizens do notvote, voluntarily giving up their voice in the government (p. 10).

Citizenship in The Community Means Principle 3: Other citizens do not know or care about what is going on in their community, until a prison is built in their neighborhood, orthe crime rate grows (p. 10).
Citizenship in The Community Means Principle 4: Unless they are upset about a particularissue, most citizens leave the decisions to elected representatives and local activists (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Citizenship in The Community Means): People who feel connected to their community tend toparticipate (p. 10).
Step 2 (Citizenship in The Community Means): The more active citizens are in their community, withties to a school, youth groups, businesses, and service clubs, the more interest they (p. 10).
Step 3 (Citizenship in The Community Means): Thatis why longtime residents often hold local offices (p. 10).
Step 4 (Citizenship in The Community Means): You have a chance now to build connections in your own community (p. 10).

pamphlet_excerpts: Using an electronic mapping tool: Organization of one typical county government Municipalities A charter is aformal, legaldocument thatdefines theboundaries of acity (p. 14).
Using an electronic mapping tool Principle 2: Municipalities (cities, towns, villages, and boroughs) aredensely populated urban areas with local governments (p. 14).
Using an electronic mapping tool Principle 3: The state creates them by charters or other legislation, which thenserve as local constitutions (p. 14).
Using an electronic mapping tool Principle 4: Municipal governments are organized according to their charters (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Using an electronic mapping tool): The most widely used form of city government is themayor-council charter (p. 14).
Step 2 (Using an electronic mapping tool): Voters elect a mayor as the chief executive and a council as its legislature (p. 14).
Step 3 (Using an electronic mapping tool): For cities larger than 5,000 people, the average size of a city council is seven members, buthuge cities like New York City may have as many (p. 14).
Step 4 (Using an electronic mapping tool): Depending on how many formal powers are given to the mayor, the mayor-council form of government often isdescribed as a "strong-mayor (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: Constitution of The United States: Amendments to the Constitution The Constitution is a flexible document that adapts to thechanging needs of American society (p. 18).
Constitution of The United States Principle 2: Since the Bill of Rightswas adopted, the Constitution has been amended 17 times (p. 18).
Constitution of The United States Principle 3: The 11th Amendment (1795) prohibits a citizen of onestate or a citizen of another country from suing another statein federal court (p. 18).
Constitution of The United States Principle 4: However, a citizen may file suit in federalcourt against state authorities for depriving that person of constitutional rights (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Constitution of The United States): The 12th Amendment (1804) requires members of the Electoral College to cast two separate ballots: one for president and one for vice president (p. 18).
Step 2 (Constitution of The United States): When the Founding Fathers wrote Article II of the Constitution, they planned one election for bothpresident and vice president (p. 18).
Step 3 (Constitution of The United States): Electors each hadtwo votes to cast for two people without specifying the office (p. 18).
Step 4 (Constitution of The United States): The person with the most votes becamepresident and the runner-up became vice president (p. 18).

Purposes for Creating Principle 2: Six purposes for creating the United Principle 2: Since the Bill of Rightswas adopted, the Constitution has been amended 17 times (p. 18).

Purposes for Creating Principle 3: Six purposes for creating the United Principle 3: The 11th Amendment (1795) prohibits a citizen of onestate or a citizen of another country from suing another statein federal court (p. 18).

Purposes for Creating Principle 4: Six purposes for creating the United Principle 4: However, a citizen may file suit in federalcourt against state authorities for depriving that person of constitutional rights (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Purposes for Creating): Step 1 (Six purposes for creating the United): The 12th Amendment (1804) requires members of the Electoral College to cast two separate ballots: one for president and one for vice president (p. 18).

Step 2 (Purposes for Creating): Step 2 (Six purposes for creating the United): When the Founding Fathers wrote Article II of the Constitution, they planned one election for bothpresident and vice president (p. 18).
Step 3 (Purposes for Creating): Step 3 (Six purposes for creating the United): Electors each hadtwo votes to cast for two people without specifying the office (p. 18).
Step 4 (Purposes for Creating): Step 4 (Six purposes for creating the United): The person with the most votes becamepresident and the runner-up became vice president (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Branches of The United States: Three Branches of The United: This separation of powers and system of checks and balances prevented any one branch from becomingtoo powerful (p. 27).

Branches of The United States Principle 2: Three Branches of The United Principle 2: The Constitution established a bicameral (two-chamber) legislature consisting of the Senate and the House of Representativesso that one chamber (p. 27).
Branches of The United States Principle 3: Three Branches of The United Principle 3: The Senatehas 100 members; two senators are elected from each state (p. 27).

Branches of The United States Principle 4: Three Branches of The United Principle 4: The House of Representatives has 435 members; the number of representatives from each state is based on the population of the state according (p. 27).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Branches of The United States): Step 1 (Three Branches of The United): The Constitution does not fix the number of members in the House of Representatives, instead allowing Congress to determine the total (p. 27).
Step 2 (Branches of The United States): Step 2 (Three Branches of The United): As the population of the United States increased, so did the number of House members (p. 27).

Step 3 (Branches of The United States): Step 3 (Three Branches of The United): Congress worried that adding more memberswould cripple the ability to do business in the House, so it passed the Reapportionment Act (p. 27).
Step 4 (Branches of The United States): Step 4 (Three Branches of The United): Boundaries of congressional districts are redrawn to keep the populations of voting districts equal (p. 27).

pamphlet_excerpts: Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard: Amendments to the Constitution The Constitution is a flexible document that adapts to thechanging needs of American society (p. 15).
Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard Principle 2: Since the Bill of Rightswas adopted, the Constitution has been amended 17 times (p. 15).
Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard Principle 3: The 11th Amendment (1795) prohibits a citizen of onestate or a citizen of another country from suing another statein federal court (p. 15).
Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard Principle 4: However, a citizen may file suit in federalcourt against state authorities for depriving that person of constitutional rights (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard): The 12th Amendment (1804) requires members of the Electoral College to cast two separate ballots: one for president and one for vice president (p. 15).
Step 2 (Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard): When the Founding Fathers wrote Article II of the Constitution, they planned one election for bothpresident and vice president (p. 15).
Step 3 (Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard): Electors each hadtwo votes to cast for two people without specifying the office (p. 15).
Step 4 (Citizenship in the Nation Core Field Standard): The person with the most votes becamepresident and the runner-up became vice president (p. 15).

pamphlet_excerpts: Watch the national evening news: As you watch the evening news on television or read a newspaper, consider how the national issues covered relate to whatyou have already read (p. 41).
Watch the national evening news Principle 2: Do thetopics affect a citizen's rights and freedoms (p. 41).
Watch the national evening news Principle 3: Are the senators and the presidentdeadlocked over an issue like health care or Social Security (p. 41).
Watch the national evening news Principle 4: Did the Supreme Court rule on a controversial case (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Watch the national evening news): In countries where freedom of the press and the right tofree speech do not exist, the government controls mass media (p. 41).
Step 2 (Watch the national evening news): Citizens know only what their leaders are willing to tell them (p. 41).
Step 3 (Watch the national evening news): But in the United States, citizens have the right to know the truth (p. 41).
Step 4 (Watch the national evening news): If you want your opinion and your vote to matter, you must make consistent efforts to seek information (p. 41).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Visit a place that is listed as a National Historic Landmark or that is on the National Register of Historic Places. Tell your counselor what you learned about the landmark or site and what you found interesting about it. (b) Tour your state capitol building or the U. S. Capitol. Tell your counselor what you learned about the capitol, its function, and the history. (c) Tour a federal facility. Explain to your counselor what you saw and what you learned about its function in the local community and how it serves this nation. (d) Choose a United States national monument that interests you. Using books, brochures, the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission), and other resources, find out more about the monument. Tell your counselor what you learned, and explain why the monument is important to this country's citizens.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Representatives in The United States): Step 1 (Name your representatives in the United): You can write a letter online orsend a letter by mail (p. 14).

Step 3 (Representatives in The United States): Step 3 (Name your representatives in the United): The Honorable John Smith The greeting: Dear Senator Smith: Member of the House of Representatives The address: The Honorable Mary Doe The greeting: Dear (p. 14).

Step 4 (Representatives in The United States): Step 4 (Name your representatives in the United): Senators and representatives want to know what youthink, but they receive thousands of letters each month (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: Citizenship in the world means: The Declaration of Independence is a unique contractbetween citizens and government (p. 13).
Citizenship in the world means Principle 2: Governments are instituted among Men, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed (p. 13).
Citizenship in the world means Principle 3: The right to a free trial, for example, obligates U. S. citizens to serve on juries (p. 13).
Citizenship in the world means Principle 4: The right to vote obligates them to be informed about important issues and the candidates' positions (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Citizenship in the world means): Because the government rules with the consent of the citizens, Americans must understand and exercise their constitutional rights, or risk (p. 13).
Step 2 (Citizenship in the world means): In the United States, serving on a jury when called is a civic duty; it is also one way that the right to a free trial is protected (p. 13).
Step 3 (Citizenship in the world means): U. S. citizens live in an open society where it is safe to think outloud (p. 13).
Step 4 (Citizenship in the world means): We freely express our opinions, exchange ideas, and evendisagree in public (p. 13).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Explain international law and how it differs from national law. Explain the role of international law and how international law can be used as a tool for conflict resolution. (b) Using resources such as major daily newspapers, the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission), and news magazines, observe a current issue that involves international trade, foreign exchange, balance of payments, tariffs, and free trade. Explain what you have learned. Include in your discussion an explanation of why countries must cooperate in order for world trade and global competition to thrive. (c) Select TWO of the following organizations and describe their role in the world. (1) United Nations and United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) (2) International Court of Justice (The World Court) (3) International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) (4) World Organization of the Scout Movement (5) World Health Organization (WHO) (6) Amnesty International (7) International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) (8) Cooperative for American Relief Everywhere (CARE) (9) European Union

Step 3 (International law and how it differs): In more than 60 countries around the world, CAREprovides food, disaster aid, health care training, self-help development programs, and economic (p. 64).
Step 4 (International law and how it differs): As an independent organization, CARE partners with other humanitariangroups and builds relationships with governments to influencepolicy (p. 64).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (A government is represented abroad): A visa is a permit to enter another country and must be issued by the country one wishes to enter (p. 85).
Step 2 (A government is represented abroad): It is a specialseal stamped on a valid passport that indicates an official of that country has approved the visit (p. 85).
Step 3 (A government is represented abroad): Prior to leaving, thetraveler should apply for avisa, if required by thatparticular country, at theappropriate foreign embassyor nearest (p. 85).

Step 4 (A government is represented abroad): An alien (foreignnational) wishing to enter the United States must apply for a visa outside the United States at embassies and consulates worldwide (p. 85).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following (with your parent or guardian's permission) and share with your counselor what you have learned:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following (with your parent or guardian's permission) and share with your counselor what you have learned: (a) Visit the website of the U. S. State Department. Learn more about an issue you find interesting that is discussed on this website. (b) Visit the website of an international news organization or foreign government, OR examine a foreign newspaper available at your local library, bookstore, or newsstand. Find a news story about a human right realized in the United States that is not recognized in another country. (c) Visit with a student or Scout from another country and discuss the typical values, holidays, ethnic foods, and traditions practiced or enjoyed there. (d) Attend or participate in a World Organization of the Scouting Movement (WOSM) event such as the World Scout Jamboree, World Scout Moot, World Scout Congress, Jamboree Over The Air, or Jamboree Over The Internet. Attendance at a national or regional Jamboree sponsored by a WOSM-National Scout Organization is also allowed. (e) Participate in or attend an international event in your area, such as an ethnic festival, concert, or play.

(c) Identify the conditions that must exist before performing CPR on a person.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Dehydration, caused by lack of water in the body, can occur in cold orwarm weather, anytime a person is sweating profusely and/or notdrinking enough (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Avoid dehydration by drinking plenty of fluids andeating enough throughout the day to keep your body well-balanced (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: If youbecome weary or develop a headache or body aches, or if you becomeconfused, rest in the shade and sip water until the symptoms subside (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: If the freezing continues, the area will stiffen andbecome grayish-white in color (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): To treat the victim, thaw theaffected area only if there is no risk of refreezing (p. 28).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Put cold fingers under the armpit and the warm palm of your hand on frostbitten nose, ears, or cheeks (p. 28).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In a shelter, if possible, put cold feet on a companion's barebelly, or immerse the affected area in lukewarm water, nowarmer than 108 degrees (p. 28).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If blisters develop, apply a large steriledressing (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying: Present yourself properly dressed for belaying: Webbing designed for climbing is available in avariety of sizes, lengths, and materials such asnylon, Spectra, and Dyneema (p. 49).

Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying Principle 2: Present yourself properly dressed for belaying Principle 2: Tubularwebbing (usually 1") is used to form tied-seatharnesses; for anchors used by belayers andrappellers; and for other uses in climbing, rappelling (p. 49).
Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying Principle 3: Present yourself properly dressed for belaying Principle 3: A piece of webbing can be tied into a loop known as a runner with a water knot (p. 49).

Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying Principle 4: Present yourself properly dressed for belaying Principle 4: Webbing can be purchasedas a runner or sling and is pre-sewn by the Belayers use tubular webbing tomanufacturer (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying): Step 1 (Present yourself properly dressed for belaying): Climbers use runners, oranchor themselves securely (p. 49).

Step 2 (Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying): Step 2 (Present yourself properly dressed for belaying): Like all climbing rope, all webbing can beharmed by friction, dirt, and long exposure tosunlight or harsh weather (p. 49).
Step 3 (Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying): Step 3 (Present yourself properly dressed for belaying): Dispose of webbing that shows any sign of damage or that has anunknown history (p. 49).

Step 4 (Yourself Properly Dressed for Belaying): Step 4 (Present yourself properly dressed for belaying): Take time to store equipment correctly so that it will last longer and be in good shape the next time youwant to use (p. 49).

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Core Field Standard: Whenever you are climbing, rappelling, or belaying onrock faces, wear a helmet that has been specifically designed for climbing (p. 42).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 2: A helmet will protect your head against stones and debris falling from above, and may prevent injuries if youcollide with a rock face during a fall (p. 42).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 3: A chin strap helps keep aclimber's helmet from falling off or shifting (p. 42).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 4: The helmets, hardware, and ropes used for climbing, rappelling, and belaying have been developedover more than 150 years of mountaineering (p. 42).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Core Field Standard): The UIAA (Union Internationale des Associations d'Alpinisme) is a group of mountain-travelexperts who set standards and testing procedures (p. 42).
Step 2 (Climbing Core Field Standard): The CE (Conformité Européenne, which translates to European Community) maintains similar standards for excellence (p. 42).
Step 3 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Allropes, harnesses, helmets, and hardware used by Scouts for climbing, rappelling, and belaying must bespecifically designed for climbing (p. 42).
Step 4 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Wear a properly fittedhelmet when climbing above shoulder height whether you are on a rock face, tower, or artificial wall (p. 42).

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Core Field Standard: For tying together the ends of two ropes, the most reliable knotis the double fisherman's knot (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 2: It can also be used to secure the ends of a piece of cord to form a runner (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 3: Half of a doublefisherman's knot (also known as a barrel knot) can be used as a stopper knot at the end of a rope (p. 53).
Climbing Core Field Standard Principle 4: Lay about 2 feet of the ends of two ropes alongside oneanother, ends opposite (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Loosely loop one rope end twice around the other, then thread the end of that rope through the loops (p. 53).
Step 2 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Carefully tighten the two parts of the knot, then slide them (p. 53).
Step 3 (Climbing Core Field Standard): If they don't fit together neatly, the knot is incorrectly tied (p. 53).
Step 4 (Climbing Core Field Standard): The knot is commonlytied with accessory cord by a climber to ascend a rope or to secure abelay system in order to release the belayer (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Harness, Helmet and Gloves: Using a harness that fits properly helpsmake climbing and rappelling safer, morecomfortable, and fun (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 2: Commercially made climbing harnesses usually require only thatyou put your legs through leg loops and then secure the waiststrap with a buckle (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 3: The leg loops of some harnesses can beadjusted; you should just be able to slip two fingers between theloop and your thigh (p. 57).

Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 4: If the harnesses available to you are notadjustable, you will need to choose one that fits your body snuglybut not tight enough to restrict circulation (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): A 30-foot length of nylon tubular webbing can be wrappedaround your body and tied in special ways to form a reliabletied harness for climbing (p. 57).
Step 2 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): Each tied harness must be tied exactly rightevery time to ensure your safety (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Directly Belay Rope: Climbing: Verbal Signals for Climbers and Belayers Verbal signals allow a climber and a belayer to communicate and worktogether as a team even if they cannot (p. 65).
Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 2: Climbing Principle 2: Get in the habit ofusing verbal signals every time you are climbing or belaying (p. 65).

Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 3: Climbing Principle 3: Arrange the rope so that your stronger hand (usually your right hand if you are right-handed) will be the brake hand, thehand closest to the free end (p. 65).
Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 4: Climbing Principle 4: Exchange verbalsignals (see the boxed text later in this chapter) with a climber (p. 65).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 1 (Climbing): As the climber ascends, pull through the belay device any slack that forms in the rope, and let the loose rope pile up next to your feet (p. 65).
Step 2 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 2 (Climbing): While holding the rope firmly with your brake hand, slideyour guide hand out along the rope (p. 65).
Step 3 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 3 (Climbing): Keeping slack in the rope to a minimum will limit thelength of a fall if the climber slips (p. 65).
Step 4 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 4 (Climbing): Running the rope through a belay deviceallows a belayer to stop a fall easily, justby moving the belay rope to one side (p. 65).

Step 4 (Ways to store rope, hardware): Wear a properly fittedhelmet when climbing above shoulder height whether you are on a rock face, tower, or artificial wall (p. 42).

pamphlet_excerpts: Different Ways to Store: Three Different Ways to Store: A modern gold ingot Before people used coins inexchange for goods, they traded with hand-fashioned gold andsilver pieces called ingots (p. 21).
Different Ways to Store Principle 2: Three Different Ways to Store Principle 2: Thesevaried in size and shape as well as in value (p. 21).
Different Ways to Store Principle 3: Three Different Ways to Store Principle 3: At every transaction, the merchant or trader had toweigh each ingot and verify that the metal was genuine (p. 21).
Different Ways to Store Principle 4: Three Different Ways to Store Principle 4: Later, ingots were stamped with aseal that verified the weight, contents, and purity of themetal (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Different Ways to Store): Step 1 (Three Different Ways to Store): People realized that itwas much easier to do business with stamped ingots (p. 21).
Step 2 (Different Ways to Store): Step 2 (Three Different Ways to Store): The most famous of these first coins are from the Greek kingdom of Lydia (locatedin modern-day western Turkey) (p. 21).

Step 3 (Different Ways to Store): Step 3 (Three Different Ways to Store): They are made of electrum (a natural alloy of gold and silver) and carry a stamped lion'shead on the obverse and crude markings on the reverse (p. 21).

Step 4 (Different Ways to Store): Step 4 (Three Different Ways to Store): Coins made of electrum did not alwayscontain equal portions of gold and silver, so the value among coins differed even if the weights were equal (p. 21).

requirements.req_text: Do the following and explain to your counselor the design features, designer name, designer initials, and where to find them for each item: (a) Collect a one-cent coin from the year group: 1959-2008 (that is, dated between 1959 and 2008) and a one-cent coin from the year group 2010-present. Explain how and why the one-cent coins issued in 2009 were different from either of the other two year groups. (b) Collect two five-cent coins, one from each of these year groups: 1959-2003 and 2006-present. Explain how and why the five-cent coins issued in 2004-2005 were different from either of the other two year groups. (c) Collect a ten-cent coin from 1965-present. (d) Collect a twenty-five-cent coin from 1965-1998, two examples from the 50-State Quarter®/territories Program 1999-2009, two designs from the America the Beautiful® program 2010-2021 and two designs from the American Women Quarter® program (2022-2024). Explain the purpose of each of those programs. (e) Collect a half dollar coin from 1965-present. (f) Collect a dollar coin from each of the following design groups: Susan B. Anthony (1979-1981, 1999); Sacagawea (2000-2008); and U. S. Presidents (2007-2016, 2020).
