pamphlet_excerpts: Match A Fly Rod Line: Lines vary by weight, and must be matched to the rod (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 2: They come in different styles (called tapers) and colors and are designed either to float on the surface of the water or to sink to different depths (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 3: Intermediate lines, for example, sink very slowly and can be fished just below the surface (p. 13).
Match A Fly Rod Line Principle 4: Heavily weighted lines sinkquite rapidly and are designed to get down deep very quickly (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Match A Fly Rod Line): Most fly-fishing is done with floating lines, which are the easiest to cast and control (p. 13).
Step 2 (Match A Fly Rod Line): But there are times and conditions whenfish lie deeply in the water and are not feeding at or near the surface (p. 13).
Step 3 (Match A Fly Rod Line): A sinking line is then useful to get the fly down to them (p. 13).
Step 4 (Match A Fly Rod Line): Sinking lines usuallycome in drab, darker colors so that the fish cannot spot them (p. 13).

Step 4 (Tie Proper Knots to Prepare): Attach the backing to the reel spool with an arbor knot (p. 24).

pamphlet_excerpts: Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders: Use these flies to catch trout, bass andpanfish on the water's surface (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 2: Traditional trout flies that float are called dry flies (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 3: They aredesigned to imitate the adultforms of mayflies, caddis flies, and other insects that trout and other fish feed (p. 38).
Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders Principle 4: Anglers usedry flies to catch fish that arefeeding on surface-hatchinginsects (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): The dry flies are tied inpatterns to look like the specificspecies of insect (p. 38).
Step 2 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): This is calledmatching the hatch, and itis one of the most importantprinciples in fishing (p. 38).
Step 3 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): If you seefish feeding on a specific insectthen you should use a fly thatclosely imitates this food source (p. 38).
Step 4 (Essential Fly-Fishing Knots and Leaders): In addition to shape, color andmovement, the size of the fly isalso important when matching the hatch (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: Ability to Cast A Fly: A large plastichoop (such as a hula hoop) makes anexcellent target for practicingcasting (p. 33).
Ability to Cast A Fly Principle 2: Make sure your thumb is on top of therod's cork grip and that you have a firm hold (p. 33).
Ability to Cast A Fly Principle 3: Now, strip out 20 to 30 feet of line from the reel (p. 33).
Ability to Cast A Fly Principle 4: You might want to make a mark 30 feet from the line tip, using a waterproof marker (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ability to Cast A Fly): With that length of line in front of you, more or less in a straight line, start with the rod tip down near the ground orthe surface of the water (p. 33).
Step 2 (Ability to Cast A Fly): Smoothly accelerate the rod through the vertical, or 12 o'clock, position and then stop it abruptly (p. 33).
Step 3 (Ability to Cast A Fly): This loads the rod like a spring and then vigorously launches the fly line up and behind (p. 33).
Step 4 (Ability to Cast A Fly): The line will soar up and behind you in a loop that willquickly straighten (p. 33).

intro_notes: NOTE: Scouts must remember to follow the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code while on field trips and when collecting specimens. Make sure you have permission of the land manager prior to taking any samples for your collection. Collecting is prohibited in most National and State Parks. Pictures or sketches may suffice for a collection and limit impacted disturbances. NOTE: The official merit badge pamphlets are now free and downloadable HERE or can be purchased at the Scout Shop.

pamphlet_excerpts: Collect and identify wood samples: Whatever its origins, damage from certain insects, diseases, fires, and invasive species often can be reduced if the forest is healthy (p. 28).
Collect and identify wood samples Principle 2: Pieces of wood are valuable in identifying and understanding the trees from which they came (p. 28).

Collect and identify wood samples Principle 3: Appearance, color, grain, texture, weight, general feel, and sometimes even the aroma of a wood all are clues to its growing patterns, strengths (p. 28).
Collect and identify wood samples Principle 4: Each year during the spring and summer, most trees increasetheir diameter by adding two new layers of wood (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Collect and identify wood samples): The layer formed by the cambium in the spring grows quickly (p. 28).
Step 2 (Collect and identify wood samples): Because the cells are large, this springwood looks light in color (p. 28).
Step 3 (Collect and identify wood samples): Because the cells are smaller, this summerwood appears darker (p. 28).
Step 4 (Collect and identify wood samples): When a tree is cut or a core sample taken, the light anddark layers show as alternating rings of light and dark wood (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Contributions forests: Forests are among Earth's great filters for cleansing the atmosphere and replenishing it with oxygen (p. 45).
Contributions forests Principle 2: Carbon dioxide is also producedwhen plants and animals decay and when wood, coal, gasoline, and other carbon-based materials burn (p. 45).
Contributions forests Principle 3: Plants must absorb carbon dioxide in order to survive (p. 45).
Contributions forests Principle 4: In achemical reaction charged with sunlight, chlorophyll allows plants to combine water with carbon dioxide to produce the simplesugars plants use (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Contributions forests): The process is called photosynthesis, making something with the aid of light (p. 45).
Step 2 (Contributions forests): A by-product of photosynthesis is the oxygen animals need for survival (p. 45).
Step 3 (Contributions forests): Plants absorbing carbon dioxide can store it, a process calledsequestration, and slow its return to the atmosphere (p. 45).
Step 4 (Contributions forests): Carbon is storedin a tree's trunk and roots, and in the soil of a forest (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Forest management means: The main treatments making up silvicultural systemsinvolve the felling of trees and the regeneration of a new forest for the future (p. 55).
Forest management means Principle 2: Systems that result in trees of approximately the same age are called even-aged systems (p. 55).
Forest management means Principle 3: Systems that result in trees of many ages are termed uneven-aged systems (p. 55).
Forest management means Principle 4: Each system includes steps to establish seedlings and actions to encourage the health andproductivity of a developing stand (p. 55).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Forest management means): Some tree species grow bestin an even-aged forest, while others grow best in uneven-agedstands (p. 55).
Step 2 (Forest management means): Clear-cutting is the harvesting of alltrees in an area except those that are necessary to maintainwater quality, fish habitat (p. 55).
Step 3 (Forest management means): The clear-cut can then be regenerated by broadcastingseeds, from sprouts, or by planting seedlings (p. 55).
Step 4 (Forest management means): The new trees will have equal access to sunlight (p. 55).

requirements.lead_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a managed public or private forest area with the manager or a forester who is familiar with it. Write a brief report describing the type of forest, the management objectives, and the forestry techniques used to achieve the objectives. (b) With a knowledgeable individual, visit a current or past logging operation or wood-using manufacturing plant. Write a brief report describing the following: (1) The species and size of trees harvested or used (2) The origin of the forest or stands of trees utilized (e. g., planted or natural) (3) The forest's successional stage, its future, and, if it is a past logging operation, the regeneration that is occurring, whether planted or natural (4) Where the trees are coming from (land ownership) or where they are going (type of mill or processing plant) (5) The products that are made from the trees (6) How the products are made and used (7) How waste materials from the logging operation or manufacturing plant are or were disposed of or utilized (c) Take part in a forest-fire prevention campaign in cooperation with your local fire warden, state wildfire agency, forester, or counselor. Write a brief report describing the campaign, how it will help prevent wildfires, and your part in it.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 1 (Do ONE of The Following): Get permission in advance if you want to take photographs during your visit (p. 71).

Step 2 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 2 (Do ONE of The Following): Do some research on the forest, loggingoperation, or manufacturing plant you plan to visit, and think about some of the questions you wantanswered (p. 71).

Step 3 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 3 (Do ONE of The Following): In a managed forest, for example, you can find out about the management objectives and the forestry techniques used to achieve thoseobjectives (p. 71).

Step 4 (Managed Public or Private Forest): Step 4 (Do ONE of The Following): You might also research or ask about the species of trees grown, the silvicultural systemused, or whether replanting is done with seedlingsor seeds (p. 71).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Your merit badge counselor and parents can helpyou arrange a visit to a managed forest, a loggingoperation, or a manufacturing plant that useswood (p. 75).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: You can see for yourself how the work of forestry is carried (p. 75).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: You also will haveopportunities to visit with forestry professionals andlearn more about their backgrounds, training, andresponsibilities (p. 75).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Plan the trip well in advance so that the forestry professionals will have time to prepare for your visit (p. 75).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Get permission in advance if you want to take photographs during your visit (p. 75).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Do some research on the forest, loggingoperation, or manufacturing plant you plan to visit, and think about some of the questions you wantanswered (p. 75).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In a managed forest, for example, you can find out about the management objectives and the forestry techniques used to achieve thoseobjectives (p. 75).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): You might also research or ask about the species of trees grown, the silvicultural systemused, or whether replanting is done with seedlingsor seeds (p. 75).

Terms for Game Analysis Principle 2: The following terms, difficulty, balance, depth, complexity, pace, replay value, and age appropriateness, describe the nature of the play experience (p. 49).
Terms for Game Analysis Principle 3: They are useful tools forcomparing different games (p. 49).
Terms for Game Analysis Principle 4: Difficulty describes how easy or hard it is for a player tocomplete a game objective (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Terms for Game Analysis): As a designer, you can adjust gamedifficulty in many ways (p. 49).
Step 2 (Terms for Game Analysis): Electronic games often have settings, such as novice, standard, and expert, that adjust difficulty bychanging the strength of the player (p. 49).
Step 3 (Terms for Game Analysis): Board gamesor card games may include a second, simpler set of rules fornew players (p. 49).
Step 4 (Terms for Game Analysis): Balance is a description of the relative strength of differentresources, mechanics, objectives, or starting states (p. 49).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Pick a game where the players can change the rules or objectives (examples: basketball, hearts, chess, kickball). Briefly summarize the standard rules and objectives and play through the game normally. (b) Propose changes to several rules or objectives. Predict how each change will affect gameplay. (c) Play the game with one rule or objective change, observing how the players' actions and emotional experiences are affected by the rule change. Repeat this process with two other changes. (d) Explain to your counselor how the changes affected the actions and experience of the players. Discuss the accuracy of your predictions.

Change at least one rule, mechanic, or objective from your first version of the game, and describe why you are making the change. Play the game again. Record in your game design notebook whether or not your change had the expected effect. (c) Repeat 6(b) at least two more times and record the results in your game design notebook.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Blind test your game): Begin a playtesting session by handing the testers any rules orinstruction sheets that you have written to go with the prototypecomponents (p. 82).

Step 3 (Blind test your game): During the playtest, if the players get confusedby the rules or stuck, they should make up whatever rules theyneed for play to continue (p. 82).
Step 4 (Blind test your game): This is what would happen if someonebought a new board or card game and the rules were confusingor incomplete (p. 82).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers and Professional Pathways: Work within the game industry is not a career everyone can pursue no matter how hard they try, but that does not meangame design cannot be incorporated (p. 23).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 2: Comingup with a fun, exciting, and balanced ruleset is a good skill tohave in almost any career (p. 23).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 3: Teachers can employ game elements in the classroom to make learning a more engaging, participatoryexperience (p. 23).
Careers and Professional Pathways Principle 4: You can also use the psychology of rewarding tasks to get yourself to do things you would not normally want (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers and Professional Pathways): If you have a game that you want to pitch to a publisher, rememberthese tips. • Show your best, mostfinished, and most ofall fun game (p. 23).
Step 2 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Makesure that the testers arehaving a blast whenthey play your game (p. 23).
Step 3 (Careers and Professional Pathways): Be prepared to hand over all the game design documentation. • Nondisclosure Agreements (NDAs) protect you and your game idea (p. 23).
Step 4 (Careers and Professional Pathways): It is good practice to get anyone who is looking at your game to signan NDA (p. 23).

Step 3 (Honeybees Are Used in Pollinating): First, they practice what biologists call flower fidelity (p. 59).
Step 4 (Honeybees Are Used in Pollinating): That is, on a foraging trip they visit only one kind of flower sothat when they transfer pollen it is to a flower that can use (p. 59).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following and record weekly observations. Discuss the results of your project with your counselor. (a) Build a compost bin and maintain it for 90 days. (b) Build a vermicompost bin (worm compost bin) and maintain it for 90 days. (c) Build a hydroponic garden containing three vegetables or herbs, or three ornamental plants. Maintain this garden through harvest or flowering, or for 90 days. (d) Build one water garden, either in a container (at least 12 by 6 inches and 6 inches deep), or in the ground as a small, decorative pond no larger than 6 by 3 feet and 24 inches deep. Maintain the water garden for 90 days. (e) Prepare a honey super for use on a hive or colony. Remove a filled honey super from the hive or colony and prepare the honey for sale. (f) Grow a garden of your own using soil from seed or plantings to harvest or for 90 days, whichever is earlier. This can be an outdoor garden or indoors using appropriate containers, and should include at least three types of plants approved by your counselor.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in gardening. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (b) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in gardening to pursue a personal hobby and/or healthy lifestyle. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

pamphlet_excerpts: You Have Learned: Then you must know where to go tofind accurate answers (p. 17).
You Have Learned Principle 2: If your family moved to the United States from another country, it is important to askyour parents or guardians and other relatives (p. 17).
You Have Learned Principle 3: Even if you are not formally interviewing allthese people, write down or record the information they tell (p. 17).
You Have Learned Principle 4: Not all the information someone tells you is necessarilycorrect (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (You Have Learned): Relationships (such as great-uncle Ralph was Grandpa Erickson's brother) are usually correct (p. 17).
Step 2 (You Have Learned): But names, places, and dates may not be accurate (p. 17).
Step 3 (You Have Learned): Double-check the information you gather against other records (p. 17).
Step 4 (You Have Learned): It can be fun to talk to them and discover what they have and to hear what they know (p. 17).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in geocaching activities, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Discuss first aid and prevention for the types of injuries or illnesses that could occur while participating in geocaching activities, including cuts, scrapes, snakebite, insect stings, tick bites, exposure to poisonous plants, heat and cold reactions (sunburn, heatstroke, heat exhaustion, hypothermia), and dehydration. (c) Discuss how to properly plan an activity that uses GPS, including using the buddy system, sharing your plan with others, and considering the weather, route, and proper attire.

pamphlet_excerpts: Global Positioning System GPS Works: GPS technology can beused anywhere in the world 24 hours a day because the system ofsatellites circles Earth all the time, and some number of them (p. 11).
Global Positioning System GPS Works Principle 2: The system works in any kind of weather anddoes not require any setup fee or subscription charge (p. 11).
Global Positioning System GPS Works Principle 3: A GPS receiver (GPSr) calculates its position by carefully timing thesignals sent by the 24 to 30 GPS satellites high above Earth (p. 11).
Global Positioning System GPS Works Principle 4: At anygiven time, there are usually several satellites over any given placeon Earth (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): Each satellite continually transmits data that indicates itslocation and the current time (p. 11).
Step 2 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): All GPS satellites transmit signals at the same instant, but the signals arrive at a GPS receiver at slightlydifferent times (p. 11).
Step 3 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): The farther the receiver is from a satellite, thelonger the signal takes to reach the receiver (p. 11).
Step 4 (Global Positioning System GPS Works): The receiver uses the arrival time of each signal to measure the distance to each satellite (p. 11).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) If a Cache to Eagle® series exists in your council, visit at least three of the locations in the series. Describe the projects that each cache you visit highlights, and explain how the Cache to Eagle® program helps share our Scouting service with the public. (b) Create a Scouting-related Travel Bug® that promotes one of the values of Scouting. Release your Travel Bug into a public geocache and, with your parent or guardian's permission, monitor its progress at www. geocaching. com for 30 days. Keep a log, and share this with your counselor at the end of the 30-day period. (c) Set up and hide a public geocache, following the guidelines in the Geocaching merit badge pamphlet. Before doing so, share with your counselor a three-month maintenance plan for the geocache where you are personally responsible for those three months. After setting up the geocache, with your parent or guardian's permission, follow the logs online for 30 days and share them with your counselor. You must archive the geocache when you are no longer maintaining it. (d) Explain what Cache In Trash Out (CITO) means, and describe how you have practiced CITO at public geocaches or at a CITO event. Then, either create CITO containers to leave at public caches, or host a CITO event for your unit or for the public.

Make sure you have permission from the land manager prior to taking any samples for your collections. Collecting is prohibited in most National and State Parks. Consider purchasing from commercial rock and mineral shops or from home garden stores. Pictures or sketches may suffice for a collection and limit impacted disturbances. requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (b) Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site. (c) Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (d) Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site.

sub_requirements.text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. sub_requirements.label: (d)
sub_requirements.text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: Even if you are not interested in a career in geology, it is good to learn more about our Earth (p. 89).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Knowledge of geology makes Earth even more interesting (p. 89).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: To learn moreabout geologytake an earthscience coursein high school, or two or morecollege coursesin geology (p. 89).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Geology is a wide field with many career choices (p. 89).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Hydrogeologists help find water underground and can plan how much to use so you will not run (p. 89).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Many geologists are involved in the exploration of and/orthe production of natural resources, like oil and gas, coal, ironore, copper, gold (p. 89).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A professional geologist must earn at least a four-yearcollege degree (bachelor's degree) in geology, geophysics, environmental geology (p. 89).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): In manyfields a master's degree (two years beyond a bachelor's degree) may be necessary (p. 89).

pamphlet_excerpts: Safety on the golf course: You may have seen golfers lick the dirt off their golf ball so the ball will roll true or to hold a used tee in their mouth (p. 53).
Safety on the golf course Principle 2: Toxic substances on the courses may cling to the ball and tee (p. 53).
Safety on the golf course Principle 3: Theseinclude fertilizers, pesticides, weed killers, and animal excrement (p. 53).
Safety on the golf course Principle 4: Somegolfers who have a habit of cleaning their golf balls by licking themdevelop hepatitis, an inflammation of the liver (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safety on the golf course): It is best to always carry a towel in your golf bag and dampen it to wipe your ball clean (p. 53).
Step 2 (Safety on the golf course): There are a few first-aid issues that apply especially to golfers and golfing (p. 53).
Step 3 (Safety on the golf course): When we lose more water than we take in, we becomedehydrated (p. 53).
Step 4 (Safety on the golf course): Symptoms of mild dehydration include increasedthirst, dry lips, and dark yellow urine (p. 53).

requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you. (b) Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): Soon the days of using a simple Frisbee® graduated to the modern golf disc, with the triangular beveled-edge discpatented by Dave Dunipace in 1983 (p. 50).
Step 2 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): This disc provides theplayer a next-level experience (p. 50).
Step 3 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): With most of the disc'sweight in the rim, the golfdisc flies farther and moreaccurately, even in the wind (p. 50).
Step 4 (Traditional Golf / Disc Golf): Only one disc is needed to enjoy the game, but as playersimprove and get more active in thesport, a range of discs can come into play (p. 50).

pamphlet_excerpts: Differences Between Continuous Tone Line: The halftone dots are so small, the human eye cannot see the individual dots unless they are magnified, but the eye does see anoverall effect (p. 44).
Differences Between Continuous Tone Line Principle 2: The arrangement of the halftone dots creates this effect (p. 44).
Differences Between Continuous Tone Line Principle 3: The halftone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look dark are big and fill most of the halftone dot area (p. 44).
Differences Between Continuous Tone Line Principle 4: The halftone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look light are small and fill very little of thehalftone dot area (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): Generally, halftones are made from a continuous-toneimage, such as a traditional photograph (p. 44).
Step 2 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): In the past, thecontinuous-tone image was photographed through a specialscreen that created a halftone version of the original (p. 44).
Step 3 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): Today it is more common to take a continuous-tone image and scan it into a computer or to take a picture with a digital camera (p. 44).
Step 4 (Differences Between Continuous Tone Line): Thecomputer software then converts the digital file into a pattern ofsmall halftone dots that make up an image (p. 44).

requirements.lead_text: Produce the design you created for requirement 3 using one of the following printing processes:
requirements.req_text: Produce the design you created for requirement 3 using one of the following printing processes: (a) Offset lithography. Make a layout, and produce a plate using a process approved by your counselor. Run the plate and print at least 50 copies. (b) Screen printing. Make a hand-cut or photographic stencil and attach it to a screen that you have prepared. Mask the screen and print at least 20 copies. Resource: Screen Printing Tutorial (video) (c) Electronic/digital printing. Create a layout in electronic form, download it to the press or printer, and run 50 copies. If no electronic interface to the press or printer is available, you may print and scan a paper copy of the layout. (d) Relief printing. Create a layout in electronic form, download it to the press or printer, and run 50 copies. If no electronic interface to the press or printer is available, you may print and scan a paper copy of the layout.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Postpress Operations): Other methods of binding generally are for single-sheetprinted material, where each page is printed on a separatesheet (p. 73).

Step 3 (Postpress Operations): Spiral and plastic comb binding require the pages to bepunched with holes before the wire or plastic binding is applied (p. 73).
Step 4 (Postpress Operations): Stitching, a one-step operation using a thin wire called spoolwire, is the oldest of the methods and the most economical (p. 73).

pamphlet_excerpts: Careers & Professional Pathways: A binderysupervisor coordinates operationsin the bindery, schedules jobs, andsupervises and trains workers (p. 81).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: A binderyworker may prepare and tendone or more automated machines that do cutting, scoring, folding, stitching, taping, and gluing (p. 81).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: In large binderies, the work isdone on an assembly line, withworkers performing one or twotypes of tasks (p. 81).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: A perfect-binder setter sets up andcontrols a binding machine that gathers magazine or booksignatures, glues them, and adds the cover to magazines (p. 81).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A bookbinder handbinds books, usually working on special editions and custom binding, andrepairs old and rare books (p. 81).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Bookbinders learn by training with the relatively few experts in the field (p. 81).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 1 (Select three of the professions): In most states, the PA must have a formal workingarrangement with a physician in order to practice (p. 16).

Step 2 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 2 (Select three of the professions): Undergraduate education in a variety ofscience/health disciplines will prepare thestudent for the graduate program (p. 16).

Step 3 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 3 (Select three of the professions): Some PAprograms will require the applicant to havehad some experience in a health care setting (p. 16).
Step 4 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 4 (Select three of the professions): Hospital, outpatientclinics, community health clinics, private practices, and prisons (p. 16).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 1 (Select three of the professions): They may also provide radiation therapy treatments (p. 47).

Step 3 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 3 (Select three of the professions): Education: Courses include anatomy, radiologictechniques, patient positioning, equipment protocols, radiationphysics and radiation safety as well as basic patient care (p. 47).

Step 4 (Health Care Professions Careers and Pathways): Step 4 (Select three of the professions): Radiologic Technologists require four-year bachelor's degrees and Technicians require a two-year associate degree (p. 47).

Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): That is easy to do on hot summer days when you arethirsty (p. 48).

pamphlet_excerpts: Hiking is an aerobic activity: Setting off on a hike without properly preparing can havedisastrous results (p. 33).
Hiking is an aerobic activity Principle 2: Make sure you are ready, from your physical condition to the best gear for the trip (p. 33).
Hiking is an aerobic activity Principle 3: To enjoy hiking to the fullest, you will want to be in goodshape (p. 33).
Hiking is an aerobic activity Principle 4: That is why requirement 3 calls for developing a plan for conditioning yourself (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): Begin with short trips, increasing the length of your journeys as you become more fit (p. 33).
Step 2 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): A goodway to prepare for Scout hikes is to walk when­ever you canrather than riding in a car or relying on public transit (p. 33).
Step 3 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): The word aerobic means "with oxygen." Aerobic activitiesincrease the rate of your breathing and your heartbeat, andpush your body to use oxygen (p. 33).
Step 4 (Hiking is an aerobic activity): Aerobic training can strengthen your circula­tory and respiratory systems, add mass to muscles and bones, burn excess fat, and lead toimprovements (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Under the supervision of your parent: Toggles in a circuit breaker flip to "off" or to a centerposition for both short circuits and circuit overloads (p. 24).

Under the supervision of your parent Principle 2: To reset the circuit and restore power, flip the switch to full "off" and then back to "on." Circuit breakerfuses have a resetbutton or switch (p. 24).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 3: When blown, they can be reactivated with the buttonor switch (p. 24).
Under the supervision of your parent Principle 4: Push the switch to the "off" position, then back to the "on" position (p. 24).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Under the supervision of your parent): The main electrical service entrance to your home isthrough a service panel containing fuses, circuit breakers, orboth (p. 24).
Step 2 (Under the supervision of your parent): The panel usually is located in the basement or utilityroom, or in a closet on an outside wall (p. 24).

Step 3 (Under the supervision of your parent): An older home canhave more than one service entrance, and many homes haveadditional disconnect panels for outside supplies, such as airconditioner (p. 24).
Step 4 (Under the supervision of your parent): Never replace a fuse with one that has the improper amperage rating or size (p. 24).

requirements.lead_text: Under the supervision of your parent, guardian, or counselor, do THREE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Under the supervision of your parent, guardian, or counselor, do THREE of the following: (a) Paint a wall or ceiling. (b) Repair or replace damaged tile, linoleum, or vinyl flooring. (c) Install drapery or curtain rods and then hang drapes or curtains. (d) Repair a hole in drywall. (e) Secure a picture, plant hanger, or other object approved by your parent or guardian to drywall using anchors. (f) Reinforce a picture frame. (g) Mend an object made of china, glass, or pottery. (h) Fix a drawer slide or fix/replace cabinet pulls.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to this merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include, with your parent or guardian's permission, an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from this merit badge to pursue a hobby or healthy lifestyle. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): The smoother thesurface you arepainting, and the smoother thefinish you want, the shorter the napyou should use (p. 45).

Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Removing it is such a high-risk job that it is best left to aprofessional (p. 45).

pamphlet_excerpts: Equine Conformation and Lameness Signs: It includes the horse'sskeletal and muscular structures and all of the physical features and proportions that are characteristic of its breed (p. 13).

Equine Conformation and Lameness Signs Principle 3: A well-proportioned horse will be well-balanced, which allowsit to move efficiently and makes it less prone to unsoundnessand strain (p. 13).
Equine Conformation and Lameness Signs Principle 4: A well-balanced conformation will give the horse alonger working life and help it maintain a better temperament (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Equine Conformation and Lameness Signs): As you choose your horse, keep the followingthings in mind (p. 13).
Step 2 (Equine Conformation and Lameness Signs): It should be muscular and themuscles should look evenlybuilt, giving the horse abalanced shape (p. 13).
Step 3 (Equine Conformation and Lameness Signs): Look for a well-shapedhead that is proportional to the rest of the body (p. 13).
Step 4 (Equine Conformation and Lameness Signs): Ahead that is too big or small will upset the balance of thehorse's overall appearance (p. 13).

pamphlet_excerpts: Importance of Hoof Care: A horse's usefulness depends greatly on thecondition of its hooves, which need dailyinspection and attention to stay healthy (p. 39).
Importance of Hoof Care Principle 2: In addition, long-term exposure to bacteria can lead to infections (p. 39).
Importance of Hoof Care Principle 3: Starting when a horse is about 6 weeks old, the hoovesshould be leveled with a rasp (file) by a horseshoer (farrier) to prevent the bones from growing (p. 39).
Importance of Hoof Care Principle 4: Lifting, inspecting, and cleaning the hooves daily will prepare the horse for thepossible next step of shoeing (p. 39).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Importance of Hoof Care): Use the hoof pick to carefully clean thebottom of each hoof from heel to toe (p. 39).
Step 2 (Importance of Hoof Care): Rasping and shoeing should be doneonly by a farrier (p. 39).
Step 3 (Importance of Hoof Care): A hoof pick probably will be the most importantitem in your grooming kit (p. 39).
Step 4 (Importance of Hoof Care): Shoes help preventexcessive hoof wear under rocky conditions (p. 39).

pamphlet_excerpts: Groom A Horse: Here are the steps to help you care for the hooves (p. 40).
Groom A Horse Principle 2: Step 1, Put a halter on the horse and tie it to a secure fence, rail, or post attachment with a quick-release knot (p. 40).
Groom A Horse Principle 3: Make sure the horse is standing square with its weight evenly distributed (p. 40).
Groom A Horse Principle 4: Step 2, Stand beside the horse's left foreleg, facing toward the tail (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Groom A Horse): Run your left hand down the leg so the horse is aware that you are going to do something (p. 40).
Step 2 (Groom A Horse): Many horses will lift thefoot when the hand reaches the pastern (just below the fetlockjoint and above the hoof) (p. 40).
Step 3 (Groom A Horse): Step 4, If your horse still does not pick up its foot, leanagainst the horse slightly, pushing its weight to the otherforeleg while trying steps (p. 40).
Step 4 (Groom A Horse): A professional shoer at work A shod horse's hooves should be picked daily (p. 40).

pamphlet_excerpts: Determine What and How Much: Although horses are built to forage, it is not always practical to put a horse out to pasture (p. 52).
Determine What and How Much Principle 2: When feeding, there are a few rules to follow. • Provide an amount of feed appropriate to the horse's activity level (p. 52).
Determine What and How Much Principle 3: Too much feed can cause digestive and circulatoryproblems (p. 52).
Determine What and How Much Principle 4: Too little feed can lead to a loss of energy, and itcould harm the horse's overall condition (p. 52).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Determine What and How Much): If your horseis stabled, giveit clean waterbefore feeding. • Do not feed a horse that is tired or overheated (p. 52).
Step 2 (Determine What and How Much): Let a horsecool off sufficiently after exercise or work before allowingit to eat. • Water is critical for a horse's health (p. 52).
Step 3 (Determine What and How Much): It helps produce saliva and other fluids, regulates body temperature, carries nutrientsthrough the body, and is important for digestion (p. 52).
Step 4 (Determine What and How Much): A horse can drink from 4 to 15 or more gallons of water each day, depending on the weather, amount of work, and its ageand size (p. 52).

Step 4 (Saddle and Bridle That You): Step 4 (Name 10 parts of the saddle): Hundreds of bitdesigns are available, but one of the most common is the eggbutt snafflebit (p. 11).

pamphlet_excerpts: Safety With Horses: Before you handle a horse, you should know afew safety rules (p. 9).
Safety With Horses Principle 2: Because horses can sense if you are afraid, be confident yet careful around them (p. 9).
Safety With Horses Principle 3: Prevent accidents and injuries by followingthese rules. • Ground Safety -Never startle a horse (p. 9).
Safety With Horses Principle 4: You might startle it and cause it to kick, which could result in a serious injury (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safety With Horses): The leader of a wild herd usually is an older mare that the other horses respect (p. 9).
Step 2 (Safety With Horses): She leads the herd to food and safety andeven settles disputes, sometimes using discipline (p. 9).

requirements.req_text: On level ground, continuously do the following movements after safely mounting the horse. Do them correctly, at ease, and in harmony with the horse. (a) Walk the horse in a straight line for 60 feet. (b) Walk the horse in a half-circle of not more than 16 feet in radius. (c) Trot or jog the horse in a straight line for 60 feet. (d) Trot or jog the horse in a half-circle of not more than 30 feet in radius. (e) Halt straight. (f) Back up straight four paces. (g) Halt and dismount.

pamphlet_excerpts: On level ground, continuously: Never back ahorse by pullingor jerking on the mouth (p. 49).
On level ground, continuously Principle 2: As you teach your horse to move backward with a halter, remember that horses dislike moving backward (p. 49).
On level ground, continuously Principle 3: Your horse'sfirst reaction might be to raise its head and plant its hind feet (p. 49).
On level ground, continuously Principle 4: However, there is an effective way to teach your horse to back (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (On level ground, continuously): Step 1, Stand on the left side of the horse, near thewithers, with the lead rope in your right hand (p. 49).
Step 2 (On level ground, continuously): Use the rope tobump the horse's forefeet back while using your left hand tokeep the horse's nose straight (p. 49).
Step 3 (On level ground, continuously): Just move the horse back a step at a time while saying "back." It might help to have the horse facing a wall sothat it can't go forward (p. 49).
Step 4 (On level ground, continuously): Step 2, If the horse won't move, push the horse at thechest, where the muscles join (p. 49).

Step 3 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Today, more than half of American Indians live outside the reservations that were set aside for them by the federalgovernment (p. 91).
Step 4 (Different American Indian cultural areas): Many live in big cities; others live in smallercommunities and rural areas (p. 91).

pamphlet_excerpts: Life Might Have Been: Describe How Life: This pamphlet will help youtake that important first step in your journey of discovery (p. 9).
Life Might Have Been Principle 2: Describe How Life Principle 2: Usethe information here as a starting point to learn more about American Indians and Ameri­can heritage (p. 9).
Life Might Have Been Principle 3: Describe How Life Principle 3: You might want to focus on only one tribe to fulfill all of the merit badge requirements (p. 9).
Life Might Have Been Principle 4: Describe How Life Principle 4: You might want to learn moreabout Indian life in general before Euro­peans came, as well asafter they arrived (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Life Might Have Been): Step 1 (Describe How Life): You might also investigate how Indians live and work today and carry on their ancient traditions (p. 9).
Step 2 (Life Might Have Been): Step 2 (Describe How Life): Ask your school or public librarian for books and other materials about different Indian groups (p. 9).
Step 3 (Life Might Have Been): Step 3 (Describe How Life): If you have anatural history museum in your area, ask the curator or personin charge for information (p. 9).
Step 4 (Life Might Have Been): Step 4 (Describe How Life): See if your town or city has an American Indian center, oran Indian tribal council or similar governing group (p. 9).

pamphlet_excerpts: Museum Either In-person or Virtually: Visit a museum either in-person: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and revivingtheir arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 37).

Museum Either In-person or Virtually Principle 2: Visit a museum either in-person Principle 2: Many havechosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 37).
Museum Either In-person or Virtually Principle 3: Visit a museum either in-person Principle 3: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in themodern world (p. 37).

Museum Either In-person or Virtually Principle 4: Visit a museum either in-person Principle 4: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part ofmodern society (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 1 (Visit a museum either in-person): There is no easy answer, and no one knowswhat the future holds (p. 37).

Step 2 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 2 (Visit a museum either in-person): The history of American Indians is filled with the names ofmen and women who are remembered for deeds that set themapart from others (p. 37).
Step 3 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 3 (Visit a museum either in-person): They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 37).

Step 4 (Museum Either In-person or Virtually): Step 4 (Visit a museum either in-person): Some, like Pocahontas, Sacajawea, Hahyonhwatha (known as "Hiawatha"), and Tecumseh, livedcenturies ago (p. 37).

pamphlet_excerpts: Life Cycles: The most accurate observation of an insect in nature comes from watching it undisturbed (p. 35).
Life Cycles Principle 2: When observing insects in their habitat, be careful to leave them unharmed in the place thatyou found them (p. 35).
Life Cycles Principle 3: The Seven Principles of Leave No Trace and the Outdoor Code apply to alloutdoor activities, including insect study (p. 35).
Life Cycles Principle 4: Requirements for the Insect Study merit badge call for you to not only observe insects, but in somecases, to collect them (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Life Cycles): As with any trek in the outdoors, there are some basicguidelines to follow when searching for insects. 1 (p. 35).
Step 2 (Life Cycles): When you embark on your insect safari, prepare a trip plan, or at the very least, tell an adult where you are going (p. 35).
Step 3 (Life Cycles): It isalso a good idea to take a friend with you. 2 (p. 35).
Step 4 (Life Cycles): It is a good idea to wear long pants, a long-sleeved shirt, ahat, and closed shoes to keep ticks, chiggers, and insects from biting you or hitching (p. 35).

pamphlet_excerpts: Conservation Migration Route Insect: Conservation: Monarch butterfly chrysalis The chrysalis is a shiny, transparent green with several spots of gold (p. 22).
Conservation Migration Route Insect Principle 2: Conservation Principle 2: It hangs from the leaf for several days to about three weeks, dependingon the weather (p. 22).

Conservation Migration Route Insect Principle 3: Conservation Principle 3: Near the end of this period, the chrysalis turns very dark (almost black), and the wing pattern of the adult butterfly can be seenbeneath the thin skin (p. 22).
Conservation Migration Route Insect Principle 4: Conservation Principle 4: Finally, the bottom of the chrysalis splits and out crawls the adultmonarch butterfly (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 1 (Conservation): Its wings gradually expand and harden, and thebutterfly starts to use its long, hollow, coiled "tongue" to sucknectar from flowers (p. 22).
Step 2 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 2 (Conservation): Usually, the adult will live four to six weeks, feeding occasionallybut mostly just wandering from field to field (p. 22).
Step 3 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 3 (Conservation): The last brood of summer, however, will migrate south, often in large numbers and journeying anincredible 2,500 miles (p. 22).
Step 4 (Conservation Migration Route Insect): Step 4 (Conservation): This brood lives longer, some of the monarchs livethrough the winter in Mexico or along the southern coast of California (p. 22).

Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 2: Many are involved in education and outreachprograms at natural historymuseums, nature centers, zoos, conservation agencies, and extension offices (p. 91).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 3: Forensic entomologists helpin police investigations byexamining insects that inhabitdecomposing remains (p. 91).
Careers & Professional Pathways Principle 4: Forexample, insects can helpestablish the time of death (p. 91).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Among the first insects toarrive on a newly dead body are blowflies, and a femaleblowfly usually lays eggs within a very short time after arriving (p. 91).
Step 2 (Careers & Professional Pathways): A researcher whoknows how long it takes blowfly eggs to reach these differentstages can estimate the time of the victim's death (p. 91).
Step 3 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Few people are employed full-time as forensic entomologists (p. 91).
Step 4 (Careers & Professional Pathways): Most are affiliated with colleges or universities, teachentomology or biology, and do research (p. 91).

requirements.lead_text: Think of an item you would like to invent that would solve a problem for your family, troop, chartered organization, community, or a special-interest group. Then do the following, while keeping a notebook to record your progress.
requirements.req_text: Think of an item you would like to invent that would solve a problem for your family, troop, chartered organization, community, or a special-interest group. Then do the following, while keeping a notebook to record your progress. (a) Talk to potential users of your invention and determine their needs. Then, based on what you have learned, write a statement describing the invention and how it would help solve a problem. This statement should include a detailed sketch of the invention. (b) Create a model of the invention using clay, cardboard, or any other readily available material. List the materials necessary to build a working prototype of the invention. (c) Share the idea and the model with your counselor and potential users of your invention. Record their feedback in your notebook.

Step 3 (Freedom of the press): The person falsely accused cansue the journalist and news organization in civil court (p. 20).
Step 4 (Freedom of the press): Journalists should respect people's privacy, their right to be left alone, out of public view (p. 20).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Option A, Newspaper, Magazine, and Online Journalism. (Ask your parent or guardian's permission for the online option.) Do ALL of the following: (1) On the same day, read a local news source or newspaper, a national news source or newspaper, a news magazine (online or printed), and a social media news feed. From each source, clip, read, and compare a story about the same event. Tell your counselor how long each story is and how fair and accurate the stories are in presenting different points of view. Tell how each source handled the story. (2) Visit the office of a newspaper, magazine, or internet news site. Ask for a tour of the various divisions (editorial, business, and printing). During your tour, talk to an executive from the business side about management's relations with reporters, editors, and photographers, and what makes a "good" newspaper, magazine, or internet news site. Note: If there are no opportunities for in-person visits in your community, a virtual visit is acceptable with the news site of your choice, provided your counselor approves this option in advance. (You can request a virtual visit with Scout Life magazine ) (b) Option B, Radio and Television Journalism. Do ALL of the following: (1) All on the same day, watch a local and national network newscast, listen to a radio newscast, and (with your parent or guardian's permission) view a national broadcast news source online. List the different news items and features presented, the different elements used, and the time in minutes and seconds and the online space devoted to each story. Compare the story lists and discuss whether the stories are fair and accurate. Explain why different news outlets treated the stories differently and/or presented a different point of view. (2) Visit a radio or television station. Ask for a tour of the various departments, concentrating on those related to news broadcasts. During your tour, talk to the station manager or other station management executive about station operations, particularly how management and the news staff work together, and what makes a "good" station. If possible, go with a reporter to cover a news event.

requirements.lead_text: Discuss the differences between a hard news story and a feature story. Explain what the five W's and H are. Then do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Discuss the differences between a hard news story and a feature story. Explain what the five W's and H are. Then do ONE of the following: (a) Choose a current or an unusual event of interest to you, and write either a hard news article OR a feature article about the event. Gear the article for print OR online OR audio OR video journalism. Share your article with your counselor. (b) With your parent or guardian's permission and counselor's approval, interview someone in your community who is influential because of his or her leadership, talent, career, or life experiences. Then present to your counselor either a written or oral report telling what you learned about this person. (c) With your parent or guardian's permission and counselor's approval, read an autobiography written by a journalist you want to learn more about. Write an article that tells what you learned about this person and the contributions this person has made to the field of journalism. (d) Attend a Scouting event and write a 200-word article (feature or hard news) about the event. Use either the inverted pyramid style or the chronological style. Review the article with your counselor, then submit it to your community newspaper or Scouting America local council or district newsletter for consideration.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the hazards you are most likely to encounter while participating in kayaking activities, including weather and water-related hazards, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that can occur while kayaking: blisters, cold-water shock and hypothermia, heat-related illnesses, dehydration, sunburn, sprains, and strains. (c) Review the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy. Explain to your counselor how this applies to kayaking.

pamphlet_excerpts: Out The Major: Name and point out the major: In selecting a kayak paddle, the most important thing toconsider is the comfort of the paddle in your hands (p. 29).
Out The Major Principle 2: Name and point out the major Principle 2: Qualitypaddles have an oval shaft, which provides better control andcomfort and helps you set the correct angle (p. 29).
Out The Major Principle 3: Name and point out the major Principle 3: Most paddles havestraight shafts, but a few designs are bent at the grip positions to ease strain on the wrists (p. 29).
Out The Major Principle 4: Name and point out the major Principle 4: Paddles for recreational kayaks are normally sized in centimeters, withtypical lengths between 200 and 220 centimeters (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Out The Major): Step 1 (Name and point out the major): Given these differences, a general rule of thumb for sizing akayak paddle is to hold the paddle above your head horizontally (p. 29).
Step 2 (Out The Major): Step 2 (Name and point out the major): With your elbows at 90-degree angles, your hands should be 6 to 8 inches from the throat on either end of the paddle (p. 29).
Step 3 (Out The Major): Step 3 (Name and point out the major): The blades of kayak paddles come in various designs (p. 29).
Step 4 (Out The Major): Step 4 (Name and point out the major): Largeblades provide more power per stroke; smaller blades take lessenergy per stroke and are gentler to arm and shoulder joints (p. 29).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Using a properly equipped kayak): Step 1, The rescuer pulls and the paddlerin the water pushes the capsized kayakacross the deck of the rescue boat so bothends (p. 56).

Step 3 (Using a properly equipped kayak): The paddler in the watershould hold on to the end of the rescue boator hold on to the end of the capsized kayak (p. 56).
Step 4 (Using a properly equipped kayak): Step 2, Once the boat is empty, therescuer flips it away from himself andturns the kayak upright (p. 56).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (As a solo paddler, use): The draw stroke starts by rotating theupper body so you are looking out to theside of the boat (p. 75).

Step 3 (As a solo paddler, use): For the catch position, place thepaddle in the water out away from theboat and your hips so the power face of the blade faces (p. 75).
Step 4 (As a solo paddler, use): Keep the top handhigh so the shaft and the blade stay fairlystraight up and down (vertical) (p. 75).
