pamphlet_excerpts: Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid: Responsibility and Safety in Snow Sports Reporting an Accident Be aware of the ski area's procedure for reporting accidents (p. 19).
Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid Principle 2: Make it a habit to check with the local ski patrol for instructions on accident reporting before you head (p. 19).

Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid Principle 3: At Alpine ski resorts, one common method of reportingaccidents is to send someone from your group to the bottom of the nearest lift and inform a lift (p. 19).

Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid Principle 4: Remember to includeimportant details: the exact location of the accident, the type ofinjuries, the number of people hurt, and their conditions (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid): Snow sports, like other activities, have their own set of precautions and unique risks (p. 19).
Step 2 (Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid): The conditions described here representthose for which any safety-conscious person should be prepared (p. 19).
Step 3 (Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid): You should perform first aid only if help from the ski patrol ortrained medical personnel is unavailable (p. 19).
Step 4 (Sprains, Fractures & Cold-Weather First Aid): Hypothermia occurs when the body islosing more heat than it can generate (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: International Trail-marking System: Another thing snow sport enthusiasts need to become familiar with is the international trail-marking system (p. 18).
International Trail-marking System Principle 2: This system has been designed to help users identify the trails best suited to their level of ability as well as hazards within a ski area (p. 18).
International Trail-marking System Principle 3: The signs arethere for everyone's safety and should always be followed (p. 18).

International Trail-marking System Principle 4: Each ski area determines whether a trail is a green circle (beginner), blue square (intermediate), black diamond (advanced), or double black diamond (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (International Trail-marking System): Nordic andsnowshoe trails often use this system as well (p. 18).
Step 2 (International Trail-marking System): Terrain parks usean "orange pill" to identify terrain features (p. 18).
Step 3 (International Trail-marking System): There may or maynot be ratings to indicate difficulty (p. 18).
Step 4 (International Trail-marking System): No two slopes ortrails are exactly the same, eventhough they mighthave the samedifficulty rating (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up: Activities such asrunning, soccer, biking, and hiking are great ways to To enjoy snow sports, you must be in good physical condition (p. 25).
Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up Principle 2: Be sure to take the time to prepare your body for the sport (p. 25).
Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up Principle 3: Start your warm-up with some activity to get your musclesready, such as jogging briefly (p. 25).
Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up Principle 4: Then perform these stretches, holding each one a minimum of 30 seconds up to two minutes. to keep in shapeyear-round (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up): Use a wall or something solid tolean into, one leg forward and one leg back (p. 25).
Step 2 (Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up): Keep the back leg straight and push into the wall until you can feel the calf stretch (p. 25).
Step 3 (Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up): While standing, bend from the waist with your legs straight (p. 25).
Step 4 (Winter Fitness, Conditioning & Warm-Up): Stretchyour hands toward the ground until you feel the back of your legs stretching (p. 25).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Downhill (Alpine) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate each of the required skills. (1) Show how to wax and maintain your skis and use/maintain your release bindings. Explain the international DIN standard and what it means to skiers. (2) Explain the American Teaching System and a basic snowskiing progression. (3) Discuss the different types of Alpine skis. Demonstrate two ways to carry skis and poles safely and easily. (4) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (5) On a gentle slope, demonstrate some of the beginning maneuvers learned in skiing. Include the straight run, gliding wedge, wedge stop, sidestep, and herringbone maneuvers. (6) On slightly steeper terrain, show linked wedge turns. (7) On a moderate slope, demonstrate five to 10 christies. (8) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (9) Demonstrate the ability to ski in varied conditions, including changes in pitch and snow conditions. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (10) Name the major ski organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (b) Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag. (c) Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions. (d) Option D, Snowshoeing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name the parts of a snowshoe. (2) Explain how to choose the correct size of snowshoe. (3) Describe the different types of snowshoes and their specialized uses. Discuss factors to consider when choosing a snowshoe. (4) Explain how to properly care for and maintain snowshoes. (5) List the items you would take on a one-day snowshoe hike. (6) Describe areas that are best for snowshoeing. Discuss some advantages and dangers of backcountry snowshoeing. (7) Discuss the benefits of snowshoeing. (8) Demonstrate the most efficient ways to break trail, climb uphill, travel downhill, and traverse a slope. (9) Demonstrate your ability, on a 2-mile snowshoe hike, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive snowshoers may complete a 1-mile hike with prior approval from their counselor. (10) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Downhill (Alpine) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate each of the required skills. (1) Show how to wax and maintain your skis and use/maintain your release bindings. Explain the international DIN standard and what it means to skiers. (2) Explain the American Teaching System and a basic snowskiing progression. (3) Discuss the different types of Alpine skis. Demonstrate two ways to carry skis and poles safely and easily. (4) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (5) On a gentle slope, demonstrate some of the beginning maneuvers learned in skiing. Include the straight run, gliding wedge, wedge stop, sidestep, and herringbone maneuvers. (6) On slightly steeper terrain, show linked wedge turns. (7) On a moderate slope, demonstrate five to 10 christies. (8) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (9) Demonstrate the ability to ski in varied conditions, including changes in pitch and snow conditions. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (10) Name the major ski organizations in the United States and explain their functions.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Cross-Country (Nordic) Skiing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show your ability to select, use, and maintain equipment for cross-country skiing in safety and comfort. (2) Explain the reasons for common rules, including no walking on ski trails, one-way ski direction, no pets, and no skiing on snowmobile trails. (3) Discuss classic, skating, touring, and telemark skis. (4) Discuss the basic principles of waxing for cross-country ski touring. (5) Discuss the differences between cross-country, backcountry/ski touring, ski mountaineering, and downhill/telemark skiing. (6) List the items you would take on a one-day ski tour. (7) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass. (8) On a gentle, packed slope, show some basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the straight run, traverse, side slip, step turn, wedge stop, and wedge turn maneuvers. (9) On a cross-country trail, demonstrate effective propulsion by showing proper weight transfer from ski to ski, pole timing, rhythm, flow, and glide. (10) Demonstrate your ability, on a 4-mile tour, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive skiers may complete a 1-mile tour with prior approval from their counselor. (11) Demonstrate several methods of dealing with steep hills or difficult conditions. Include traverses and kick turns going uphill and downhill, sidesteps, and pole drag.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Snowboarding. Do ALL of the following: Note: Generally, a gentle slope will be a trail designated by a green circle, a slightly steeper slope will be a green circle or blue square trail, and an intermediate slope will be a blue square trail. However, your counselor should determine what type of hill is most suited to your skill level and allows you to demonstrate the required skills. (1) Discuss forward-fall injuries. (2) Show your ability to select the correct equipment for snowboarding and to use it for safety and comfort. (3) Show how to use and maintain your own bindings, and explain the use of the different binding methods. Explain the need for leashes. (4) Discuss the four types of snowboards. Demonstrate how to carry a snowboard easily and safely. (5) Demonstrate how to ride one kind of lift and explain how to ride two others. (6) Demonstrate the basic principles of waxing a snowboard. (7) Do the following: (a) On a gentle slope, demonstrate beginning snowboarding maneuvers. Show basic ways to control speed and direction. Include the sideslipping maneuver. (b) On slightly steeper terrain, show traversing. (8) On a moderate slope, demonstrate an ollie, a nose-end grab, and a wheelie. (9) Make a controlled run down an intermediate slope. (10) Demonstrate your ability to ride in varied conditions, including changes in pitch, snow conditions, and moguls. Maintain your balance and ability to turn. (11) Name the major snowboarding organizations in the United States and explain their functions.

sub_requirements.text: Option D, Snowshoeing. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name the parts of a snowshoe. (2) Explain how to choose the correct size of snowshoe. (3) Describe the different types of snowshoes and their specialized uses. Discuss factors to consider when choosing a snowshoe. (4) Explain how to properly care for and maintain snowshoes. (5) List the items you would take on a one-day snowshoe hike. (6) Describe areas that are best for snowshoeing. Discuss some advantages and dangers of backcountry snowshoeing. (7) Discuss the benefits of snowshoeing. (8) Demonstrate the most efficient ways to break trail, climb uphill, travel downhill, and traverse a slope. (9) Demonstrate your ability, on a 2-mile snowshoe hike, to cope with an average variety of snow conditions. Note: Adaptive snowshoers may complete a 1-mile hike with prior approval from their counselor. (10) Demonstrate the proper use of a topographic map and compass.

pamphlet_excerpts: Snow Sports Specialized Field Options: All-mountain skis come in a variety of flexes and side cuts (p. 37).
Snow Sports Specialized Field Options Principle 2: Racing skis are designed for high speeds and hard snow (p. 37).
Snow Sports Specialized Field Options Principle 3: They generally have a stiff flex that can make turning moredifficult, but that makes the ski more stable at higher speeds (p. 37).
Snow Sports Specialized Field Options Principle 4: Racing skis are specialized for turning around gates, and theside cut determines how wide a turn the skis can make (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Snow Sports Specialized Field Options): Twin-tip skis are turned up at the tip and the tail and aredesigned for performing on jumps, rails, and half-pipes (p. 37).
Step 2 (Snow Sports Specialized Field Options): They can be skied all over the mountain, but their design makesmany conditions outside the terrain park more challenging (p. 37).

Step 3 (Snow Sports Specialized Field Options): Most boots for downhill skiing consist of a plastic outer shell for support and an inner shell of material designed to mold to the foot for comfort (p. 37).
Step 4 (Snow Sports Specialized Field Options): Boots come in a variety of widths, and they have buckles on the outer shell that allow a skier to adjust the amount of tension (p. 37).

pamphlet_excerpts: Soil Formed Soil They: Tell What Soil: Fertile soil can supply the complete nutritional needs of agrowing plant (p. 21).
Soil Formed Soil They Principle 2: Tell What Soil Principle 2: The three principal plant nutrients are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (p. 21).
Soil Formed Soil They Principle 3: Tell What Soil Principle 3: Aplant that lacks an essential nutrient will show physical signs of the deficiency (p. 21).
Soil Formed Soil They Principle 4: Tell What Soil Principle 4: Chemical soil tests help determine how much of which nutrients are needed for the best growth of differentkinds of plants (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Soil Formed Soil They): Step 1 (Tell What Soil): For centuries, people who lived along the banks of rivers and streamshave recognized that the annual floods that covered their land (p. 21).
Step 2 (Soil Formed Soil They): Step 2 (Tell What Soil): In 1699, John Woodward experimented by growing plants in water containingdiffering amounts of sediment (p. 21).
Step 3 (Soil Formed Soil They): Step 3 (Tell What Soil): He found that the plant growthimproved as the amount of sediment in water increased (p. 21).
Step 4 (Soil Formed Soil They): Step 4 (Tell What Soil): Loose and crumblysoil has manypores for water and air, it hasgood structure (p. 21).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (A watershed): The way people in cities along a river use water and the kinds of wastes they put into the river will affectindustries, businesses, and cities farther (p. 58).
Step 2 (A watershed): Remember, the care and use of land in your watershed is important (p. 58).
Step 3 (A watershed): Fires that have swept through watersheds in thewestern United States and have been followed by heavy andprolonged rains have washed huge amounts (p. 58).
Step 4 (A watershed): In some places, mudslides have carried houses and other buildings (p. 58).

Step 3 (Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle): When the water vapor in cloudscondenses, we get the rain, snow, sleet, or hail that falls on Earth, called precipitation (p. 30).
Step 4 (Drawing to show the hydrologic cycle): As air masses move across the land, the air picks up moremoisture (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Meant By Water Pollution: Tell What Is Meant: Often, the effluent resulting from primary treatment requiressecondary treatment (p. 78).

Meant By Water Pollution Principle 2: Tell What Is Meant Principle 2: The wastewater repeats all the steps ofprimary treatment and then one of two processes for furtherorganic waste decomposition (p. 78).
Meant By Water Pollution Principle 3: Tell What Is Meant Principle 3: Both processes depend onbiological action and both require oxygen (p. 78).
Meant By Water Pollution Principle 4: Tell What Is Meant Principle 4: The oxygen issupplied through aeration, that is, by spraying the effluentinto the air or by pumping air (p. 78).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 1 (Tell What Is Meant): In one process, the effluent goes from the primary settlingtank to a trickling filter (p. 78).
Step 2 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 2 (Tell What Is Meant): There, it passes slowly over stones or other material where biological growths decompose the wasteleft in the effluent (p. 78).

Step 3 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 3 (Tell What Is Meant): The stones and other material in the tricklingfilter provide as much surface area as possible with oxygen sothat the biological growths can live (p. 78).
Step 4 (Meant By Water Pollution): Step 4 (Tell What Is Meant): While the effluent remainsin the sludge tank, it is continuously aerated (p. 78).

Write a report of more than 500 words about the soil and water and energy conservation practices you saw. (1) An agricultural experiment (2) A managed forest or woodlot, range, or pasture (3) A wildlife refuge or a fish or game management area (4) A conservation-managed farm or ranch (5) A managed watershed (6) A waste-treatment plant (7) A public drinking water treatment plant (8) An industry water use installation (9) A desalinization plant (b) Plant 100 trees, bushes, and/or vines for a good purpose. (c) Seed an area of at least one-fifth acre for some worthwhile conservation purposes, using suitable grasses or legumes alone or in a mixture. (d) Study a soil survey report. Describe the things in it. Using tracing paper and a pen, trace over any of the soil maps, and outline an area with three or more different kinds of soil. List each kind of soil by full name and map symbol. (e) Make a list of places in your neighborhood, camps, school ground, or park that have erosion, sedimentation, or pollution problems. Describe how these could be corrected through individual or group action. (f) Carry out any other soil and water conservation project approved by your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Conservation on the Land: Conservation buffers are small areas or strips of land kept in permanent vegetation (p. 49).
Conservation on the Land Principle 2: These areas thenhelp control soil erosion and pollution by breaking upand slowing the movement of runoff, sediment, and other pollutants within fields (p. 49).
Conservation on the Land Principle 3: The USDA launched the National Conservation Buffer Initiative in 1997 (p. 49).
Conservation on the Land Principle 4: Through this initiative, public and private agencies are working together to helplandowners create 2 million miles of conservationbuffers (p. 49).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Conservation on the Land): Grassed contour buffer strips cover an entire field in Iowa (p. 49).
Step 2 (Conservation on the Land): Professional conservationists have solved many conservationproblems (p. 49).
Step 3 (Conservation on the Land): Some practices may be suitable only for application oncroplands, rangelands, or forestlands (p. 49).
Step 4 (Conservation on the Land): Because plants are the greatprotectors of land surfaces, most practices involve the use andmanagement of plants so that they can hold soil (p. 49).

pamphlet_excerpts: Purpose of Space Exploration: The United States, Russia, and other countries wanted alarger, longer-lasting facility to do long-term research in space (p. 69).
Purpose of Space Exploration Principle 2: The space shuttle had supported some research, but flights had been too few and too short (p. 69).
Purpose of Space Exploration Principle 3: A bigger spacestation also would provide better researchsupport services (such as data transmission) than the shuttle could ever provide (p. 69).
Purpose of Space Exploration Principle 4: Purposes of the ISS The million-pound ISS is the largestconstruction project ever attemptedin space (p. 69).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Purpose of Space Exploration): The International Space Station has severalpurposes (p. 69).
Step 2 (Purpose of Space Exploration): One of the most important is that the ISS provides a constant presence in space (p. 69).
Step 3 (Purpose of Space Exploration): Since November 2000, there have been from two to 13 (when the space shuttleorbiter was docked) astronauts and cosmonauts at a time livingin space (p. 69).
Step 4 (Purpose of Space Exploration): The research done aboard the ISS may lead to breakthroughs in medicine, engineering, and technology that willhave practical uses for humanity (p. 69).

pamphlet_excerpts: Collector's Card With A Picture: Design a collector's card: Richard Branson (1950- ) and Burt Rutan (1943- ) founded Virgin Galactic, an early commercial spaceflight companyoffering customers suborbital flights (p. 23).

Collector's Card With A Picture Principle 2: Design a collector's card Principle 2: They used an innovativelaunch system designed by Rutan featuring a carrier aircraft and a suborbital rocket-powered spaceplane as a secondstage (p. 23).

Collector's Card With A Picture Principle 3: Design a collector's card Principle 3: Overcoming a number of technical setbacks including a fatal crash, the company would lead the way in commercialspaceflight (p. 23).
Collector's Card With A Picture Principle 4: Design a collector's card Principle 4: Its test pilots earned the first commercial astronautwings, award by the FAA in 2004 (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 1 (Design a collector's card): Elon Musk (1971- ) formed Space Exploration Technologies (SpaceX) in 2002 to build rockets that could inexpensivelycarry payloads to low Earth orbit (p. 23).

Step 2 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 2 (Design a collector's card): After years of successful rocket launches, the company begantransporting cargo to the International Space Station in October 2012 in its Dragon (p. 23).
Step 3 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 3 (Design a collector's card): For requirement 2, create a collector's card of your favorite spacepioneer (p. 23).
Step 4 (Collector's Card With A Picture): Step 4 (Design a collector's card): Give details of the person's contribution tospaceflight, including dates, missions, and other accomplishments (p. 23).

pamphlet_excerpts: Launch and Recover A Model: Build, launch, and recover a model: Model rocketry is a great way to learn about space exploration (p. 25).

Launch and Recover A Model Principle 2: Build, launch, and recover a model Principle 2: The rocket you build won't reach space, but the science andtechnology that goes into your rocket is the same as NASA usesin launching giant rockets (p. 25).
Launch and Recover A Model Principle 3: Build, launch, and recover a model Principle 3: Model rockets are made of paper, balsa wood, plastic, glue, and paint (p. 25).

Launch and Recover A Model Principle 4: Build, launch, and recover a model Principle 4: You build them with simple tools such as amodeling knife, sandpaper, scissors, rulers, and paintbrushes (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Launch and Recover A Model): Step 1 (Build, launch, and recover a model): Model rockets are powered by solid propellant rocket engines (p. 25).

Step 2 (Launch and Recover A Model): Step 2 (Build, launch, and recover a model): Depending on the size and design of the rocket and the power of the engine, model rockets may fly only 50 feet high or up to a half mile (p. 25).

Step 3 (Launch and Recover A Model): Step 3 (Build, launch, and recover a model): You can purchase model rocket kits and engines online, through mail-order catalogs, and in toy and hobby shops (p. 25).

Step 4 (Launch and Recover A Model): Step 4 (Build, launch, and recover a model): Ifyou can borrow a rocket launcher, you can buy everything youneed to complete requirement 3 for less than $20 (p. 25).

(c) Design a robotic mission to another planet, moon, comet, or asteroid that will return samples of its surface to Earth. Name the planet, moon, comet, or asteroid your spacecraft will visit. Show how your design will cope with the conditions of the environments of the planet, moon, comet, or asteroid.

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Risks in sports): If you feel a hot spot developing, stop immediately and protect the tender area by applying anadhesive bandage or moleskin (p. 87).
Step 2 (Risks in sports): If a blister must be drained, first wash the blister with mildsoap and water (p. 87).
Step 3 (Risks in sports): Prick the edge of the blister with a needle that has been sterilized in a flame (p. 87).
Step 4 (Risks in sports): Cover itwith an adhesive bandage or other sterile dressing (p. 87).

Step 3 (Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration): If you truly disagree with the officiating after the game, it is acceptable to write a letter to the league commissioner orofficiating (p. 22).
Step 4 (Warm-Up, Cool-Down, and Hydration): Also considertaking a course to qualify as an official (p. 22).

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) With guidance from your counselor, establish a suitable personal training program that you will follow throughout your competition season (or for three months). (b) Create a chart or other tracking system, and document your training, practice, and development during this time. (c) Demonstrate proper technique to play each sport effectively and avoid injury. (d) List and describe the equipment needed for each sport, including protective equipment and any specialized clothing. (e) List and explain the rules and proper etiquette of each sport. (f) Draw and explain a diagram of the playing area for each sport. (g) Participate in each sport as a competitive individual or as a member of an organized team for one season (or for three months). (h) At the end of the season, share your completed chart with your counselor and discuss how your participation in the sports you chose has affected you mentally and physically.

Topical Stamp Collecting Principle 2: Define topical stamp collecting Principle 2: A collector can, for example, focus on stamps of the United States while specializing in trains as a topical collection (p. 20).

Topical Stamp Collecting Principle 3: Define topical stamp collecting Principle 3: A variety of definitive and commemorative stamps andpostal stationery can make an interesting and inexpensive type of collection (p. 20).
Topical Stamp Collecting Principle 4: Define topical stamp collecting Principle 4: Covers, or envelopes, showing different postalrates and classes make a challenging collection (p. 20).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 1 (Define topical stamp collecting): Even advertising covers used to promote different products can be collected (p. 20).

Step 2 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 2 (Define topical stamp collecting): Without spending a cent, you can easily collect 50 to a hundreditems that reflect the complexity of the modern mail system, from your family's (p. 20).
Step 3 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 3 (Define topical stamp collecting): Some collectors specialize inmeter imprints and labels (p. 20).

Step 4 (Topical Stamp Collecting): Step 4 (Define topical stamp collecting): These can be collected historically, going back to the many types used since the 1920s or focusing on current usealone (p. 20).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Design a stamp, cancellation, or cachet. (b) Visit a post office, stamp club, or stamp show with an experienced collector. Explain what you saw and learned. (c) Write a review of an interesting article from a stamp newspaper, magazine, book, or website (with your parent or guardian's permission). (d) Research and report on a famous stamp-related personality or the history behind a particular stamp. (e) Describe the steps taken to produce a stamp. Include the methods of printing, types of paper, perforation styles, and how they are gummed. (f) Prepare a two- to three-page display involving stamps. Using ingenuity, as well as clippings, drawings, etc., tell a story about the stamps and how they relate to history, geography, or a favorite topic of yours.

requirements.lead_text: Mount and show, in a purchased or homemade album, ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Mount and show, in a purchased or homemade album, ONE of the following: (a) A collection of 250 or more different stamps from at least 15 countries (b) A collection of a stamp from each of 50 different countries, mounted on maps to show the location of each (c) A collection of 100 or more different stamps from either one country or a group of closely related countries (d) A collection of 75 or more different stamps on a single topic. (Some interesting topics include Scouting, birds, insects, the Olympics, sports, flowers, animals, ships, holidays, trains, famous people, space, and medicine.) Stamps may be from different countries. (e) A collection of postal items discovered in your mail by monitoring it over a period of 30 days. Include at least five different types listed in requirement 3.

Step 3 (Set an instrument): This is especially useful when thenearest survey monuments are far away (p. 19).

Meaning of sustainability in your own Principle 2: Sustainable, then, relates to methods of harvesting or using resources in ways that do not squander or permanently damage them (p. 15).
Meaning of sustainability in your own Principle 3: A sustainablelifestyle or society meets today's needs without depleting (completely using up) natural resources for future generations (p. 15).
Meaning of sustainability in your own Principle 4: At its heart are the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which are urgent calls for action by all developed anddeveloping countries (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Meaning of sustainability in your own): Achieving sustainability requires balancing environmental, social, and economic needs (p. 15).
Step 2 (Meaning of sustainability in your own): Forever." This will require navigating trade-offs between short-term and long-term benefits (p. 15).
Step 3 (Meaning of sustainability in your own): You might ask yourself what role you play in sustainabilityand what you can do to help sustain Earth (p. 15).
Step 4 (Meaning of sustainability in your own): Earning the Sustainability merit badge is the first big step in educatingyourself and increasing your awareness about the topic (p. 15).

Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Create a sketch depicting how you would design a sustainable community and be prepared to explain how the housing, work locations, shops, schools, and transportation systems affect energy, pollution, natural resources, and the economy of the community. (b) Identify one unsustainable practice in your community and develop a written plan to fix it. (c) Identify five sustainability factors in housing and rate your own home's sustainability against these factors.

requirements.lead_text: Energy. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Energy. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Learn about the sustainability of different energy sources, including coal, gas, geothermal, hydro power, nuclear, petroleum, solar, and wind. Identify three common energy sources in the United States and describe how the production and consumption of each of these energy sources affects sustainability. (b) List eight ways your family consumes energy, such as gas appliances, electricity, heating systems or cooling systems, and transportation. For one home- and one transportation-related energy use, list three ways to help reduce consumption, reduce your carbon footprint, and be a better steward of this resource. (c) List five ways you and your family could reduce energy consumption in your home, such as adjusting your thermostat, window shades, opening windows, reducing hot-water temperature, and minimizing water consumption. Identify the benefits and risks of each idea and implement if possible.

pamphlet_excerpts: Sustainability Core Field Standard: Close windowdrapes to keepheat out insummer, and open the drapes to letin the warm sunin wintertime (p. 62).
Sustainability Core Field Standard Principle 2: By using less fuel and less electricity and reducing the amount of trash you create, you can reduce your carbon footprintdramatically (p. 62).
Sustainability Core Field Standard Principle 3: Start by turning off computers, televisions, andlights when you are not using them (p. 62).
Sustainability Core Field Standard Principle 4: Unplug small appliances and phone chargers, etc., when they are not in use (p. 62).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Sustainability Core Field Standard): Lower thetemperature in your home to 68 degrees or lower in winter, andraise it to 78 degrees or higher when running an air conditionerin (p. 62).
Step 2 (Sustainability Core Field Standard): Turn off your heat or air conditioner entirely andopen screened windows for natural ventilation when the weatheris comfortable (p. 62).
Step 3 (Sustainability Core Field Standard): Here are more tips for reducing your carbon footprint: Buy local and buy organic (p. 62).
Step 4 (Sustainability Core Field Standard): When possible, buy organic or "fair trade." There's a better chance the food was grown inan eco-friendly way (p. 62).

requirements.lead_text: Stuff. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Stuff. Do ONE of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) Create a list of 15 items of your personal "stuff." Classify each item as an essential need (such as soap) or a desirable want (such as a video game). Identify any excess "stuff" you no longer need, working with your family, if possible. Donate, repurpose, or recycle those items you can. (b) List five ways having too much "stuff" affects you, your family, your community, AND the world. For each of the five ways, consider the following aspects: the financial impact, time spent, maintenance, health, storage, and waste generation. Identify practices that can be used to avoid accumulating too much "stuff." (c) Research the impact waste has on the environment (land, water, air). Find out what the trash vortex is and how it was formed. Explain the number system for plastic recyclables and which plastics are more commonly recycled. Identify the average lifespan of one electronic device in your household, and whether it can be recycled in whole or part.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following and discuss with your counselor:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following and discuss with your counselor: (a) The United Nations lists 17 Sustainable Development Goals. These include Zero Hunger, Clean Water and Sanitation, Affordable and Clean Energy, Sustainable Cities and Communities, Responsible Consumption and Production, Climate Action, Life Below Water, and Life on Land. Pick one of these eight and summarize the goal and its current and future impact on you, your family, community, and the world. (b) Identify how the planetary life-support systems (soil, climate, freshwater, atmospheric, nutrient, oceanic, ecosystems, and species) support life on Earth and interact with one another. Share what happens to the planet's sustainability when these systems are disrupted by natural events or human activity. (c) Identify how product life cycles (the cycle of design, sourcing, production, use, and disposal or reuse) influence current and future sustainability. Choose one common product to demonstrate how the full product life cycle would apply. (d) Learn how the world's population affects the sustainability of Earth. Discuss three human activities that may contribute to putting Earth at risk, now and in the future. (e) Explain the term species (plant or animal) decline. Share the human activities that contribute to species decline, what can be done to help reverse the decline, and its impact on a sustainable environment. (f) Find a world map that shows the pattern of temperature change for a period of at least 100 years. Identify three factors that scientists believe affect the global weather and temperature. Discuss how climate change impacts sustainability of food, water, or other resources.

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) On a campout or other outdoor Scouting activity that you attend, make notes on the sustainability practices you and your fellow Scouts practice. Step 3 (On a campout or other outdoor): Work with your family to adopt sustainable practices (p. 23).
Step 4 (On a campout or other outdoor): Although notrequired, you can meet with your family and talk about how conservation and stewardship relate to sustainability (p. 23).

pamphlet_excerpts: Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat: Review with your counselor how Scouting: Spinal injuries can occur from diving into shallow orobstructed water (p. 25).
Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat Principle 2: Review with your counselor how Scouting Principle 2: Rescuers must be very careful when a spinalinjury is suspected (p. 25).
Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat Principle 3: Review with your counselor how Scouting Principle 3: Spinal injuries can be fatal or can cause paralysis (p. 25).
Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat Principle 4: Review with your counselor how Scouting Principle 4: If the victim is not handled properly, additional serious injury could result (p. 25).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 1 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): Moving a victim is an extremely delicatetask best left to trained emergency personnel, but if no one elseis present you may need to act (p. 25).

Step 2 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 2 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): In a swimming accident, youmay have to move the victim to prevent drowning or to performrescue breathing (p. 25).

Step 3 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 3 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): When tending to a suspected spinal injury victim, move the victim's head, neck, and back as little as possible (p. 25).
Step 4 (Safe Swim Defense and Safety Afloat): Step 4 (Review with your counselor how Scouting): Thetechnique used to limit this movement is called in-line stabilization (p. 25).

Swimming Strokes Principle 2: If your breaststroke is a vigorous, bobbing stroke as usedin competition, it is not satisfactory for this requirement (p. 41).
Swimming Strokes Principle 3: Doing the backstroke using a frog kick rather than a whip kick also is unacceptable for this requirement (p. 41).
Swimming Strokes Principle 4: You also are required to swim the specified strokes in a "strong manner." This means no rest stops and no gasping, panting finishes (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Swimming Strokes): The stroke sequence begins with the morestrenuous strokes and moves through to the more restfulstrokes, with the last stroke (p. 41).
Step 2 (Swimming Strokes): You shouldfollow the stroke sequence as presented in the requirement (p. 41).
Step 3 (Swimming Strokes): Ifyou complete the swim "in a strong manner" in the specifiedsequence, then you should be rested and able to continue wellbeyond the 150-yard (p. 41).
Step 4 (Swimming Strokes): On the following pages, you will find the required strokesillustrated and explained as you should swim them to completerequirement 3 (p. 41).

pamphlet_excerpts: Swim continuously for 150 yards: To earn the Swimming merit badge you must demonstrateyour swimming strength and stroke proficiency byswimming 150 yards using a combination of fivestrokes (p. 41).
Swim continuously for 150 yards Principle 2: If your breaststroke is a vigorous, bobbing stroke as usedin competition, it is not satisfactory for this requirement (p. 41).
Swim continuously for 150 yards Principle 3: Doing the backstroke using a frog kick rather than a whip kick also is unacceptable for this requirement (p. 41).
Swim continuously for 150 yards Principle 4: You also are required to swim the specified strokes in a "strong manner." This means no rest stops and no gasping, panting finishes (p. 41).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Swim continuously for 150 yards): The stroke sequence begins with the morestrenuous strokes and moves through to the more restfulstrokes, with the last stroke (p. 41).
Step 2 (Swim continuously for 150 yards): You shouldfollow the stroke sequence as presented in the requirement (p. 41).
Step 3 (Swim continuously for 150 yards): Ifyou complete the swim "in a strong manner" in the specifiedsequence, then you should be rested and able to continue wellbeyond the 150-yard (p. 41).
Step 4 (Swim continuously for 150 yards): On the following pages, you will find the required strokesillustrated and explained as you should swim them to completerequirement 3 (p. 41).

pamphlet_excerpts: Water rescue methods by reaching: Spinal injuries can occur from diving into shallow orobstructed water (p. 22).
Water rescue methods by reaching Principle 2: Rescuers must be very careful when a spinalinjury is suspected (p. 22).
Water rescue methods by reaching Principle 3: Spinal injuries can be fatal or can cause paralysis (p. 22).
Water rescue methods by reaching Principle 4: If the victim is not handled properly, additional serious injury could result (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Water rescue methods by reaching): Moving a victim is an extremely delicatetask best left to trained emergency personnel, but if no one elseis present you may need to act (p. 22).
Step 2 (Water rescue methods by reaching): In a swimming accident, youmay have to move the victim to prevent drowning or to performrescue breathing (p. 22).
Step 3 (Water rescue methods by reaching): When tending to a suspected spinal injury victim, move the victim's head, neck, and back as little as possible (p. 22).
Step 4 (Water rescue methods by reaching): Thetechnique used to limit this movement is called in-line stabilization (p. 22).

Step 3 (In Water Over Your Head): A tuck surface dive is another option you can use to fulfillrequirement (p. 56).
Step 4 (In Water Over Your Head): Instead of lifting your legs as you would for apike surface dive, pull your knees toward your chest and pushthem upward as you point your head (p. 56).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Surface Dives): Never attempt to plunge headfirst below waves at a beach (p. 15).
Step 2 (Surface Dives): Diving is permitted in clear water at least 7 feet deep from a dock, pier, or platform that is no more than 18 inches above the water surface (p. 15).
Step 3 (Surface Dives): However, if your state, city, or local community requires a water depthgreater than 7 feet, it is important to abide by that mandate (p. 15).
Step 4 (Surface Dives): Remember that it is theweight of your legs aboveyou that pushes you downinto the water (p. 15).

pamphlet_excerpts: Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic: Regular exercise may be the single most important thing aperson can do to live a long and healthy life (p. 62).

Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic Principle 2: Studies ofpeople who live to great ages, into their 90s andbeyond, indicate that these people have at least onething in common: regular, consistent (p. 62).
Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic Principle 3: While exercise has a wide variety of benefits, the mostremarkable are the prevention of heart disease and the strengthening of bones (p. 62).
Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic Principle 4: The relationship between exercise and heart diseasehas been investigated extensively (p. 62).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic): The results arealways the same: The physically active have less heartdisease (p. 62).
Step 2 (Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic): The impact of exercise on heart disease is, in part, due to its beneficial effects on the other risk factors ofheart disease (p. 62).
Step 3 (Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic): People who exercise regularly are much less likely to beoverweight because exercise burns calories (p. 62).
Step 4 (Health Benefits of Regular Aerobic): In fact, the combination of exercise and losingweight often allows people with hypertension (high blood pressure) to control it without taking (p. 62).

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Visit a textile plant, textile products manufacturer, or textile school or college. Report on what you saw and learned. (b) Weave a belt, headband, placemat, or wall hanging using a simple loom that you have made yourself. (c) With a magnifying glass, examine a woven fabric, a nonwoven fabric, and a knitted fabric. Sketch what you see. Explain how the three constructions are different. (d) Make a piece of felt. (e) Make two natural dyes and use them to dye a garment or a piece of fabric. (f) Waterproof a fabric. (g) Demonstrate how to identify fibers, using microscope identification or the breaking test.

requirements.lead_text: Discuss with your counselor the safety precautions that should be practiced when working in a theater to protect the cast and crew. Then do THREE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Discuss with your counselor the safety precautions that should be practiced when working in a theater to protect the cast and crew. Then do THREE of the following: (a) Act a major part in a full-length play; or act a part in three one-act plays. (b) Direct a play. Cast, rehearse, and stage it. The play must be at least 10 minutes long. (c) Design the set for a play or a theatrical production. Make a model of it. (d) Design the costumes for five characters in a theatrical production set in a historical time. (e) Show skill in hair and makeup design. Make up yourself or a friend as a historical figure, a clown, an extraterrestrial, or a monster as directed. (f) With your counselor's approval, help with the building and painting of the scenery for a theatrical production. (g) With your counselor's approval, design the lighting for a play; or help install, focus, color, program, and operate the lighting for a theatrical production. (h) With your counselor's approval, help install, focus, equalize, program, and operate the sound for a theatrical production. (i) Serve as the stage manager for a theatrical production. Document all cues and stage setups in your calling script. (j) Serve as musical director for a musical theater production.

requirements.lead_text: Preventing Impaired Driving. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Preventing Impaired Driving. Do the following: (a) Explain why a distracted driver must not operate a motor vehicle. List five common distractions, explain how driver distractions contribute to traffic accidents, and tell how drivers can minimize distractions. (b) Explain why a driver impaired by alcohol, drugs, or other substances must not operate a motor vehicle. Describe how alcohol, cold medications, and prescription and illegal drugs affect driving abilities. For the state where you live, find out what is the legal blood alcohol concentration and what are the consequences for driving while intoxicated or driving under the influence. Find out what the open-container law is in your state. (c) Explain why a fatigued driver must not operate a motor vehicle. Describe how drivers must plan to be alert for safely transporting families, friends, Scouts, and themselves. (d) Describe mistakes that new drivers make, how those mistakes increase their risk of collisions, how drivers can reduce this risk, and how driving behavior affects automobile insurance rates.

pamphlet_excerpts: Vehicle Safety: Safety belts are the most effective device for preventing seriousinjuries and reducing fatalities in motor vehicle crashes (p. 37).
Vehicle Safety Principle 2: Studieshave shown that people who wear seat belts reduce their risk of serious injury by 50 percent and reduce the risk of fatalinjury by 45 percent (p. 37).
Vehicle Safety Principle 3: Safety belts also keep passengers properlypositioned to fully benefit from the protection provided by airbags (p. 37).
Vehicle Safety Principle 4: Research has shown that the chances of being killed arefive times greater when the occupant is thrown from a vehicle (p. 37).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Vehicle Safety): Properly worn safety belts help prevent passengers from beingejected (p. 37).
Step 2 (Vehicle Safety): Crash victims who wear safety belts are more likely to be unhurt, alert, and able to escape quickly (p. 37).
Step 3 (Vehicle Safety): Always wear a safety belt and make sure that all other passengers areproperly restrained (p. 37).
Step 4 (Vehicle Safety): The NHTSA says that growing up safe is a four-step process (p. 37).

requirements.lead_text: Auto Maintenance and Safety Checkups. With adult supervision and using a vehicle that you have access to, do the following:
requirements.req_text: Auto Maintenance and Safety Checkups. With adult supervision and using a vehicle that you have access to, do the following: (a) Demonstrate that all driving lights and signaling lights are clear and operational. Show where the switches are for these lights. Explain how drivers use lights to drive safely and courteously and to communicate with other drivers. (b) Explain issues that might affect the driver's ability to see through the front, rear, and side windows. Demonstrate with a smear-and-clear test if the windshield wiper blades will clear the windshield completely or need to be replaced. Describe instances in good and bad weather when windshield wipers are important to safe driving. (c) Demonstrate how to find the vehicle's recommended tire pressures, how to check tire pressures, and how to check for adequate tire tread depth. Explain why proper tire pressure and tread depth are important to traction, stopping distances, tire wear, and fuel economy. (d) Check the vehicle for tools needed to change a flat tire or to use tire sealant to fix a puncture. Demonstrate you know how to change a flat tire and how to use tire sealant. (e) In a location away from traffic hazards, mark off the reaction distances and braking distances that a car will travel as it makes an emergency stop at 25, 55, and 70 miles per hour on level dry and level wet pavement. Discuss how these distances change for normal and impaired drivers, for day and night driving, and for weather conditions. Note: Use the graphics template in the Traffic Safety merit badge pamphlet or one approved by your counselor to set up this demonstration.

Traffic Safety and the Law Principle 2: Scoutsalways have backup plans in case of emergencies (p. 51).
Traffic Safety and the Law Principle 3: Safe driving meanssharing the road with other drivers and being aware of thosewho are using the road (p. 51).

Traffic Safety and the Law Principle 4: Safe driving also means sharing the road with everybody who uses it, including pedestrians, bicycles, motorcycles, trucks, buses, and stray or wild animals (p. 51).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Traffic Safety and the Law): Riding a bike in traffic with bigger, faster, heavier four-wheeledvehicles is often dangerous and scary (p. 51).
Step 2 (Traffic Safety and the Law): The number of bicycles and vehicles sharing the road continues to grow every year andso, too, do accidents involving (p. 51).
Step 3 (Traffic Safety and the Law): In traffic, bicycles are considered vehicles and traffic laws thatapply to cars also apply to bicyclists (p. 51).
Step 4 (Traffic Safety and the Law): Rules of the road to helpensure bicycle safety include the following: • Always ride on the right side of the road, with traffic, just ascars (p. 51).

pamphlet_excerpts: Sharing the Road: Always wear a helmet when you are on a motorcycle, regardless of whether your state requires them (p. 55).
Sharing the Road Principle 2: Ahelmet will help protect you from serious, oftenfatal, head injuries (p. 55).
Sharing the Road Principle 3: On a motorcycle, a person does not have theprotection that a car's metal body structure affords, so amotorcyclist is much more vulnerable to injury (p. 55).
Sharing the Road Principle 4: For this reason, motorcyclists must drive extremely defensively (p. 55).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Sharing the Road): These safety guidelines also apply to street-legal scooters and mopeds (p. 55).
Step 2 (Sharing the Road): Vehicles that are not street legal, such as go-carts and all-terrainvehicles (ATVs), should not be used for transportation on any publicroad (p. 55).
Step 3 (Sharing the Road): Pedestrian safety is a serious issue because people whoare walking across a roadway lose in any accident with avehicle (p. 55).
Step 4 (Sharing the Road): Each year, nearly 5,000 pedestrians die in trafficcrashes (p. 55).

requirements.lead_text: Careers. Explore careers related to traffic safety. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. Your research methods may include, with your parent or guardian's permission, an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career.

pamphlet_excerpts: Major truck lines serving your town: On the highway, there are tractor-trailers for general cargo, trucks that hauldirt, trucks that deliver new cars to a showroom, and trucks that carry bulk (p. 10).
Major truck lines serving your town Principle 2: In your neighborhood, you may haveseen special trucks that pick up trash or recycling materials (p. 10).
Major truck lines serving your town Principle 3: Refrigerated trucks deliver frozen produce to retailers (p. 10).
Major truck lines serving your town Principle 4: Flatbedtrucks are used to move cargo that is not easily stowed, loadedinto, or unloaded from the more common tractor-trailer (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Major truck lines serving your town): Before meeting with your counselor, think of the differenttypes of trucks you have seen and what they transport (p. 10).
Step 2 (Major truck lines serving your town): The next couple of pages show several of the more common truckson the road (p. 10).
Step 3 (Major truck lines serving your town): There are a couple of ways you can find out which major truck lines serve your town (p. 10).
Step 4 (Major truck lines serving your town): Look in the yellowpages of your local telephone directory or, if you have a computer, search on the internet (with your parentor guardian's) (p. 10).

Truck Transportation Careers and Pathways Principle 2: Visit a truck terminal and complete Principle 2: As the trucking industry grew, it became so important to theeconomy of the United States that the federal governmentstepped in to set some rules (p. 18).

Truck Transportation Careers and Pathways Principle 3: Visit a truck terminal and complete Principle 3: Through the Motor Carrier Act of 1935, the government regulated where a trucking company, orcarrier, could operate and what it could charge (p. 18).

Truck Transportation Careers and Pathways Principle 4: Visit a truck terminal and complete Principle 4: An agency known as the Interstate Commerce Commission enforced these rules, which were very helpful at the time theywere introduced (p. 18).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Truck Transportation Careers and Pathways): Step 1 (Visit a truck terminal and complete): By the 1970s, these regulations were out-of-date and anobstacle to competition in the trucking industry (p. 18).

Step 2 (Truck Transportation Careers and Pathways): Step 2 (Visit a truck terminal and complete): The government recognized the situation and, starting with the Motor Carrier Act of 1980, the trucking industry became largelyderegulated (made) (p. 18).
Step 3 (Truck Transportation Careers and Pathways): Step 3 (Visit a truck terminal and complete): Further controls were liftedthrough the 1990s, and by 1995 the ICC was eliminated (p. 18).

Step 4 (Truck Transportation Careers and Pathways): Step 4 (Visit a truck terminal and complete): Today, the trucking industry is monitored by several government agencies that are primarily concerned with truck registration, driver licensing (p. 18).

pamphlet_excerpts: Roles A Veterinarian Plays: Aquaculture medicine uses the principles of veterinarymedicine to maintain healthycolonies of fish and other aquaticanimals (p. 22).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 2: This field of veterinarymedicine is distinct from otherareas of aquatic science, such as marine biology (p. 22).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 3: As the worldpopulation grows, aquaculture will help provide an adequatefood supply, and the work ofaquaculture veterinarians will be critical (p. 22).
Roles A Veterinarian Plays Principle 4: Students interested in aquaculture medicine must earn a doctorate in veterinary medicine (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Postgraduate training inaquaculture medicine is offered at some schools of veterinarymedicine (p. 22).
Step 2 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Many opportunities, especially in the coming years, await individuals trained in aquaculture medicine (p. 22).
Step 3 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): You might not hear much about public health veterinariansbecause most of them work for local, state, and federal agencies (p. 22).
Step 4 (Roles A Veterinarian Plays): Veterinarians who work in public health are the silent sentinelsprotecting America's public health and our quality of life (p. 22).

pamphlet_excerpts: Role A Veterinarian Plays: The Human-Animal Bond and the Veterinarian If you have a pet, you know how special that pet (p. 41).
Role A Veterinarian Plays Principle 2: Ask yourself why you feel the way you do about your pet (p. 41).
Role A Veterinarian Plays Principle 3: Theanswers from your deepest feelings reflect your experience with the human-animal bond (p. 41).

Step 2 (Role A Veterinarian Plays): Veterinarians can do this by being compassionate advisers foran animal's health-care needs throughout the animal's lifetime (p. 41).
Step 3 (Role A Veterinarian Plays): This includes providing quality medical care and giving advice to people about animal care, preventive medical care, and howto choose (p. 41).
Step 4 (Role A Veterinarian Plays): Hieroglyphics on the Egyptian pyramids illustrate thehuman-animal bond, and Roman legends tell about it in storiessuch as "Romulus and Remus (p. 41).

(c) Review the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy. Tell how it applies to water sports.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: A body temperature of 105 degrees or greater is a life-threatening medicalcondition and requires immediate medical treatment by health-care (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Heatstroke is a life-threatening condition; call for medical assistanceimmediately (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: While waiting for medical personnel to arrive, work to lower the victim's temperature (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Move the person to an air-conditioned or shadyarea (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Loosen tight clothing and further cool the victim by fanning and applying wet towels (p. 28).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If possible, immerse or spray the person with cold water (p. 28).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Ifyou have ice packs, wrap them in a thin barrier (such as a thin towel) and place them under the armpits and against the neck and groin (p. 28).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If the personis able to drink, give small amounts of cool water (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Showing reasonable control: To keep the board from wobbling, putslightly moreweight on your front foot than onyour back foot as the boat begins Alternate Method for Deepwater (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 2: Youmay prefer to start out with the wakeboard partially rotated uptoward the front foot (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 3: Begin with the wakeboard out in front ofyou and parallel to the water's surface (p. 59).
Showing reasonable control Principle 4: Keep your knees bent and hold the rope handle with your arms straight (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Showing reasonable control): When you are in position and ready, shout out "Hit it!" to letthe driver know to accelerate (p. 59).
Step 2 (Showing reasonable control): As soon as the boat starts to pull, twist at the hips to turn the front of the board up and toward the boat (p. 59).
Step 3 (Showing reasonable control): Keeping your knees bent, transfer more weight to your back foot as the boatpulls (p. 59).
Step 4 (Showing reasonable control): Alternate starting position to pull you out of the water (p. 59).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a troop trek planning session, a Scout says 'weather' and 'climate' mean the exact same thing when packing gear for High Adventure. How does the Weather Merit Badge Pamphlet distinguish weather from climate?
quiz_item.question: During a troop trek planning session, a Scout says 'weather' and 'climate' mean the exact same thing when packing gear for High Adventure. How does the Weather Merit Badge Pamphlet distinguish weather from climate?
options: A. Weather describes the day-to-day state of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, while climate is the long-term average of weather patterns over 30 or more years.
B. Weather only measures rainfall and snow, whereas climate only measures wind speed and barometric pressure.
C. Climate changes every hour with passing fronts, while weather remains constant across an entire continent.
D. Weather only affects sailors and aviators, while climate only affects farmers and outdoor construction crews.
choices: A. Weather describes the day-to-day state of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, while climate is the long-term average of weather patterns over 30 or more years.
B. Weather only measures rainfall and snow, whereas climate only measures wind speed and barometric pressure.
C. Climate changes every hour with passing fronts, while weather remains constant across an entire continent.
D. Weather only affects sailors and aviators, while climate only affects farmers and outdoor construction crews.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Weather describes the day-to-day state of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, while climate is the long-term average of weather patterns over 30 or more years.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Meteorology studies day-to-day atmospheric conditions (weather), while climate measures long-term regional averages over decades (Official Scouting America Weather Merit Badge Pamphlet, p. 10).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Your patrol is camping when the NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts a 'Tornado Warning' for your county, versus a 'Tornado Watch' issued two hours earlier. What is the critical difference and required action?
quiz_item.question: Your patrol is camping when the NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts a 'Tornado Warning' for your county, versus a 'Tornado Watch' issued two hours earlier. What is the critical difference and required action?
options: A. A Watch means a tornado has been spotted on the ground; a Warning means conditions might become favorable tomorrow.

B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.
D. Wait until you see hail larger than golf balls before checking your family or troop emergency shelter plan.
choices: A. A Watch means a tornado has been spotted on the ground; a Warning means conditions might become favorable tomorrow.

B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.
D. Wait until you see hail larger than golf balls before checking your family or troop emergency shelter plan.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under NWS and BSA Weather Pamphlet standards, a Watch means 'be prepared' (conditions are favorable), whereas a Warning means 'take action immediately' because life-threatening weather is occurring or imminent (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: At least two sources of weather: The first weather satellite, known as TIROS-1, waslaunched in the spring of 1960 (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 2: It was highly successfulat giving meteorologists their first overall view of entirestorm systems (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 3: Since then, satellites have become muchmore sophisticated, allowing a nearly continuous watchover the entire Earth (p. 33).
At least two sources of weather Principle 4: NOAA has two satellite systems: polar-orbiting satellites and geostationary satellites (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (At least two sources of weather): The satellite systems are named Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES) and Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (p. 33).
Step 2 (At least two sources of weather): The polar-orbiting satellites circle Earth, passingover or near the poles at a height of approximately 520 miles (p. 33).
Step 3 (At least two sources of weather): Theytravel around the globe several times each day (p. 33).
Step 4 (At least two sources of weather): The polar-orbitingsatellites are placed in sun-synchronous orbits, which means theypass over the same spot at the same time each day (p. 33).

B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
C. A high-pressure ridge where sinking air creates heavy blizzards and stationary fog.
D. A stationary pressure trough where wind stops completely and humidity drops to zero.
choices: A. A warm front that brings several days of calm, cloudless skies and rising barometric pressure.

B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
quiz_item.question: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
options: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
choices: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds suspend and cycle freezing droplets into layered hailstones while collisions between ice crystals and soft hail (graupel) build high-voltage charge separation that arcs as lightning (p. 34).

quiz_item.question: When tracing the hydrologic (water) cycle diagram for Requirement 7, how do evaporation, transpiration, condensation, and precipitation work together to move water between the ocean, atmosphere, and land?
options: A. Solar energy evaporates liquid water from oceans and lakes (plus plant transpiration) into invisible water vapor, which rises, cools, and condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei before falling as precipitation and returning via surface runoff and groundwater infiltration.
B. Condensation turns liquid river water directly into underground aquifers without entering the atmosphere.
C. Precipitation moves water upward from the soil into clouds, while evaporation pulls rain down to Earth.
D. The water cycle creates brand-new water molecules each summer and destroys them each winter.
choices: A. Solar energy evaporates liquid water from oceans and lakes (plus plant transpiration) into invisible water vapor, which rises, cools, and condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei before falling as precipitation and returning via surface runoff and groundwater infiltration.
B. Condensation turns liquid river water directly into underground aquifers without entering the atmosphere.
C. Precipitation moves water upward from the soil into clouds, while evaporation pulls rain down to Earth.
D. The water cycle creates brand-new water molecules each summer and destroys them each winter.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Solar energy evaporates liquid water from oceans and lakes (plus plant transpiration) into invisible water vapor, which rises, cools, and condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei before falling as precipitation and returning via surface runoff and groundwater infiltration.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Solar heating drives evaporation and plant transpiration; rising moist air cools to its dew point (condensation) to form clouds, which release precipitation that replenishes rivers, groundwater, and oceans (p. 42).

quiz_item.question: For Requirement 8, how does a densely paved city ('urban heat island') alter local weather compared to surrounding rural forests, and how do sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions affect precipitation?
options: A. Dark asphalt and concrete absorb and re-radiate solar heat with less vegetation cooling—raising urban temperatures by 2°F to 10°F and boosting downwind convective showers—while SO2 and NOx react with atmospheric moisture to form acid rain.
B. Concrete buildings reflect 100% of sunlight and make cities 15°F colder than surrounding forests in summer.
C. Acid rain is caused purely by natural ocean salt spray and has no connection to fossil-fuel combustion.
D. Urban heat islands eliminate all cloud formation and stop the greenhouse effect.
choices: A. Dark asphalt and concrete absorb and re-radiate solar heat with less vegetation cooling—raising urban temperatures by 2°F to 10°F and boosting downwind convective showers—while SO2 and NOx react with atmospheric moisture to form acid rain.
B. Concrete buildings reflect 100% of sunlight and make cities 15°F colder than surrounding forests in summer.
C. Acid rain is caused purely by natural ocean salt spray and has no connection to fossil-fuel combustion.
D. Urban heat islands eliminate all cloud formation and stop the greenhouse effect.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Dark asphalt and concrete absorb and re-radiate solar heat with less vegetation cooling—raising urban temperatures by 2°F to 10°F and boosting downwind convective showers—while SO2 and NOx react with atmospheric moisture to form acid rain.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Urban heat islands retain heat in masonry and asphalt while reducing evapotranspiration, and industrial/vehicle emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides form sulfuric and nitric acids in rainwater (p. 48).

pamphlet_excerpts: Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps: Recall that weather is the condition of the atmosphere over aparticular area for a short time (p. 66).
Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 2: Climate is the average of theweather over a region for a longer time, such as 30 years (p. 66).

Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 3: The word climate comes from the Greek word klima, meaning "angle." This name was used because the angle atwhich the sun strikes Earth largely determines (p. 66).
Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps Principle 4: At the equator, the sun is nearly straight overhead most of the year, so most of the equatorial region is hot (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): Poleward from the equator, theclimate gradually shifts from hot to cold (p. 66).
Step 2 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): This tilt (about 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular) remains the same allyear as seen from deep space (top) but changes relative to the sun (p. 66).
Step 3 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): At thesummer solstice (the first day of summer, bottom left), the North Pole tilts toward thesun, and the sun reaches its northernmost point (p. 66).
Step 4 (Tilt of Earth's Axis Helps): This is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere (p. 66).
