quiz_item.scenario_prompt: For Requirement 9, why does the Northern Hemisphere experience warm summer weather in June and cold winter weather in December, and why are polar regions colder than the equator?
quiz_item.question: For Requirement 9, why does the Northern Hemisphere experience warm summer weather in June and cold winter weather in December, and why are polar regions colder than the equator?
options: A. Earth's orbit brings the planet 50 million miles closer to the sun every June and farther away in December.

B. Earth's rotational axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane, causing sunlight to strike the equator nearly perpendicularly year-round while striking the poles at a low oblique angle and tilting the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun in June.
C. The sun burns hotter in July and cools down in January on a 12-month solar cycle.
D. Ocean currents reverse direction every six months when the moon crosses the equator.
choices: A. Earth's orbit brings the planet 50 million miles closer to the sun every June and farther away in December.

B. Earth's rotational axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane, causing sunlight to strike the equator nearly perpendicularly year-round while striking the poles at a low oblique angle and tilting the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun in June.
C. The sun burns hotter in July and cools down in January on a 12-month solar cycle.
D. Ocean currents reverse direction every six months when the moon crosses the equator.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Earth's rotational axis is tilted 23.5 degrees relative to its orbital plane, causing sunlight to strike the equator nearly perpendicularly year-round while striking the poles at a low oblique angle and tilting the Northern Hemisphere toward the sun in June.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt—not distance from the sun—governs solar incidence angle and day length across latitudes and seasons (p. 21).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Make one of the following instruments: wind vane, anemometer, rain gauge, or hygrometer. Keep a daily weather log for one week using information from this instrument as well as from other sources such as local radio and television stations, NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards, and internet sources (with your parent or guardian's permission). Record the following information at the same time every day: wind direction and speed, temperature, precipitation, and types of clouds. Be sure to make a note of any morning dew or frost. In the log, also list the weather forecasts from radio or television at the same time each day and show how the weather really turned out. (b) Visit a National Weather Service office or talk with a local radio or television weathercaster, private meteorologist, local agricultural extension service officer, or university meteorology instructor. Find out what type of weather is most dangerous or damaging to your community. Determine how severe weather and flood warnings reach the homes in your community.

pamphlet_excerpts: Measuring and Recording the Weather The most obvious way to study theweather is to observe actual events and keep a record of what you see (p. 61).
Measuring and Recording the Weather Principle 2: Daily observations of temperature, wind, pressure, clouds, andrainfall can help you understand how theatmosphere behaves (p. 61).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Measuring and Recording the Weather): You can obtain readings from your owninstruments, from local television or radio, and from internet sites devoted to meteorology (p. 61).

Step 3 (Measuring and Recording the Weather): Keep a 30-dayrecord based on local weather forecasts and your own observations (p. 61).
Step 4 (Measuring and Recording the Weather): Make and record observations at the same time each day (p. 61).

quiz_item.question: When building and siting a thermometer, barometer, or rain gauge for your Requirement 10 daily weather observation log, what instrument placement rule ensures accurate readings?
options: A. Mount the thermometer in direct afternoon sunlight against a dark brick wall and place the rain gauge directly beneath a leafy maple tree.

B. Mount the thermometer in a ventilated, shaded shelter away from heat-radiating surfaces, and place the rain gauge in an open, level area at least twice as far from trees or buildings as those obstacles are tall.
C. Keep the rain gauge and wind vane inside an enclosed garage so wind cannot tip them over.
D. Record your 30-day weather log from memory on the final day instead of taking daily measurements at a consistent time.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During your 5-minute outdoor weather safety talk to your troop (Requirement 11), you explain safety rules for lightning, flash floods, and tornadoes. Which protocol is accurate?
quiz_item.question: During your 5-minute outdoor weather safety talk to your troop (Requirement 11), you explain safety rules for lightning, flash floods, and tornadoes. Which protocol is accurate?
options: A. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule (shelter when thunder follows flash within 30 seconds; wait 30 minutes after last thunder), move immediately to higher ground during flash-flood warnings ('Turn Around, Don't Drown'), and shelter in an interior basement or lowest-floor room away from windows during a tornado.
B. Lightning cannot strike unless rain is actively falling directly overhead, so clear-air thunder more than 10 seconds away is harmless.
C. During a tornado warning in the backcountry, climb to the highest exposed ridge to watch the funnel cloud.
D. If caught in a flash flood while driving to camp, drive faster through flooded low-water crossings to beat rising water.
choices: A. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule (shelter when thunder follows flash within 30 seconds; wait 30 minutes after last thunder), move immediately to higher ground during flash-flood warnings ('Turn Around, Don't Drown'), and shelter in an interior basement or lowest-floor room away from windows during a tornado.
B. Lightning cannot strike unless rain is actively falling directly overhead, so clear-air thunder more than 10 seconds away is harmless.
C. During a tornado warning in the backcountry, climb to the highest exposed ridge to watch the funnel cloud.
D. If caught in a flash flood while driving to camp, drive faster through flooded low-water crossings to beat rising water.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Apply the 30/30 lightning rule (shelter when thunder follows flash within 30 seconds; wait 30 minutes after last thunder), move immediately to higher ground during flash-flood warnings ('Turn Around, Don't Drown'), and shelter in an interior basement or lowest-floor room away from windows during a tornado.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): A 30-second flash-to-bang interval means lightning is within 6 miles, six inches of fast-moving floodwater can knock an adult off their feet, and tornado safety requires sheltering on the lowest interior level or a low ditch away from trees/vehicles (p. 62).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During a troop trek planning session, a Scout says 'weather' and 'climate' mean the exact same thing when packing gear for High Adventure. How does the Weather Merit Badge Pamphlet distinguish weather from climate?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During a troop trek planning session, a Scout says 'weather' and 'climate' mean the exact same thing when packing gear for High Adventure. How does the Weather Merit Badge Pamphlet distinguish weather from climate?
options: A. Weather describes the day-to-day state of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, while climate is the long-term average of weather patterns over 30 or more years.
B. Weather only measures rainfall and snow, whereas climate only measures wind speed and barometric pressure.
C. Climate changes every hour with passing fronts, while weather remains constant across an entire continent.
D. Weather only affects sailors and aviators, while climate only affects farmers and outdoor construction crews.
choices: A. Weather describes the day-to-day state of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, while climate is the long-term average of weather patterns over 30 or more years.
B. Weather only measures rainfall and snow, whereas climate only measures wind speed and barometric pressure.
C. Climate changes every hour with passing fronts, while weather remains constant across an entire continent.
D. Weather only affects sailors and aviators, while climate only affects farmers and outdoor construction crews.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Weather describes the day-to-day state of the atmosphere at a specific time and place, while climate is the long-term average of weather patterns over 30 or more years.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Meteorology studies day-to-day atmospheric conditions (weather), while climate measures long-term regional averages over decades (Official Scouting America Weather Merit Badge Pamphlet, p. 10).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Your patrol is camping when the NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts a 'Tornado Warning' for your county, versus a 'Tornado Watch' issued two hours earlier. What is the critical difference and required action?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Your patrol is camping when the NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts a 'Tornado Warning' for your county, versus a 'Tornado Watch' issued two hours earlier. What is the critical difference and required action?
options: A. A Watch means a tornado has been spotted on the ground; a Warning means conditions might become favorable tomorrow.

B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.
D. Wait until you see hail larger than golf balls before checking your family or troop emergency shelter plan.
choices: A. A Watch means a tornado has been spotted on the ground; a Warning means conditions might become favorable tomorrow.

B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
C. Both Watch and Warning mean the storm has already passed your campsite and outdoor activities can resume.
D. Wait until you see hail larger than golf balls before checking your family or troop emergency shelter plan.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. A Watch means atmospheric conditions favor severe thunderstorm and tornado development (stay alert and prepared); a Warning means hazardous weather or a tornado is imminent or occurring on radar/ground (take immediate shelter now).
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Under NWS and BSA Weather Pamphlet standards, a Watch means 'be prepared' (conditions are favorable), whereas a Warning means 'take action immediately' because life-threatening weather is occurring or imminent (p. 14).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Looking at a surface weather map (Requirement 4), your patrol sees a blue line with triangles pointing southeast advancing toward a warm, humid air mass. What frontal system is approaching and what weather should the troop expect?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Looking at a surface weather map (Requirement 4), your patrol sees a blue line with triangles pointing southeast advancing toward a warm, humid air mass. What frontal system is approaching and what weather should the troop expect?
options: A. A warm front that brings several days of calm, cloudless skies and rising barometric pressure.

B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
C. A high-pressure ridge where sinking air creates heavy blizzards and stationary fog.
D. A stationary pressure trough where wind stops completely and humidity drops to zero.
choices: A. A warm front that brings several days of calm, cloudless skies and rising barometric pressure.

B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
C. A high-pressure ridge where sinking air creates heavy blizzards and stationary fog.
D. A stationary pressure trough where wind stops completely and humidity drops to zero.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. An advancing cold front where dense cold air wedges abruptly under warm moist air, forcing rapid vertical uplift, towering cumulonimbus clouds, gusty winds, and potential squall-line thunderstorms.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Cold fronts (blue triangles) push dense cold air beneath lighter warm air, causing steep vertical lifting, rapid cumulus/cumulonimbus buildup, and sudden showers or thunderstorms followed by cooler, drier air (p. 29).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During a summer afternoon thunderstorm (Requirement 5), your patrol observes jagged lightning bolts and half-inch hailstones. What physical mechanism inside a cumulonimbus cloud produces both hail and lightning?
options: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
choices: A. Gentle horizontal breezes blowing across flat stratus clouds below 2,000 feet.

B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
C. Direct solar radiation melting high-altitude cirrus clouds without any vertical air motion.
D. Ocean tides pulling warm air downward into a high-pressure center.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Powerful vertical updrafts and downdrafts cycling water droplets above and below the freezing level (accreting layered ice for hail) while colliding ice crystals and graupel separate electrical charges that discharge as lightning.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Strong updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds suspend and cycle freezing droplets into layered hailstones while collisions between ice crystals and soft hail (graupel) build high-voltage charge separation that arcs as lightning (p. 34).

requirements.req_text: After successfully completing requirements 1 through 5, use the equipment you prepared for the welding process in 5(b) to do the following: (a) Using a metal scribe or soapstone, sketch your initial onto a metal plate, and weld a bead on the plate following the pattern of your initial. (b) Cover a small plate (approximately 3" x 3" x 1/4") with weld beads side by side. (c) Tack two plates together in a square groove butt joint. (d) Weld the two plates together from 6(c) on both sides. (e) Tack two plates together in a T joint, have your counselor inspect it, then weld a T joint with fillet weld on both sides. (f) Tack two plates together in a lap joint, have your counselor inspect it, then weld a lap joint with fillet weld on both sides.

requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in whitewater activities, including branches and trees in water along a shore and stretching across the stream, rocks, hydraulics over ledges or low-head dams, strong wind, low water or air temperature, and thunder and lightning storms. Explain what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review with your counselor the prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that could occur while participating in whitewater activities: cold-water shock; hypothermia; head, neck, and back injuries; heat-related illnesses; sunburn; dehydration; blisters; bruises; cuts; sprains and strains; shoulder dislocation; and submersion injuries. (c) Discuss with your counselor the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy and the American Whitewater safety guidelines, including the use of helmet and life jackets.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Cool the victim immediately through immersion with cold packs in the groin area and armpits (p. 21).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Increase the body's fluid level by having a conscious victim sip water (p. 21).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: Sunburn is an inflammation of the skin caused by toomuch exposure to the sun (p. 21).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Shoulder dislocations are one of the most serious injuries associated with whitewater activities (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): A shoulder becomes dislocatedwhen the ball at the end of the upper arm bone slips out of thesocket at the shoulder (p. 21).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): This can happen when a paddlerattempts a maneuver such as a high brace that involves reaching overhead to gain leverage with the paddle (p. 21).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Any stroke ormaneuver in which the arm is fully extended and then rotatedrearward so the elbow is behind the shoulder puts the shoulderjoint (p. 21).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): You can reduce the likelihood of such an injury by making sure you keep a slight bend inyour elbows and by keeping your grip or upper hand (p. 21).

pamphlet_excerpts: Ferrying Upstream and Downstream: Upstream (forward) ferries and downstream (back) ferries moveyou sideways across the current (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 2: In an upstream ferry, you faceupstream and paddle forward with your bow at an angle to thecurrent (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 3: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 30).
Ferrying Upstream and Downstream Principle 4: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and backpaddle with your stern pointed upstream at anangle to the current (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): You move across the current in the direction your stern is facing (p. 30).
Step 2 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): To perform a successful upstream ferry, begin by turningyour boat until it faces upstream (p. 30).
Step 3 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): As you start paddling, adjust the ferry angle, the angle of the boat compared to theupstream, to about 10 degrees (p. 30).
Step 4 (Ferrying Upstream and Downstream): If you are moving out of aneddy into the current, enter the current as if you were doing a peel out by exiting the eddy at about a 45-degree angle (p. 30).

pamphlet_excerpts: Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites: Canoeists and kayakers use backstrokes to backpaddle, that is, to slow or reverse the forward motion of the boat (p. 56).
Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites Principle 2: As you paddle downstream, you will want to stop in an eddy torest or to scout a rapid below (p. 56).
Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites Principle 3: The maneuver to enter an eddywhile heading downstream is called an eddy turn (p. 56).
Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites Principle 4: Later you will learn how to exit an eddy using a peel (p. 56).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): When you havelearned how to move in and out of eddies with confidence andease, you will have passed a major whitewater skills milestone (p. 56).
Step 2 (Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): Entering an eddy while moving downstream in a boat can bechallenging, especially if the current is fast (p. 56).
Step 3 (Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): The three importantcomponents of an eddy turn are angle, speed, and edge or tilt (p. 56).
Step 4 (Whitewater Swimmer and Boating Prerequisites): Aim thebow so it crosses the eddy line as close as possible to the top of the eddy (p. 56).

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Option A, Tandem Canoeist. Do ALL of the following strokes and techniques on calm water: (1) Demonstrate the following strokes in the bow: cross forward, bow draw, cross bow draw, bow pry, and sculling draw. (2) Demonstrate the following strokes in the stern: stern draw, stern pry, sculling draw, and forward with stern pry. (3) Demonstrate a high brace, low brace, and righting pry. (b) Option B, Solo Canoeist. Do ALL of the following strokes and techniques on calm water: (1) Demonstrate the following strokes: cross forward, bow draw, cross bow draw, stern draw, pry, stern pry, sculling draw, and forward with stern pry. (2) Demonstrate a high brace, low brace, and righting pry. (c) Option C, Solo Kayaker. Do ALL of the following strokes and techniques on calm water: (1) Demonstrate the following strokes: bow draw, rudder, and sculling draw. (2) Demonstrate a high brace and low brace.

pamphlet_excerpts: Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker: In the peel out, note how both paddlers use their left knees to lean into and tilt the boat into the turn (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 2: An offside peel out incorporates all the same features of the onside peel out except that the turning strokes are different (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 3: For kayakers, the opposite paddle blade is used for the turningstroke (p. 50).
Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker Principle 4: After crossing the eddy line, solo canoeists can use avariety of turning strokes, including a forward sweep or crossbow draw (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): Tandem canoeists use a combination of a cross-bowdraw in the bow while the stern paddler does a low bracingreverse sweep or simply powers (p. 50).
Step 2 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): The paddle shaft should be vertical and move in a path 2 to 3 feet long next to the side of the boat (p. 50).
Step 3 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): Angle the blade at 45 degrees, as if you were spreading butter on a slice of bread, and move the paddle from side to side (p. 50).
Step 4 (Tandem Canoeist / Solo Canoeist / Solo Kayaker): At the end of each stroke, move the blade back in the opposite direction with the forwardedge (p. 50).

pamphlet_excerpts: Importance of Communication: Remember: River right andriver left alwaysrefer to the rightside or the left side of the river as if you were facingdownstream (p. 33).
Importance of Communication Principle 2: Teammates should discusstheir run on an ongoing basis and make adjustments to anyplan as needed (p. 33).
Importance of Communication Principle 3: Even asmall riffle can muffle words, and roaring rapids often drownout speech altogether (p. 33).
Importance of Communication Principle 4: For emergencies or times when talk isdifficult, river runners make use of whistles and paddle signals to communicate (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Importance of Communication): Review river signals before the beginning ofevery trip (p. 33).
Step 2 (Importance of Communication): To respond that you are OK to someone signalingyou, return the same signal (p. 33).
Step 3 (Importance of Communication): The time of year, fallen trees, andrainfall are justseveral elements that can transform a normally saferoute into adangerous one (p. 33).
Step 4 (Importance of Communication): Always scoutahead, plan your run, and identifyseveral optionsin case your run does not goas planned (p. 33).

Step 3 (Ability to Read A Class): Step 3 (Your ability to read a Class): Rapidsmay feature drops in which the water abruptly descends overrocks or a ledge (p. 26).
Step 4 (Ability to Read A Class): Step 4 (Your ability to read a Class): Current describes the continuous movement of water in a certain direction (p. 26).

requirements.req_text: Wearing a proper life jacket and being appropriately dressed for the weather and water conditions, perform the following skills in moving water in a properly equipped whitewater craft of your choice (tandem canoe, solo canoe, or solo kayak). pamphlet_excerpts: Wearing a proper life jacket: Upstream (forward) ferries and downstream (back) ferries moveyou sideways across the current (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 2: In an upstream ferry, you faceupstream and paddle forward with your bow at an angle to thecurrent (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 3: You move across the current in the direction your bowis pointing (p. 46).
Wearing a proper life jacket Principle 4: To perform a downstream ferry, you face downstream and backpaddle with your stern pointed upstream at anangle to the current (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wearing a proper life jacket): You move across the current in the direction your stern is facing (p. 46).
Step 2 (Wearing a proper life jacket): To perform a successful upstream ferry, begin by turningyour boat until it faces upstream (p. 46).
Step 3 (Wearing a proper life jacket): As you start paddling, adjust the ferry angle, the angle of the boat compared to theupstream, to about 10 degrees (p. 46).
Step 4 (Wearing a proper life jacket): If you are moving out of aneddy into the current, enter the current as if you were doing a peel out by exiting the eddy at about a 45-degree angle (p. 46).

pamphlet_excerpts: Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others As you will recall, a throw rope is a floating rope that is stored in a throw bag (p. 71).
Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 2: The rope will pay out neatly when the bagis tossed (p. 71).

Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 3: A throw bag or a neatly coiled throw rope shouldalways be secured in your craft so that it will be handy in a rescue situation but is not an entrapment (p. 71).
Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others Principle 4: Allow theremainder of the rope to stay in the bag (p. 71).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Be sure that the mouth of the bag is onlyhalfway open (p. 71).
Step 2 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Step 2, Get the attention of the person in the water by yelling, "Rope!" or giving a single blast of your whistle (p. 71).
Step 3 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Step 3, Grasp or step on the freeend of the rope and toss the bag at the swimmer (p. 71).
Step 4 (Using a Throw Rope to Rescue Others): Ifyou miss, quickly restuff the bagor make arm-length coils of rope and try again (p. 71).

requirements.lead_text: Participate in one or more whitewater trips using either a canoe or kayak on a Class I and/or Class II river. The trip(s) must involve at least six hours of paddling time. For each trip:
requirements.req_text: Participate in one or more whitewater trips using either a canoe or kayak on a Class I and/or Class II river. The trip(s) must involve at least six hours of paddling time. For each trip: (a) Help to prepare a written plan, specifying the route (put-ins and takeouts), schedule, equipment, safety precautions, and emergency procedures. (b) Determine local rules and obtain permission from landowners and land managers in advance. (c) Explain what steps have been taken to comply with Scouting America Safety Afloat and the American Whitewater safety guidelines. (d) Show how to protect personal and group equipment from water and how to load and secure the containers in boats to be used in the trip. Execute the plans with other paddlers. (e) Explain to your counselor how well your plans worked for each trip taken.

requirements.lead_text: Hazards and First Aid. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Hazards and First Aid. Do the following: (a) Show or explain first aid for, and prevention of, injuries and conditions that could occur in backcountry settings, including: (1) Dehydration (2) Heatstroke (3) Hypothermia (4) Shock (5) Blisters (6) Eye injuries (7) Ankle and knee sprains (8) Bug bites of chiggers, ticks, mosquitoes, and biting gnats (9) Bee stings (10) Bites of spiders (11) Sting of a scorpion (12) Bite of a wild mammal (13) Bite of a venomous snake (b) Explain how the Scout Basic Essentials address hazards of survival situations and are basic to a survival kit. (c) Explain how a trip plan could help prevent a wilderness survival situation.

pamphlet_excerpts: Wet Forests: While forests can offer an abundance of materials for makingshelters and building campfires, they can also be challenging, especially if the weather (p. 43).
Wet Forests Principle 2: The shade of a forest floor canfeel chilly, and dampness can make it seem even colder (p. 43).
Wet Forests Principle 3: As in other settings, do what you must to keep yourself and othersdry and warm, and be on guard against hypothermia (p. 43).
Wet Forests Principle 4: Dense forests can make signaling to rescuers difficult (p. 43).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Wet Forests): Youmight need to move a short distance to a meadow, streambank, or other open area visible from an aircraft (p. 43).
Step 2 (Wet Forests): Consider your options carefully, though, before changing locations (p. 43).
Step 3 (Wet Forests): Mark your route clearly in case you need to find your way back (p. 43).
Step 4 (Wet Forests): Rest in a high, shady spotduring the day, then complete necessary activities in the cool of the eveningor early morning (p. 43).

pamphlet_excerpts: Fire Building: The importance of a fire means that you should spendplenty of time getting it right (p. 31).
Fire Building Principle 2: As with most survival skills, practicing when you are not in an emergency situation is the best way to become good (p. 31).
Fire Building Principle 3: It is especially important topractice using fire-lighting methods other than matches andlighters, a magnifying lens, flint and steel, and fire (p. 31).
Fire Building Principle 4: A good way to think about a campfire is to consider it a tool to be used for specific and important uses (p. 31).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Fire Building): If you come to thebackcountry prepared not to need a fire, carrying a stove andfuel, for example, you can make an informed choice (p. 31).
Step 2 (Fire Building): Be mindful of any temporarybans against open flames in the area (p. 31).
Step 3 (Fire Building): In a survival situation, you might not have a stove or theclothing and gear to stay warm without a fire (p. 31).
Step 4 (Fire Building): Even so, taketime to build your fire in a manner that does not harm theenvironment (p. 31).

Step 3 (Signaling Lost Stranded Could): Step 3 (Signaling): Flags, banners, and contrasting colors can be part of your signaling efforts (p. 36).
Step 4 (Signaling Lost Stranded Could): Step 4 (Signaling): If you can see rescuers, wave a shirt over your head or attach it to a pole and wave it as a flag (p. 36).

pamphlet_excerpts: 6. Drink Water: Drink Water It bears repeating: Drink plenty of water (p. 40).
6. Drink Water Principle 2: You can survive for days without food, but inhot weather without water, only hours (p. 40).
6. Drink Water Principle 3: Dehydration happens in cold weather, too, even though you may not feel as thirsty (p. 40).
6. Drink Water Principle 4: The best rule is to drink plenty of water, enoughso that your urine is clear, whenever you arein the outdoors (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (6. Drink Water): Ideally you will be able to find waterwhere you are, from a lake, a stream, or melting snow, or by guiding rainwater down a tarp or tent fly (p. 40).
Step 2 (6. Drink Water): Watermay have collected in depressions in rocks, in the crotches of trees, or in seeps along cliffs (p. 40).
Step 3 (6. Drink Water): The surest means of making your water safe is byboiling (p. 40).
Step 4 (6. Drink Water): Use a pot or other metal container on a stove orover a fire and bring the water to a full boil (p. 40).

requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to this merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. With permission of your parent or guardian, your research methods may include an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from the Wilderness Survival merit badge to pursue a hobby or to serve as volunteer. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursue this.

requirements.lead_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Taking Action. Do ONE of the following: (a) Develop a fire readiness plan for a wildland area with which you are familiar. The plan should include a map showing available resources, water supplies, natural and manmade barriers, and access. The plan should discuss fuel loads, available fire apparatus, structure protection needs, values at risk, medical and evacuation considerations, and potential fire suppression tactics. (b) Visit with a state or federal forestry official or your local fire warden. Discuss the causes of and types of wildland fire that occur in your area. Discuss the prime fire season(s) in your area. Identify the agency responsible for wildland fire suppression in your area. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (c) Conduct a Firewise assessment of a home or a building in the wildland-urban interface, which could include a Scout camp building or facility. Identify potential risks and fire hazards. With your counselor's approval, complete a project to reduce the wildfire risk and increase the preparedness of the building. Write a brief report about what you did and learned from the assessment and project. (d) Meet with a Fire Prevention Specialist or a local fire official to learn about fire prevention efforts in your community. From what you learned, prepare a fire prevention message (skit, video, or billboard concept) and share with your counselor and troop (or other group approved by your counselor). (e) Meet with a meteorologist or someone familiar with fire weather and discuss the fire weather concerns and typical fire seasons that exist in your area. Discuss the conditions that lead to a Fire Weather Watch or a Red Flag Warning. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Prevention is the best way to avoid cuts, nicks, and other injuries (p. 15).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: However, as a Scout working with wood and knives, you should be prepared in the event of a cut or perhaps a splinter (p. 15).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: If you are injured, stay calm and let the adultin charge know what has happened (p. 15).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: Sometimes accidents happen even when all safetyprecautions are taken (p. 15).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): For a serious cut or gash, seekmedical help immediately (p. 15).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): For minor cuts and scrapes, follow these first aid steps: Step 1, Stop the bleeding by applying pressure with a clean, absorbent cloth; if cloth (p. 15).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Step 2, If the blood soaks through, apply a second bandage on top (p. 15).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Do not take off the first bandage because that will disturb the clotting that has already taken place (p. 15).

(b) Show that you know first aid for injuries that could occur while woodworking, including splinters, scratches, cuts, severe bleeding, and shock. pamphlet_excerpts: Timber is grown, harvested, and milled: Then workers called buckers lop off the limbs and slice thetrunks into shorter lengths (logs) that are easier to handle (p. 14).
Timber is grown, harvested, and milled Principle 2: The logs are trucked, floated, or carried on railroads to asawmill (p. 14).
Timber is grown, harvested, and milled Principle 3: At the mill, logs are debarked (their bark is removed), and saws cut them into boards (lumber) (p. 14).
Timber is grown, harvested, and milled Principle 4: Small logs are often cut into boards in a single pass through a set of saws (a gang saw) that makes many cuts at once (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): Largelogs may make several passes through one saw (a headsaw) thatslices off a board at a time until the whole log is cut into lumber (p. 14).
Step 2 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): The new lumber, called green lumber, is edged and trimmed tostraighten the sides and cut into boards of standard lengths (p. 14).
Step 3 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): Lumber is graded for quality, appearance, and strength (p. 14).
Step 4 (Timber is grown, harvested, and milled): Manufacturersuse them tomake flooring, pallets, andsimilar products (p. 14).
